articles.title: Stop the War's Lindsey German: Israel more isolated than ever
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Stop the War's Lindsey German: Israel more isolated than ever since 1948
There is no organisation in Britain more popular and opposed to US plans in the Middle East and its wars around the world than the Stop the War Coalition. Even before Israel, with Western support, began its war of extermination against Palestinians in Gaza following the 7 October 2023 Al-Aqsa Flood, the coalition considered Palestine its most important cause.
The New Arab met with Lindsey German, British activist and the coalition's coordinator, at its headquarters in far-north London.
The region is like a "powder keg", German warned, as conditions "can be kept under control for a period, but not forever".
In her view, the main driving factor are two wars: the Israeli war against the Palestinians with Western support and the Israeli-American war against Iran Moreover, Israel's war of extermination in Gaza pushed campaigns in defence of Palestine to the top of the coalition's priorities.
According to German, one of the coalition's achievements was "linking the Palestinian cause to the broader context of Western and Israeli policies in the Middle East" and what she describes as "American and British imperialism", whose plans Palestinians in Gaza disrupted.
German believes that "Trump has all kinds of plans for what he will do with Gaza and the Middle East", but they have not materialised, as he "tried to force Palestinians to go somewhere, but they do not want that".
Because of this resilience, German believes Palestinians "remain a huge challenge" to the ambitions of Trump and Israel.
Greater Israel threatens Arab regimes
German highlighted how Israeli officials at various levels speak of the "Greater Israel" project, which Trump supports and his ambassador to Tel Aviv, Mike Huckabee, promotes, and seeks to seize land from Arab countries neighbouring Palestine and beyond.
She opined that no decisive practical position has been issued by the governments of the Arab countries threatened by the project because they "have strategic relations with the United States and Britain through arms deals and economic interests", which "limits their ability to adopt independent positions towards Israel".
Nevertheless, she considered that the project and all of Trump's plans for Gaza "have led to a clash with the local regimes there, because they take part of this country or that country and force Palestinians to leave their land".
German argued that Israel's plans "pose a threat to the Arab regimes themselves", requiring "political and economic action" to curb Israel's expansion by "imposing an international boycott on it because of what it is committing" in terms of crimes.
Like others who reject Israel's crimes and the complicity of the West, including Britain, German frequently drew comparisons between Israel and Russia, noting that if another country had done what Israel has done, "we would have seen a broad international reaction, as happened with Russia after the invasion of Ukraine".
Why, then, do Arab countries not take such a position towards Israel? Lindsey German answered that "this position does not come from the rulers of the Middle East because many of them have very close relations with Donald Trump and with Britain, France and the old imperial powers, and this keeps them within this Western political framework of double standards."
She compared the issue of Palestine and the position of Arab rulers towards it with the problem of Britain's National Health Service, as she believed that "everyone (in the Arab countries) supports Palestine, but we do not see government action that can actually help the Palestinians, or we see very little action".
"When looking at Palestinians in Jordan, Lebanon or anywhere else, we find that they are treated extremely badly in the camps and are considered second-class citizens. This has been the situation for 50 years, and it seems to me that this is one of the reasons why people do not rise, whether because of the Palestinian cause or because of local issues related to living conditions and wages," she added.
German said that these living conditions are somewhat similar to what is happening in Britain, but the British have not remained silent.
In her view, the reason is that "opposing the government there is much harder than it is here", and this "largely explains why there have not been more movements (for Palestine or against domestic injustices) in the Middle East".
What has America done to us?
She stressed that the Israeli-American aggression against Iran as an additional factor reinforcing the failure of Israel and America. In her view, Iran "has proved that any resistance to the United States actually has an echo and receives a degree of support" in the Middle East.
Although she sees it as extremely difficult to predict accurately what will happen, she expects that the "result (of the war) will undoubtedly be great disruption and instability".
The Stop the War Coalition coordinator cites the case of the Abraham Accords (normalisation with Israel) as another example of the impact of Israel's genocidal war on Gaza and the war on Iran in thwarting US efforts to impose Israel's presence and close the chapter on the Palestinian cause.
However, she stressed that "there is no doubt that Iran has stopped this now" because "the efforts for the Abraham Accords have effectively died" and she "does not see any possibility of reviving them".
She reiterated that credit for this outcome goes to Iran's resistance to the aggressive war, which "made it impossible" for normalisation to continue.
"If you were in government in any of these countries, the UAE or anywhere else, I should think about what we are actually getting from the Americans," she said.
Nevertheless, she quickly added, the prominent anti-war campaigner continues and "what is happening is that America launched a war on Iran with Israel, so what was the consequence? America could not, despite its enormous air power superiority, indeed its superiority in all military aspects, defeat Iran".
Fascists and the far right
Israel's position in the world after its crimes in the Palestinian territories strengthens Iran's position and weakens the chances of reviving the project to get rid of the Palestinians, German argued.
It is a state, according to her, that "has now become more isolated than at any time since its founding; its popularity has declined, and its isolation has increased", even in the United States, which has historically been Israel's strongest supporter. "This support is declining significantly, even among Jews, particularly young people".
Israel's position is no better in Britain.
Previously, according to the picture German described, the country enjoyed particular sympathy among leftists who saw it as a somewhat left-wing socialist state because of the agricultural cooperative communities (kibbutzim) and as a homeland for Jews.
"I had Jewish friends who saw it as the place they wanted to be", and "most of us tended towards Israel when the 1967 war broke out, because we saw it as a small country, and because we realised the scale of the terrible suffering that Jews had gone through, we asked: Why are people attacking them again?" she recalled.
This situation has now changed, German added, because "apart from very hardline Zionists and far-right currents–including fascists and the far right in this country (Britain)–very few people really want to defend Israel".
Among the questions now being raised more insistently than ever, particularly after the Israeli-American aggression against Iran on the pretext of preventing it from acquiring a nuclear weapon, is, according to the coalition coordinator, "Why the focus on Iran? Israel already possesses nuclear weapons, while Iran is still far from possessing such weapons".
British government waging disinformation campaign
When Andy Burnham took over as head of the British government, he announced a commitment to his predecessor Keir Starmer's policy towards the illegal war, allowing the US military to use bases inside and outside Britain to launch attacks that it considers "defensive" against Iranian territory.
"This (use) is part of the war and not self-defence, and there is no need to think about whether it is right or wrong. The bases are being used to launch offensive operations" inside Iran, German stressed.
She said that the British government's promotion of the claim that the use of the bases is "defensive" is merely part of a "disinformation campaign promoting the idea that the British rejected Trump's request" to participate in the war.
But German further said that they "did not actually reject it. They allowed Trump to use RAF Fairford, which is the only base in Europe capable of accommodating and operating the large long-range B-1, B-2 and B-52 bombers".
She pointed out that "it is also clear that they (the British and Americans) cooperate in areas such as intelligence sharing and the like", which indicates that this reflects "some of what is happening behind the scenes".
An unexpected change
The Stop the War Coalition was established in 2001 to prevent the Iraq War and was the main driving force behind the million-strong demonstrations that filled the streets of London.
However, the coalition and many anti-war activists were unable to prevent the invasion, and Tony Blair, the former Labour prime minister, took Britain into it alongside America.
Even with that defeat, the coalition did not tire over the following 25 years of organising protests against wars, particularly Israel's war of extermination against the Palestinians and the Israeli-American aggression against Iran.
German believes that without the anti-war demonstrations, Britain and America would have repeated the Iraq experience.
She said the coalition "succeeded in changing the British public's view of wars", and therefore "Britain has no longer been able since the invasion of Iraq to repeat the model of direct military occupation". Later interventions in Libya and Syria "took different forms as a result of growing popular opposition".
As for Palestine, Lindsey German credited the popular pressure exerted by the coalition and others with "pushing the Labour Party to modify some of its positions towards Palestine". Here she is referring to Burnham's widely known video about Gaza and his admission that Labour was wrong in how it initially dealt with the war in the territory, as well as his indication that he intended to take a "balanced" position on what is happening in the region.
However, she acknowledged that this will not bring about a fundamental change in the rhetoric or policy pursued by the British government, as it "will continue to arm Israel and maintain diplomatic relations with it".
Despite the growing pressure, she expected that the "Burnham government will continue to avoid talking about genocide because it does not favour using this term".
She predicted "more attempts to acknowledge that Israel has committed some bad practices, without any real change in fundamental policy, given that Britain, ultimately, has very close relations with Israel".
Lindsey German: Real madness in Britain
The Stop the War Coalition is among the pro-Palestinian organisations most affected by the conduct of Britain's ruling establishment towards the ongoing protests against Israel's extermination campaign.
Its secretary-general, Alex Kenny, is awaiting a criminal trial on charges related to an alleged breach of the conditions for protesting in support of Palestine.
His deputy, Chris Nineham, is also awaiting a hearing of his appeal, alongside Ben Jamal, director of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, against a previous ruling that convicted him on the same charge.
This is "ridiculous in every sense of the word", according to German, who attributes the ruling establishment's position to "how frightened they are" by the impact of the protests.
She added another piece of evidence of this fear, saying, "the unprecedented massive level of arrests related to Palestine over the past 25 years".
"We now have political prisoners," German said, bitterly. The tone became more bitter when asked her about the Palestine Action movement and its members detained pending investigations or those who were tried for allegedly committing criminal acts but were sentenced by the judge, contrary to the law, under provisions set out in terrorism laws under which they had not been tried.
"I look at all those people who are being arrested. Many of them are retired from the technology sector, doctors and lawyers with prestigious standing, and people who have never committed a crime in their lives. They are all being treated as criminals simply for supporting the Palestinian cause," she remarked, describing all this as "madness in every sense of the word."
She warned that criminalising protests could push some activists to adopt more escalatory methods such as "direct action" to stop the extermination, and that history will not forget.
"Be sure that this will be considered in the years ahead, and people will say that it was a complete miscarriage of justice," she said.
The coalition's priority now remains to continue building a broad mass movement that includes trade unions and various sections of society, because the major demonstrations, in her assessment, were the main factor in raising public awareness of the Palestinian cause and pushing the Labour Party to review some of its positions.

articles.title: Ukrainians marched for a month to get Mykhailo Fedorov his job back as defense minister. Then he released a video calling for elections, and the crowds stopped coming.
articles.body:
Ukrainians marched for a month to get Mykhailo Fedorov his job back as defense minister. Then he released a video calling for elections, and the crowds stopped coming.
In mid-August, a video address by former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov caused an uproar in Ukraine. In it, Fedorov argued that Ukraine needs to hold elections despite the war and spoke about corruption inside Volodymyr Zelensky’s team. Many Ukrainians, including Fedorov’s own supporters, have called the statements a misstep and criticized him sharply. Zelensky has already said that elections during the war would be a “tsunami that would split Ukraine apart.”
A source close to the Ukrainian President’s Office acknowledged to Meduza that Fedorov’s ratings have risen far enough that in an election he could be a strong rival to Zelensky and Valery Zaluzhny, the former commander in chief of Ukraine’s Armed Forces. Meduza explains what is known about Fedorov’s political intentions and how his ambitions are playing out in Ukrainian society and within the government.
Why everyone is suddenly talking about Mykhailo Fedorov
On August 18, former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov posted a video to his YouTube channel that he called an “address to the people.” It went up the day before Yevhen Khmara was appointed to lead the defense ministry, and after more than a month of protests in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities by supporters demanding Fedorov’s reinstatement.
It was the first video on the channel, which Fedorov had created that same day.
In the address, the former defense minister took up a subject that is taboo in Ukraine: elections. Ukraine last voted in presidential and parliamentary elections in 2019; subsequent votes were canceled under the martial law imposed in 2022.
Fedorov said Russia had effectively acquired “the right to determine when Ukrainians will once again be able to choose their government”:
Democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia. We are fighting precisely because we want to remain a free European state. That is why we must find a legal, safe, and realistic mechanism that will allow Ukraine to resume a fully functioning democratic process even amid a prolonged war.
Fedorov did not specify whether he meant presidential or parliamentary elections.
What do Ukrainians think about holding elections during the war?
There is broad consensus in Ukrainian society that presidential elections should be postponed until the war ends. According to the results of a March 2026 poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology, only 12% of Ukrainians think elections should be held before the fighting stops.
Not even Volodymyr Zelensky’s political rivals raise the subject in public.
Valery Zaluzhny — the former commander in chief of Ukraine’s Armed Forces, now the country’s ambassador to the United Kingdom, and until recently described as the opposition’s unity candidate — has yet to say openly that he plans to run for president. He insists that talk of voting is premature until martial law is lifted.
Ukrainian election-law expert Olha Aivazovska, responding to Fedorov’s statement on Facebook, also came out against holding elections in a country at war without the necessary preparations for an electoral process:
I see hundreds of possible scenarios the Russians could use to delegitimize the electoral process or halt it altogether. It would be a complete collapse. I agree with Fedorov that the Russians shouldn’t be the ones deciding when we hold elections, because if they could, elections would have happened long ago. …
But I am firmly against holding elections to serve someone’s political interests, without regard for the real state of the infrastructure, an analysis of the risks, and proper preparation.
Fedorov also turned to corruption in government, which he said “takes on an entirely different meaning” in wartime. In peacetime, he said, stolen money means deteriorating roads, hospitals, and schools; in wartime it means the front goes short of drones, ammunition, and the military vehicles without which the wounded cannot be evacuated.
Fedorov also said Ukraine has a “systemic crisis of governance,” one in which the political system “too often lives by its own rules.” He did not name anyone he holds responsible for the corruption or the governance crisis, but as he spoke of the “old political system,” the video cut to portraits of former President’s Office head Andriy Yermak and David Arakhamia, who leads the Servant of the People faction in the Verkhovna Rada.
The day after the video went up, an unnamed source in Zelensky’s office told the British broadcaster BBC News: “It’s extremely strange to plan elections amid missile and drone attacks. This demonstrates a complete lack of realism.”
Why Fedorov chose to make his address now
Fedorov’s address was an attempt to “enter politics,” a source close to the President’s Office told Meduza: “In essence, he laid out a political program in three points: replacing Zelensky in order to fight the war more effectively, fighting corruption (which, as he sees it, requires removing Zelensky), and uniting”:
I think Misha sincerely wants to achieve these goals. He’s very goal-oriented. And he has a personal motive: his home village, Vasylivka in the Zaporizhzhia region, is under Russian occupation.
A Ukrainian politician called it “quite logical” that the address was released now: “Talks [with the President’s Office about returning as defense minister] didn’t work out, so he’s taken the fight into politics.” The problem, the source continued, was that the President’s Office had expected “something livelier” from Fedorov. “He could have announced his own political platform and called supporters out to a series of rallies,” the source in Kyiv said. “Instead he put out media content.”
Four days after the video appeared, Zelensky again addressed Fedorov’s dismissal in comments to Ukrainian journalists. The president repeated that a “very serious” conflict had arisen between Fedorov and Oleksandr Syrskyi, then the commander in chief, over the division of authority between the defense ministry and the military command. As a result, Zelensky said, the two men stopped speaking directly and discussed matters only at meetings in the president’s office.
The president stressed that after deciding to replace the defense ministry’s leadership, he had offered Fedorov different ways of working on the team four times, and that Fedorov had turned down every one. Fedorov had said he would return only as head of the ministry.
Bringing Fedorov back to his old post was impossible — the risks to the system would have been too high, a source close to the President’s Office told Meduza. “The ‘cardboard people’ won’t start liking us again, whether or not Fedorov got his job back,” the source said. Many Ukrainians associate government embezzlement with the president’s name, the source said, and the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) is still pursuing its investigations.
“Cardboard people” is the dismissive term the source close to the President’s Office uses for the protesters supporting Fedorov.
So why are they "cardboard"?
Rallies in support of Fedorov began on July 16, the day after his dismissal. They became known as “cardboard” protests because his supporters turned up with slogans written on pieces of cardboard.
“The defense minister is being removed in the middle of effective (finally!) reforms and replaced by someone under whom you can forget about any reforms,” war veteran Dmytro Koziatynskyi wrote on social media. In July 2025, Koziatynskyi had been one of the leaders of the “cardboard” protests in defense of the independence of NABU and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO). He urged fellow protesters to gather at Franko Square in central Kyiv.
“Bring your cardboard signs, and remember this is a peaceful protest,” he said.
Protesters carried signs reading “Bring back Fedorov,” “The problem isn’t Fedorov,” “Fedorov is our hope for reform,” and “Don’t break what works.”
Rallies took place daily in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, with the largest turnout in late July. The Kyiv Independent and the news agency Reuters both counted “thousands” of participants in the “march for dialogue and reforms in defense” in Kyiv on July 31.
How Ukrainians reacted to Fedorov’s address
Fedorov’s speech left many of his supporters and Ukrainian journalists baffled. As soon as the video went online, his press service sent the link to its private chat with reporters, according to a Meduza source who belongs to that chat. The journalists, the source said, asked the press service to explain which elections Fedorov meant and what his point was in the first place.
Members of the chat found the video absurd; one wrote that “there will be a lot of memes.” Sure enough, “within a couple of hours the entire Ukrainian segment of social media was flooded with memes,” the Meduza source said with a chuckle. Many of the source’s colleagues recalled, in private conversations, an old video featuring the line “The wording’s kind of moronic,” which has since become a catchphrase. It shows the Kharkiv politicians Hennadiy Kernes and Mykhailo Dobkin recording an address to the city’s residents in 2007. Journalists who know Fedorov compared him to Dobkin and dubbed the former defense minister “Misha No. 2.”
A Ukrainian political commentator told Meduza the video address was “cringe”:
He’s sitting there at a desk looking grim, a lamp shining, the whole thing staged. In real life, he’s game for anything and improvises everything. But here it’s 10 iffy, canned minutes set to gloomy music, plenty of words about being for everything good and against everything bad.
He says we need to look for tools to hold elections. Well, yes, we do. How long have we been saying that … We need to guarantee democracy — well, sure. But it’s all generalities that are really hard to tie to any actual goal. What was the point of it?
The commentator also faulted Fedorov for “criticizing the old system”: “Never mind that you spent seven years in that system yourself? You only noticed all this once you stopped being part of it?”
He was also puzzled that Fedorov, “beginning his political story” and effectively announcing his readiness to move into opposition to Zelensky, “didn’t name him or even show him in the video,” limiting himself to photographs of Yermak and Arakhamia. The commentator suspects the former defense minister wants to “have it both ways.”
The commentator said Fedorov used the video, in effect, to accuse Arakhamia of corruption and of defending his own financial interests: “When he spoke about corruption and the harm to the country, it was Arakhamia who appeared on screen.” Some outlets, including Ukrainska Pravda, have described the head of the pro-presidential faction in the Verkhovna Rada as the principal organizer of the scheme to reshuffle the cabinet, under which Fedorov was to “disappear from the government,” the commentator said.
Fedorov draws support from some Ukrainian journalists and human rights advocates, as well as from young people and a “middle class that wants to see justice done” — groups that are sharply opposed to corruption, a source close to the President’s Office told Meduza.
“These ‘cardboard people’ are unhappy with how tightly power is centralized in the Ukrainian president’s hands, and they believe parliamentary elections would produce a new Verkhovna Rada, in which the existing single-party majority [of the Servant of the People party] would give way to a coalition,” he said. Zelensky would then have to negotiate with coalition partners, and the political process would become more democratic again. That, the source said, is the protesters’ logic.
Fedorov has worked with the political strategists Dmytro Tsarenko and Viktor Berezenko since his time at Ukraine’s Ministry of Digital Transformation, the source said. Ahead of the 2019 elections, the pair oversaw several Servant of the People lawmakers, and from early 2021 until July 2022 they even ran Zelensky’s social media accounts.
The strategists themselves confirmed in December 2024 that they were working with Fedorov. “It looks like [now] they decided the message about elections would land well with his audience. The idea that elections need to happen appeals to them. Misha took it [as the basis for his address]. But they screwed up a little here — in the end Misha turned a lot of people against himself and effectively narrowed his circle of supporters,” the Ukrainian politician said.
The political commentator believes “Fedorov’s team hit the post” — that is, they fell short of their audience’s expectations. “How could this be? Fedorov has an enormous following of young, progressive, creative people. How could they put out this shit? And why did nobody stop him at any point?” he lamented:
Even many of the people who had supported Fedorov until now are disappointed in him and stunned. As in: we came out for you, we backed you, and this is the shit you produced. After all, most of Ukrainian society believes elections during wartime are unacceptable.
Koziatynskyi, one of the main organizers of the pro-Fedorov protests, responded to the former defense minister’s video on Facebook. He thanked “everyone who came out to the protests” for helping secure the removal of Oleksandr Syrskyi as commander in chief and his replacement with Mykhailo Drapatyi.
Koziatynskyi said the main reason for the rallies, as he saw it, was the absence of communication between Ukrainian society and the authorities. For him, he said, “these protests were about dialogue and reforms, not about specific individuals.” On the idea of holding elections he was blunt:
I can’t imagine how you would technically make it possible for thousands of service members now on the front line to vote and to run for office. I’m also very worried about divisions in society during an electoral process, and about how that could affect the course of the war. In any case, street protest is definitely not the place for campaign discourse.
For his part, Oleksiy Sorokin, a political commentator at The Kyiv Independent, believes Fedorov put his political ambitions above the interests of the state.
“Zelensky himself is destroying the public support he’s had since 2022, because of self-centered decisions, corruption scandals, personnel policy, and the concentration of power. Should he lose the next election? Absolutely. But that doesn’t mean elections should be held now,” Sorokin said.
An independent Ukrainian political commentator who spoke with Meduza suggests Fedorov’s statement was meant to “stir up” the protests in his support. It didn’t work: only 100–150 people came to the Verkhovna Rada building on August 19, he said. (On July 31, Reuters correspondents had counted “thousands” of demonstrators in Kyiv.)
“After the deputies voted [to appoint Yevhen Khmara on August 19], the protesters said they’d gather outside the President’s Office that evening. Even fewer people came,” he continued. “The protests are winding down, and I think Fedorov’s statement sped up that process.”
More lawmakers voted to confirm Khmara that day than protesters gathered outside the Rada, a source close to the President’s Office said snidely.
How Fedorov’s team tried to explain what he meant in his video
In the days that followed, Fedorov made several more statements clarifying his position.
On August 21, Ukraine’s Channel 24 aired a long interview with the former defense minister, in which he clarified that he had not called for elections to be held urgently. The address, he said, was about carefully preparing electoral legislation with “the best experts in Ukraine and the world” — people he says he is “already in close touch with.”
He also said he meant parliamentary, presidential, and local elections alike. “What the sequence will be is a question for discussion with various experts,” Fedorov said.
Asked whether he would run for president, the former defense minister said he would know himself once the country was ready to hold elections.
A source close to the President’s Office believes Fedorov’s team “quickly understood that they had chosen the wrong message to begin with, and clarified that they meant not a blitzkrieg [that is, an immediate election] but a long, systemic fight” with Zelensky’s team.
In the same interview, Fedorov said he plans to set up a venture fund that will draw Western money into Ukrainian startups — for example, in producing inexpensive ballistic missiles and in the “robotization of the front line.” He also intends to create a think tank that will “generate ideas” about how to win the war and offer them to the government. And he wants to take on “civic work connected with preparing the country for the return of democracy.”
Fedorov told journalists he would soon travel to the United States for several meetings aimed at attracting investment in Ukrainian military technology projects, though he did not say whom he planned to meet.
Asked by Channel 24 whether he planned to line up the American president’s support before the elections, Fedorov said no. He stressed that discussing such questions is “Ukraine’s homework.”
Fedorov has continued making statements that appear designed to give Ukrainians a sense of his political program. On August 25, asked by Reuters journalists about Ukraine’s prospects in the war, he said: “I think there’s now a turning point that will determine our future trajectory [in the war], but it looks as though we’re gradually, slowly losing.”
What Zelensky’s team risks because of Fedorov’s public activity
Fedorov will decide which elections to contest as the situation develops, the source close to the President’s Office suggested. In the source’s view, it is still premature to talk about elections in Ukraine at all. An independent Ukrainian journalist agrees: “We really don’t know when there will be elections, and Fedorov could still flame out as a politician 150 times over.”
The 35-year-old former defense minister represents a new generation of opposition figures in Ukrainian politics, the Meduza source said. Unlike Valery Zaluzhny — who criticizes the authorities but is still officially part of the president’s team — Fedorov opposes Zelensky openly. Now, a Ukrainian official is convinced, Fedorov “will keep Zelensky’s team on edge”:
Fedorov still has a chance to fix this failure [with the video address] somehow. It will all depend on what he does next: whether he backs up his words with actions and highlights his strengths, or just goes on shooting little videos.
The journalist also points to what Fedorov’s actions have accomplished so far. Until recently, the Meduza source said, publicly calling for elections during the war came across as thoroughly fringe in Ukraine: “Mykhailo, criticized as he is, has still taken a step toward normalizing the subject — and may have pushed the people working on changes to electoral legislation [for elections under martial law] to get moving.”
Since Fedorov’s dismissal, the President’s Office has been tracking his electoral ratings alongside those of Zelensky’s other opponents, just in case, a source close to the office told Meduza. In mid-July, before Fedorov left the defense ministry, the top three presidential contenders were Zelensky, Zaluzhny, and President’s Office head Kyrylo Budanov, the source said. By mid-August, Fedorov’s rating had climbed from 2–3% to 12–15%. That pushed him abruptly into the top three and displaced Budanov, according to data from a private poll the source cited.
Fedorov now alternates between second and third place and runs roughly even with Zaluzhny, the source said. Either of them could reach a runoff against Zelensky.
The source told Meduza he is not sure Zelenskyy will run. “The election is still a long way off,” he said. The president’s disapproval rating exceeds 50%, according to the latest data, a level driven by Ukrainians’ fatigue with the war and government corruption. Such numbers usually hurt a candidate’s chances in a runoff.

articles.title: Germany reportedly considers helping fund UK nukes
articles.body:
Germany is reportedly considering helping to fund Britain’s nuclear deterrent as Berlin examines closer integration with existing UK and French nuclear forces rather than developing an independent German arsenal.
Germany is reportedly considering financial support for Britain’s nuclear deterrent as part of discussions over how European states could rely more heavily on existing British and French nuclear capabilities, the Telegraph reports.
According to an exclusive report by The Telegraph, officials in Berlin are examining whether German funding could contribute towards the UK’s nuclear programme as part of a wider attempt to strengthen Europe’s nuclear deterrence and reduce dependence on the United States.
The newspaper reports that Germany’s preference is to integrate more closely with the nuclear forces already maintained by Britain and France rather than pursue its own atomic weapons programme, with one source saying Berlin has a strong interest in seeing Europe’s existing nuclear powers increase their capabilities.
A source quoted by The Telegraph said: “We have a very strong interest that the existing nuclear powers in Europe extend their capabilities.”
The reported discussions involve London, Berlin and Paris and are said to have gathered pace as European governments consider the implications of a reduced American military commitment to the continent. Germany is reportedly looking at several forms of support, ranging from financial contributions towards the British deterrent to conventional military assistance intended to protect the infrastructure that supports it.
Among the more concrete options reported by The Telegraph is the possible deployment of German-operated Patriot air defence systems to important British nuclear sites, including HMNB Clyde at Faslane in Scotland, where the Royal Navy’s ballistic missile submarine force is based.
A British defence source cited by the newspaper reportedly regarded that type of conventional contribution as more credible than a substantial German role in building Britain’s nuclear submarines, saying: “The ability to contribute to the defence of Faslane is more credible, likely and appropriate.”
German officials are nevertheless also reported to have considered whether the country’s industrial base could contribute to future British programmes involving submarines, missiles or uranium enrichment. The same report notes doubts on the British side over whether German industry has the specialist experience necessary to play a major role in the construction and maintenance of the UK’s nuclear-powered submarine fleet.
Britain is currently replacing its four Vanguard-class ballistic missile submarines with four Dreadnought-class boats, which will carry the Trident II D5 ballistic missile and maintain the UK’s Continuous At-Sea Deterrent. London is also developing the Astraea nuclear warhead alongside the American W93 programme.
The UK’s deterrent remains sovereign in terms of decisions over nuclear use, but important parts of the programme depend upon cooperation with the United States. Trident missiles are manufactured in America and supported through facilities at Kings Bay in Georgia, while British and American warhead development also remains closely connected.
That dependence is reportedly one of the issues under discussion in Berlin. A security source quoted in The Telegraph’s report said: “There is thinking and talking about how the existing nuclear capabilities [such as Trident] may play a bigger role for the defence of Europe, and of deeper cooperation among European countries.”
The discussions would not give Germany control over British nuclear weapons, nor does the reporting suggest that Berlin would participate in decisions over their use. The proposals instead concern Germany contributing financially, industrially or with conventional military forces to the wider infrastructure supporting Britain’s deterrent.
Germany is reportedly holding similar discussions with France, whose nuclear forces remain entirely under French national control and include both submarine-launched and air-launched weapons. Paris has already opened a broader debate with European partners over the possible role of French nuclear forces in continental deterrence.

articles.title: Iran says US sanctions will achieve nothing
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US will not achieve anything with sanctions, Iran says
Iran's president insisted on Wednesday that the United States would achieve nothing with its new sanctions campaign after Washington laid out plans to collapse the country's economy.
Almost six months into their war, the two sides are locked in a stalemate, with Iran keeping the key Strait of Hormuz shut and Washington persisting with a naval counter-blockade of Iran.
Under political pressure at home over the impacts of the conflict, US President Donald Trump has pivoted away from military action to economic levers, expanding sanctions and warning of consequences for countries that do not join.
But Iran - which has already weathered decades of sanctions - has remained defiant, with officials saying they have a two-year plan to counter the pressure.
"America will not achieve anything with economic pressure at this stage, just as it was unable to achieve anything in the war," Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Wednesday, according to the country's ISNA news agency.
"We will stand firm against economic pressures, as we have done so far and will continue to do."
Iranian army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia, meanwhile, told state television Wednesday that the military had restored its combat capabilities degraded during the war, with the reconstruction of all damaged weapons systems and the import of new equipment from abroad.
On Monday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had claimed the US had "dismantled Iran's military capabilities, destroyed nearly 100 percent of its military factories, and buried its nuclear programme".
Announcing the new economic measures, Bessent said expanded secondary sanctions would target Iran's digital assets and its technology, gold, aviation and shipping sectors.
'Not in a hurry'
The US and Israel launched the war against Iran in late February, vowing to end an alleged Iranian nuclear weapons programme and threatening to topple the regime in Tehran.
Iran -- which has long denied pursuing a nuclear bomb -- responded with barrages of missiles and drones targeting US allies in the Gulf and closing the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping route for global supplies of oil and gas.
The waterway's closure has strained the world economy as shipments fail to reach major markets, pushing up the price of oil and placing pressure on Trump ahead of mid-term elections in November.
Trump had frequently claimed a deal was close, but has since backed away from diplomacy.
"I have no time schedule, none. I'm not in a hurry. I have no time schedule at all," Trump told news outlet Al Jazeera on Wednesday when asked how much time he was giving Iran for talks.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday dismissed any prospect of a deal.
"I tell you - an agreement cannot be reached," he said, calling Iran's leaders "savages".
'Total control'
In recent weeks, the conflict has come to revolve around the blockaded Strait of Hormuz. Iran says it will not reopen the vital waterway until the US meets its demands, and has frequently attacked vessels trying to cross.
Tehran has also indicated it intends to impose fees for use of the strait, which the US and others in the region fiercely oppose.
Trump insists the US navy has "total control" of the strait and has even called it US territory, but traffic there remains at a fraction of pre-war levels.
Oman, which sits on the other side of Hormuz from Iran, has been discussing with Tehran a temporary transit corridor to enable traffic to resume.
On Wednesday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards, the ideological arm of its military, said the talks with Oman included the two countries agreeing to share any revenues collected from management of the strait, accusing the US of "obstructing work" to finalise the deal.
Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi said on Tuesday that he hoped his country and Iran would "soon announce" the temporary corridor.
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi, in an interview with local media, said if the temporary route was agreed, Iran and Oman would have between 30 and 60 days to negotiate a permanent route to replace it.
He added that the Guards were involved in the talks and that the maps under discussion were drawn up by the armed forces.
(AFP)
