articles.title: Trump claims CIA director’s surprise visit to Russia is ‘semi-routine’ despite mounting speculation – live
articles.body:
Democratic states sue to block postal service from carrying out Trump's mail-in voting order
Two dozen states and the District of Columbia filed a fresh lawsuit on Wednesday to block Donald Trump’s executive order restricting mail voting in this year’s midterm elections.
The challenge comes days after the supreme court’s conservative majority lifted one injunction from a federal judge blocking parts of the president’s order.
In their new filing against the US Postal Service (USPS), the states point to concrete steps the administration has taken to carry out Trump’s directive – including a final USPS rule on ballot delivery posted Friday night.
The states said that the USPS policy is part of “a broader effort” by the Trump administration “to rewrite federal election law and usurp the authority of the states and Congress”.
And a reminder, that the constitution confers control over elections to states and Congress, not the executive.
On Monday, the supreme court did not rule on the legality of Trump’s order, but said that the states’ litigation was premature, effectively making room for further legal challenges.
A reminder that there is also a second nationwide injunction that still prevents the postal service from enforcing the order, though the justice department has argued that block should now be lifted in light of the supreme court’s ruling.
This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments:
Two dozen mainly Democratic‑led states filed a fresh lawsuit to block Donald Trump’s executive order restricting mail voting in this year’s midterm elections.
Lawyers for Lisa Cook wrote to the White House on Wednesday, rejecting a new attempt to force the Federal Reserve governor to resign for allegedly listing two properties as her primary residence on mortgage applications. The letter goes on to detail the numerous other individuals who have made the same mistake on mortgage forms, starting with Trump.
The chief spokesperson for the US Secret Service and two other communications staffers are under investigation for “potential misconduct” and have been suspended, according to the agency and media reports.
A geography professor alleges in a lawsuit filed this week in federal court in Manhattan that he was fired from his tenured position at the US Military Academy at West Point “because he taught that humans influenced climate change”.
The US army announced on Wednesday that it has awarded to $2.2bn to five contractors “to own, construct and operate nuclear microreactors on military installations” in five states.
West Point geography professor says he was fired for resisting order to stop teaching climate change to future army officers
A geography professor alleges in a lawsuit filed this week in federal court in Manhattan that he was fired from his tenured position at the US Military Academy at West Point “because he taught that humans influenced climate change” and then protested an order “that this not be mentioned in his classes” as unethical.
As first reported by Stars and Stripes, a US government-funded news outlet that cover the US military, the geographer, Adam Kalkstein, says in the suit that he was rated as an “outstanding” professor during his 17 years as a civilian employee teaching climatology to future army officers.
According to the complaint, Kalkstein says he was called into on 11 September 2025 by Joel Radunzel, a lieutenant colonel who directs the geography program at West Point.
Radunzel, the complaint says, “relayed a verbal order that professors could no longer teach about anthropogenic (human-caused) climate change and that professors must remove all mention of human causes of climate change from their courses.”
During the same meeting, Radunzel also issued “a clear threat” that if anyone in the department went to the media or politicians over the ban, “the entire department would likely be dissolved.”
“At the time, plaintiff was teaching two sections of Climatology in which he taught that humans were responsible for much of the current planetary warming trend and presented the scientific evidence, consequences, and military impacts,” the complaint explained. “Learning how humans affect the atmosphere was a fundamental component of his course which he had been teaching for many years, and the concept that humans can alter Earth’s climate is a plainly established scientific fact.”
Two months later, Kalkstein said he confronted the dean of West Point’s academic board over how hard it was to teach in line with the directive.
“I just got out of Climatology class and it’s a struggle” he recalled, “because we’re leaving our essential information. We’re only telling cadets part of the story. We’re lying to them, deceiving them. It would be like trying to teach the law without being able to even mention the Constitution. The guiding principle of any school should be to the truth ... I’m supposed to be an educator and a scientist upholding Army values, but sir, right now, I’m a liar and a fraud. What we’re doing here is wrong. It’s immoral. It’s likely illegal”.
The Dean responded angrily, according to the complaint.
Sailor who jumped from USS Abraham Lincoln charged with being absent without leave - report
A US sailor who jumped overboard from the USS Abraham Lincoln this month amid a protracted deployment at sea has been charged by the navy with harming himself to avoid duty and being absent without leave, according to his wife and charging documents reviewed by the broadcaster MS NOW.
The sailor and his wife are both 19 years old, MS NOW reports, without revealing their identities.
According to the sailor’s wife, although he jumped off the ship in a suicide attempt, he has now been charged with violating two articles of the Uniform Code of Military Justice.
The broadcaster reports:
The charging documents, which were reviewed by MS NOW, show that the sailor has been accused of violating Article 83 for “malingering,” which is defined as a service member “intentionally faking an illness or hurting themselves to avoid work, duty or service,” and Article 86 for “absence without leave,” which means a service member failed to be at their required place of duty without proper authority.
“I think they’re insane for doing this to people who need mental help,” the wife told MS NOW. “Instead of giving them help, this is just another huge stressor.”
Fed governor Lisa Cook's lawyers note that Trump and 'a third of his cabinet' had same mortgage status as her
Lawyers for Lisa Cook wrote to the White House on Wednesday, rejecting a new attempt to force the Federal Reserve governor to resign for allegedly listing two properties as her primary residence on mortgage applications.
“Governor Cook has never committed mortgage fraud or any intentional wrongdoing, and there is no legally cognizable cause for removing her from the Federal Reserve Board,” her lawyer, Abbe Lowell, wrote to in a letter to the White House Counsel, David Warrington.
Lowell cites the opinion of an expert in mortgage regulation and finance who argues that the Trump administration has failed to establish any intentional wrongdoing by Cook, “or that she benefited from the classification of either property as a ‘primary’ residence.”
The letter goes on to detail the numerous other individuals who have made the same mistake on mortgage forms, starting with Donald Trump.
The President should know firsthand that listing two properties as a ‘primary’ residence does not show intentional wrongdoing or demonstrate ‘unfit[ness] for office’. In 1993, President Trump reportedly acquired ‘primary’ residence mortgages for two different Florida homes just seven weeks apart. For each home, President Trump apparently signed a form attesting that he would occupy the property as his principal residence within 60 days and live there for at least a year. In reality, however, neither property was President Trump’s primary residence. He lived in New York and reportedly listed both Florida properties for rent.10 Surely the President does not believe himself ‘unfit for office’ because he signed these contradictory ‘primary’ mortgage documents.
Five current or former members of Trump’s cabinet have reportedly signed the same sort of mortgage application forms, Cook’s lawyer adds: Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary: Todd Blanche, the attorney general; Sean Duffy, the transport secretary and reality TV actor; Lee Zeldin, the EPA administrator; and Lori Chavez-DeRemer, the former labor secretary.
Lowell and his co-counsel, Norm Eisen, a former ethics adviser to the Obama administration, said in a statement:
“For the second time in a year, we have explained why there is no legal basis for President Trump to remove Governor Cook for cause. An inadvertent error is not fraud, as the President and a third of his cabinet should know because they reportedly did the same thing. These attacks on Governor Cook are not about real estate paperwork; they are an attempt by President Trump to force the Federal Reserve to bend to his will. Our response should put this matter to rest once and for all, but, if necessary and in keeping with the Supreme Court’s ruling, we are prepared to challenge any illegal attempt to remove Governor Cook.”
Cook, the first Black woman to serve on the central bank’s board, was appointed by then president Joe Biden in 2022 to a term that lasts until 2038.
Trump first tried to fire her last year, in a case that ended with the 5-4 US supreme court ruling, this summer, that the president does not have the authority to remove a Federal Reserve governor without cause.
Despite that loss at the nation’s highest court, Trump’s former golf caddy and social media adviser, Dan Scavino, now White House deputy chief of staff, wrote to Cook earlier this month to demand that she reply by Wednesday to a letter laying out the case for her removal.
Cook, who has called the administration’s effort to force her out a pretext to gain more power over interest rates, remains on the board.
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has rejoined the Democratic Socialists of America after not renewing her membership for seven years, amid speculation that she might run for president in 2028.
The 36-year-old New York representative and one of the country’s most prominent democratic socialists renewed her membership in the group’s national organization after reports emerged earlier this month that it had lapsed. Ocasio-Cortez initially joined the group in 2018.
In a statement on Tuesday night, the DSA announced: “Democratic Socialists of America confirms Rep Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is a member in good standing of our organization, having recently rejoined in August 2026,” according to a report in City & State New York.
It added: “Previously, the representative joined DSA in 2018 with a one-year membership, which DSA’s national leadership recently noticed had lapsed, in 2019. She has since renewed her membership as of this month.”
The DSA said it decided to disclose Ocasio-Cortez’s membership details amid reports that she could run for president in the next election cycle.
Interest in the congresswoman’s status comes as the organization has seen its ranks grow exponentially across the country, following a string of election victories from New York to Florida.
“While it is atypical for DSA to address the membership status of individuals, ongoing discussions about the 2028 presidential campaign have prompted this release … With chapters and members campaigning to draft Rep Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez as a potential Presidential Primary candidate, we believe that the status of her membership is essential information for members to have in their deliberations and discussions,” the statement said, City & State New York reported.
US Secret Service spokesman and two aides under investigation for 'potential misconduct' – reports
The chief spokesperson for the US Secret Service and two other communications staffers are under investigation for “potential misconduct” and have been suspended, according to the agency and media reports.
The spokesperson, Anthony Guglielmi, “is cooperating fully” withe the investigation, his lawyer told CNN, which first reported the news.
“Three non-law enforcement personnel at the US Secret Service have been placed on administrative leave pending an investigation into potential misconduct,” the agency said in a statement. “Per policy, this incident is being investigated by the Office of Professional Responsibility. We are unable to comment further at this time.”
The investigation comes amid an FBI leak inquiry into how the New York Times discovered that the Secret Service had raised concerns over Donald Trump using a Qatari-gifted luxury jet without the same security capabilities as older Air Force One jets to travel to Turkey for a Nato summit last month.
Guglielmi, a former chief spokesperson for the Baltimore and Chicago police departments, is being represented by Gregg Bernstein, Baltimore’s former chief prosecutor.
Oregon pledges to resist Trump's attempt to undermine its fully vote-by-mail system
In Oregon, which was the first US state to conduct fully vote-by-mail elections, governor Tina Kotek has released a statement of support for the lawsuit filed in federal court by the state’s attorney general, Dan Rayfield, seeking to block the US Postal Sertvuice with implementing Donald Trump’s executive order to restrict mail voting.
Kotek said:
“The U.S. Constitution gives power to the states to run elections. In Oregon, we uplift the right to vote and have worked hard to strengthen and expand our system to ensure everyone has a voice and that every election is safe and secure. I stand in strong support of Attorney General Rayfield’s fight against President Trump’s unconstitutional, undemocratic attempt to silence people’s voices. We’re doing everything in our power to protect Oregonians’ right to vote.”
US army to spend $2.2bn to build nuclear 'microreactors' on 5 military bases in US
The US army announced on Wednesday that it has awarded to $2.2bn to five contractors “to own, construct and operate nuclear microreactors on military installations” in five states.
“Awarding these contracts accelerates our ability to deliver safe, reliable baseload power directly to our installations,” the army secretary, Dan Driscoll, said. “We are building the energy resilience necessary to project combat power globally, without relying on potentially vulnerable external grids.”
The Pentagon statement said that it “expects more than 20 total nuclear microreactors will be built and operated” on US military installations as part of the project it calls the Janus Program, including additional private sector funding.
The selected companies and bases are: Antares Nuclear at Fort Bragg in North Carolina; BWX Technologies at Fort Campbell in Kentucky; General Atomics Electromagnetic Systems at Fort Hood in Texas; Radiant Industries at Fort Benning in Georgia; and Westinghouse Government Services at Fort Drum in New York.
The project is part of a Trump administration’s push to incentivize nuclear power, which includes billions in loans for large nuclear reactors to meet increased power demand from AI datacenters and a pilot program to boost advanced reactor designs and projects for military and civilian use. No such nuclear microreactors are supplying power to the commercial electric grid in the United States today.
During the Biden administration, the US Department of Energy published an explanatory article, headlined What is a Nuclear Microreactor?, which outlines three key features:
Factory fabricated: All components of a microreactor would be fully assembled in a factory and shipped out to location. This eliminates difficulties associated with large-scale construction, reduces capital costs and would help get the reactor up and running quickly.
Transportable: Smaller unit designs will make microreactors very transportable. This would make it easy for vendors to ship the entire reactor by truck, shipping vessel, airplane or railcar.
Self-adjusting: Simple and responsive design concepts will allow microreactors to self-adjust. They won’t require a large number of specialized operators and would utilize passive safety systems that prevent any potential for overheating or reactor meltdown.
The Council on American-Islamic Relations (Cair), the nation’s largest Muslim civil rights and advocacy organization, criticized the appointments of three pro-Israel House Democrats to the foreign affairs committee.
As we reported earlier, Debbie Wasserman Schultz, a representative from Florida, and the Missouri representative Wesley Bell will join the committee, while Jared Moskowitz, also from Florida, becomes the Democrats’ ranking member on the subcommittee for the Middle East and north Africa.
“We are deeply concerned by the appointment of three of the Israeli government’s most committed and consistent enablers,” said Edward Ahmed Mitchell, Cair’s deputy director, in a statement. “Members of Congress who want to continue giving the Netanyahu government American taxpayer money knowing it will be used to oppress and kill Palestinian men, women and children are, by definition, anti-Palestinian and out-of-step with the American people.”
Several progressives who have been critical of Benjamin Netanyhu’s leadership and the influence of the pro-Israel lobby on recent elections have won their races in recent months – most notably Abdul El-Sayed in the Democratic primary in Michigan.
Four of the nation’s leading livestock and agricultural organizations have also joined together tourge Donald Trump to reverse the proposed plan to temporarily pause higher tariffs on foreign beef imports, in an attempt to reduce grocery costs for Americans ahead of the midterm elections.
“Flooding the market with discounted foreign beef is not the way to rebuild the American cattle herd, strengthen food security, or lower grocery bills in a lasting way,” the groups write in a letter. “This announcement will discourage investment in the US cow herd and undo the progress producers have made.”
They add: “We are deeply concerned that this import strategy sacrifices long-term food security for a short-term solution. Americans deserve safe and wholesome beef free from any market distorting actions.”
This week, I’ve been reporting on the growing backlash to policy, including from several Republicans in states with sizable cattle industries who have issued rare rebukes of the president’s decision.
Federal judge lifts injunction on Trump's mail-in voting executive, paving way for further legal challenges
The federal judge who issued the injunction blocking parts of Donald Trump’s executive order curbing mail-in voting has lifted her block, after the supreme court said on Monday that the challenge from mainly Democratic-led states was premature, saying they lacked standing.
However, Judge Indira Talwani said that she would consider further challenges now that the US Postal Service had published its rule outlining how it will refuse to deliver mail-in ballots in states that refuse to give the Department of Homeland Security and other agencies access to lists of voters.
As I reported earlier, a coalition of states filed a fresh lawsuit on Wednesday to challenge the USPS policy.
And a reminder that the constitution confers control over elections to states and Congress, not the executive.
“Congress has not afforded USPS any authority whatsoever to set rules for federal elections or mail voting, even though Americans have cast ballots by mail for generations,” the states argue in the new lawsuit.
They also said although the deadline to submit mail voter lists to USPS “is still several weeks away”, the new rule “is already causing acute harm”.
“Plaintiff states or their subdivisions must immediately redesign their ballot envelopes and seek USPS review at significant costs to states,” they added.
On Truth Social, Donald Trump said that Ralph Norman, the South Carolina representative who lost the Republican primary for Senate to Darline Graham on Tuesday, had “the look” of a good congressman, but “ruined his career when he endorsed Nikki Haley”.
Trump backed Graham, after her brother, the late senator Lindsey Graham, died last month. Norman was shunned by the president as the only member of Congress to endorse Haley, the former governor of South Carolina, over Trump in the 2024 election.
The race to replace Lindsey Graham on the ballot became a stress test of the president’s support, and how effectively his endorsement can carry a candidate in deep-red pockets of the country to victory.
A federal judge has, for a second time, struck down a Texas state law banning drag performances in settings where children may be present.
In a ruling issued on Tuesday, the US district judge David Hittner said Texas cannot enforce its drag show ban. He said that the measure improperly restricts speech and violates the first amendment of the US constitution.
The Texas ban, known as Senate Bill 12, was passed in March 2023 and bans drag performers from dancing suggestively or wearing certain prosthetics on public property or in front of children, or “sexually oriented performance” presented on the premises in the presence of an individual younger than 18 years of age.
Advocacy groups sued the state after the bill’s passage, arguing the ban on “sexually oriented performance” infringed on constitutional rights. Texas’s move was just one across several states in 2023, driven by a rightwing backlash to increasing queer and transgender rights and equality. Hittner initially declared the ban unconstitutional in September 2023, but it was unblocked by the fifth US circuit court of appeals in 2025, which returned the case to the judge.
That allowed Texas attorney general, Ken Paxton, who is locked in a race for a US Senate seat against Democrat James Talarico, to resume enforcing the law earlier this year.
The new ruling prevents Paxton from enforcing the law. Paxton said he would appeal the decision. “This is a profoundly flawed decision that endangers our children and is an affront to Texas values,” Paxton on X.
In his ruling, Hittner advised anyone “who find[s] such activities as described in this case offensive” to “just don’t go”.
Trump insists that CIA director John Ratcliffe’s surprise visit to Russia is “semi-routine”, despite mounting speculation. The purpose of the visit is not yet clear, but Trump sought to temper concerns in an interview with conservative commentator Glen Beck on Wednesday. The last time a CIA director visited Moscow was in November 2021, when William Burns – Ratcliffe’s predecessor – traveled to Russia to warn against an invasion of Ukraine, which ultimately took place months later.
Democratic states sue to block postal service from carrying out Trump’s mail-in voting order. Two dozen Democratic‑led states on Wednesday filed a fresh lawsuit to block Donald Trump’s executive order restricting mail voting in this year’s midterm elections. The challenge comes days after the supreme court’s conservative majority lifted one injunction from a federal judge blocking parts of the president’s order.
New data shows a record number of arrests and deportations of immigrants in the US. The Trump administration arrested and deported a record number of immigrants in July, according to newly released government data – apprehending an average of 1,500 people and removing 1,100 people daily. Despite the administration’s insistence that it is targeting criminals, a record number of people caught in the surge of arrests in July had no prior criminal history. This confirms attorney and immigrant advocate concerns that that Trump administration is quietly ramping up its operations.
Trump touted his involvement in primary runoffs after his endorsed Republicans won elections in South Carolina and Oklahoma. The president took a moment to congratulate himself and the two candidates he backed on Tuesday – Darline Graham and Mike Mazzei. “I supported and ENDORSED two so-called ‘underdogs’ yesterday, one from South Carolina, and the other from Oklahoma, and they BOTH WON. Two great people!!!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
US designates Palestinian Action group a terrorist organization. The US treasury department has designated Palestine Action as a global terrorist group and imposed expanding US financial sanctions against the British-based organization. “Far-left extremists, their fronts and their enablers should be on notice: we will bring the full weight of our economic tools to bear,” said Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary.
Three pro-Israel Democrats will hold key roles on House foreign affairs panel. Debbie Wasserman Schultz, a representative from Florida, and Wesley Bell, from Missouri, will join the committee, while Jared Moskowitz, also from Florida, becomes the Democrats’ ranking member on the subcommittee for the Middle East and north Africa (Mena). These appointments to the House foreign affairs committee follow a succession of wins in party primaries for progressive candidates who put criticism of Israel and its actions in Gaza at the core of their campaign messages.
ICE has quietly enacted new rules to keep officers involved in deadly-force cases off the streets and on desk duty until an investigation is fully completed and they are formally cleared, the Atlantic reported last night, citing two senior ICE officials.
Previously, officers involved in such incidents – which involve firing a gun or using a chokehold, for example – could return to their regular work in the field within three days.
Per the Atlantic’s report: “The change, which has not been publicly announced, means that officers who fire their guns, choke someone, or use some other form of deadly force – even if no one is killed – will potentially be limited to performing administrative duties for much longer periods. Acting ICE Director David Venturella and other senior ICE leaders ordered the change late last month, the two senior officials said.”
Since Trump took office last year, ICE has opened fire on at least 30 people, according to Trace, a US outlet tracking such shootings. Four of these incidents were fatal.
Three pro-Israel Democrats gain key roles on House foreign affairs panel
Keely Aouga
Three pro-Israel Democrats gained key roles on the House foreign affairs committee today, with one joining as a leading Democrat in a subcommittee that oversees US-Middle East policy.
Debbie Wasserman Schultz, a representative from Florida, and Wesley Bell, from Missouri, will join the committee, while Jared Moskowitz, also from Florida, becomes the Democrats’ ranking member on the subcommittee for the Middle East and north Africa (Mena).
These appointments to the US House of Representatives foreign affairs committee follow a succession of wins in party primaries for progressive candidates who put criticism of Israel and its actions in Gaza at the core of their campaign messages.
All three recently defeated primary challengers who targeted them for their pro-Israel positions, shining a light on a potential split among establishment Democrats and new Democrats as the party works towards redefining itself.
Days before he was removed by Pete Hegseth as army chief of staff without explanation, Gen Randy George was advised by another general – who is now vying to replace him as the army’s top officer – to halt the military’s investigation into an unauthorized helicopter flyby of Kid Rock’s Tennessee estate, the Washington Post (paywall) reports, citing three people familiar with the matter.
According to the Post’s report, George “felt it was important to follow typical protocol and determine whether any safety regulations had been violated during the March 28 flyby”.
Per the report, “General Chris LaNeve, the Army’s No 2 officer, told George that Hegseth didn’t want the investigation to proceed, one person told the paper. The two others said George later confided in colleagues that he seemed troubled by the encounter with LaNeve, who suggested it would be best if the review was scuttled.”
The defence secretary reportedly requested in April that George retire immediately. Since assuming leadership at the Pentagon, he has dismissed more than a dozen high-ranking officers.
Earlier that week, Hegseth had also announced that the army personnel who piloted the two AH-64 Apache helicopters near Kid Rock’s home in Nashville would not be suspended, and he closed the investigation into the incident. Rock – real name Robert Ritchie – is a vocal Trump supporter.
In a statement to the Post, Hegseth didn’t directly address the report and instead focused on LaNeve, describing him as “precisely the kind of leader the US Army needs right now”, interested in strengthening the Army, and “not interested in playing politics in Washington”.
“He is a back-to-basics, no politics, no-nonsense General – exactly what President Trump expects,” Hegseth said. “The critics coming after him are the same out-of-touch so-called insiders who’ve spent years undermining our military with woke policies and endless wars. They hold deep grudges against any commander willing to put America and our troops first, but their days of influence are over.”
Defense department spokesperson Sean Parnell said the report amounted to a “regurgitating” of a “tired, old story simply to manufacture drama”.
Democratic states sue to block postal service from carrying out Trump's mail-in voting order
Two dozen states and the District of Columbia filed a fresh lawsuit on Wednesday to block Donald Trump’s executive order restricting mail voting in this year’s midterm elections.
The challenge comes days after the supreme court’s conservative majority lifted one injunction from a federal judge blocking parts of the president’s order.
In their new filing against the US Postal Service (USPS), the states point to concrete steps the administration has taken to carry out Trump’s directive – including a final USPS rule on ballot delivery posted Friday night.
The states said that the USPS policy is part of “a broader effort” by the Trump administration “to rewrite federal election law and usurp the authority of the states and Congress”.
And a reminder, that the constitution confers control over elections to states and Congress, not the executive.
On Monday, the supreme court did not rule on the legality of Trump’s order, but said that the states’ litigation was premature, effectively making room for further legal challenges.
A reminder that there is also a second nationwide injunction that still prevents the postal service from enforcing the order, though the justice department has argued that block should now be lifted in light of the supreme court’s ruling.
Democratic nominee for Iowa governor shuns campaign support from Joe Biden and Kamala Harris
Rob Sand, the Democratic nominee for Iowa governor, has dismissed any possible support from former president Joe Biden and vice-president Kamala Harris, as he vies to become flip the governor’s mansion blue in November.
Latest polling forecasts a tight race between Sand, a state auditor, and his Republican rival, businesman Zach Lahn. If Sand is victorious, he’d be the first Democratic governor elected in twenty years – since Chet Culver.
In an interview with Politico, Sand eschewed campaign bolstering from Biden and Harris, who unsuccessfully ran for president in 2024.
“No thanks. Let’s move on. We need some new leadership,” Sand said.
The Democratic nominee also said that he doesn’t think that Harris should mount a presidential bid in 2028.
“I think that we have a fundamentally broken two-choice political system. I don’t think that either the Democratic or the Republican parties to solve enough problems deserve special legal privileges in order to force us to pick between the lesser of two evils,” he said. “My inclination is I want it to be shaken up.”

articles.title: Italy to supply next-generation SAMP/T air defense systems, Aster 30 missiles to Ukraine in secret aid package, media reports
articles.body:
Italy to supply next-generation SAMP/T air defense systems, Aster 30 missiles to Ukraine in secret aid package, media reports
Ukraine is set to receive next-generation SAMP/T systems and additional air defense missiles by the end of the year as part of Italy’s latest military aid package, the Italian outlet La Repubblica reported on Aug. 26.
Citing its own sources, La Repubblica reported that the decision was made in secret, with the Italian government only officially announcing the transfer of civilian power generators to Ukraine. This was to sidestep internal political conflicts in Rome over continued military support for Kyiv, according to the outlet.
The package will include four SAMP/T NG air defense batteries, Aster 30 interceptor missiles, and seven long-range radars. Valued at nearly 3 billion euros ($3.5 billion), it marks Rome’s 13th military assistance package for Kyiv and will be funded through European Union loans.
The SAMP/T air defense system is co-produced by France and Italy and is capable of intercepting ballistic missiles — an urgent need for Ukraine as Russia's strikes intensify. The two countries previously provided Ukraine with earlier SAMP/T models in 2023, and again in 2024.
The upgraded SAMP/T NG systems, first available in 2025, feature a longer range and improved radar coverage compared to older versions.
read also
Paris and Rome have also agreed to authorize the production of French-Italian Aster 30 N1BT interceptor missile systems in Ukraine, according to La Repubblica. To bolster Ukraine’s air defenses amid critical shortages of interceptor missiles, Italy plans to transfer Aster 30 missiles directly from its own stockpiles by this October.
The long-range radars included in the package will be produced by the French defense company Thales and Italy's Leonardo company.
The military aid reportedly resulted from a July agreement between French President Emmanuel Macron and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, with support from their respective defense ministers.
Macron said on July 13 that France would allow Ukraine to produce French-designed cruise missiles, glide bombs, and air defense interceptors. He also said France would transfer next-generation SAMP/T air defense systems and radar systems to Ukraine.
At the time, Italy's involvement was not announced.
The reported package comes amid a dire air defense shortage in Ukraine, with July 2026 marking the worst month for civilian casualties in Ukraine since the first month of the full-scale war. Russia's increasing reliance on ballistic missile strikes on underprotected cities accounts for much of the rising death toll.

articles.title: San Francisco startup claims two-week build for jet interceptor
articles.body:
- IMPACT Drones says it built a SABLE interceptor prototype in two weeks, according to co-founder social media posts this week.
- The Y Combinator-backed startup launched its Air Defense as a Service offering on August 4 with the HUNTER and SABLE interceptors.
Y Combinator-backed startup IMPACT Drones says it built a working prototype of its high-speed interceptor drone, called SABLE, in two weeks, according to posts by the company’s two co-founders on social media.
Jasper Lortije, whom the company lists as CEO, and Alessandro Fiume, listed as founder, both posted about the prototype this week. IMPACT Drones incorporated nine weeks ago and is part of Y Combinator’s Summer 2026 batch, according to Fiume’s post.
SABLE is designed to reach 750 km/h (466 mph), Fiume said in the post. That figure differs from the 825 km/h (513 mph) design speed the company gave for SABLE at its public launch on August 4, when it first detailed the interceptor alongside a second system called HUNTER.
San Francisco-based IMPACT Drones unveiled its Air Defense as a Service offering at that August 4 launch. The company builds autonomous interceptor drones that ship inside sealed containers, which the company says can be placed at sites such as data centers, airports and power grids. When onboard sensors detect a hostile drone, an interceptor breaks through the container’s lid, launches and rams the target, guided by onboard visual navigation the company says continues to function when GPS is jammed.
HUNTER is described as a close-range, point-defense interceptor with a top speed of up to 300 km/h (186 mph), using electro-optical and long-wave infrared terminal guidance. The company has said HUNTER’s hardware lineage has been used against Shahed-136, Geran-2 and Gerbera-type drones in Ukraine.
SABLE is described as a longer-range pursuit interceptor built around a turbine engine and delta-wing airframe, intended to catch faster threats before they reach a protected site.
“SABLE and HUNTER are the cornerstones of our Air Defense as a Service offering, built to protect critical infrastructure,” Lortije wrote.
“Incoming drones keep getting cheaper and faster. Air defense has to catch up,” Fiume wrote.
“If you are responsible for protecting a data center, airport, or power grid, my inbox is open,” Fiume wrote.
IMPACT Drones is based in San Francisco and has two employees, according to its Y Combinator company profile. Lortije has an aerospace engineering background and previously worked on GNC systems, according to earlier reporting by Data Center Dynamics. Fiume previously co-founded Aerointel, a company building visual navigation and targeting software for autonomous interceptors, and lists $300,000 in revenue from European defense customers on his Y Combinator profile.
The company has said it holds more than $180 million in signed letters of intent, according to its Y Combinator listing. IMPACT Drones has targeted the third quarter of 2026 for pilot deployments of its interceptors, according to Data Center Dynamics.
The company has tied its launch to a string of drone and missile strikes on data centers this year. Data Center Dynamics reported that Amazon Web Services facilities in the United Arab Emirates were struck in March, with a further facility in Bahrain damaged in a nearby strike, and that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps later claimed a cruise missile strike on an AWS data center in Bahrain in late July.
IMPACT Drones has argued that existing air defense systems cost too much to use against low-cost drones. On its Y Combinator profile, the company says legacy effectors cost $1 million or more per shot against drones it values at around $30,000, and that its own interceptors are built to cost closer to the price of the threats they are meant to stop.

articles.title: Middle East live: Iran says Hormuz strait still closed despite transit corridor talks with Oman
articles.body:
Trump says he believes Iran’s leader is still alive but 'seriously wounded'
President Donald Trump on Wednesday said he believes Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei is “very seriously wounded”, but not dead. Khamenei has not been seen in public since the US and Israel launched the Iran war in February, prompting months of speculation over the new Iranian leader’s health. Follow our liveblog to see how the day's events unfolded.
This liveblog is no longer being updated.
This liveblog is no longer being updated.
Qatari PM to visit Iran
Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman al-Thani will visit Tehran on Thursday where he will meet a number of Iranian officials to discuss ways to de-escalate tensions, foreign ministry spokesperson Majed Al Ansari has said on X.
Iran places some foreign-based Persian-language media outlets on 'target bank'
Iran's armed forces on Wednesday said several Persian-language media outlets operating abroad were included in its "military target bank", accusing them of working for US and Israeli intelligence agencies.
In remarks published on state television, armed forces spokesman Abolfazl Shekarchi named BBC Persian, Iran International and Radio Farda among the outlets.
"These hostile media outlets are the soldiers of Zionism and America and are included in our military target bank," Shekarchi said, accusing them of being "directly connected to Mossad, CIA and enemy intelligence organisations."
"The Iranian Armed Forces do not view these news outlets as media," he added.
He did not clarify where they would be targeted.
US imposes sanctions on Palestine Action group
The US has imposed sanctions on the Palestine Action group, designating it a Specially Designated Global Terrorist, according to a notice posted on a Treasury Department website.
The UK previously banned Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation.
Palestine Action had increasingly targeted Israel-linked defence companies in Britain with a particular focus on Israel's largest defence firm Elbit Systems.
The UK's Supreme Court has said it will hear an appeal against a lower court ruling that Britain's decision to ban campaign group Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation was lawful.
Trump says believes that Iranian leader Khamenei still alive
US President Donald Trump has said he believes Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not been seen in public since taking over after his father's killing in February, remains alive.
"I don't think he's dead. He was very seriously wounded. The left side of his body, the arm, the leg, the whole thing. He was very seriously wounded. But I don't think he's dead," Trump said in an interview with conservative radio host Glenn Beck.
Dubai airport reports sharp drop in second quarter traffic due to Iran war's effects
Dubai International Airport, one of the world’s busiest hubs, has declared that it saw a sharp drop in passengers during the second quarter as the Iran war disrupted air travel and prompted many travelers to choose routes that avoided the Middle East.
The airport recorded 13 million passengers during the second quarter, following 31.5 million passengers in the first half. That was a 31.3% drop over passenger traffic in the first half of 2025, the airport said.
Air traffic in the United Arab Emirates and elsewhere in the Gulf region was disrupted by shutdowns and restrictions after the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28. The Dubai airport itself suffered minor damage in attacks from Iran.
Iran and Oman reach agreements on share of Hormuz and revenues, Revolutionary Guards say
Iran and Oman have reached agreements on their share of the Strait of Hormuz and its revenues, Iran's Revolutionary Guards spokesperson said, according to a report by the semi-official Tasnim news agency on Wednesday.
The spokesperson said the US was obstructing negotiations between Oman and Iran, leading to them being delayed.
Weapons systems damaged during war 'rebuilt', Iran army says
Iran's army on Wednesday said all weapons systems that were damaged so far in the Middle East war have been "rebuilt" and that new systems have been imported to the country.
"Systems in all branches of the military, including those that were damaged, have been rebuilt, and new systems have also been imported," said army spokesperson, Mohammad Akraminia, according to state TV.
"New systems have come through the defense industry and the army, and some have also been imported from abroad, and this equipment has enhanced our combat capabilities," he added.
The United States and Israel initiated the Middle East war with a massive wave of strikes against Iran on February 28, triggering Iranian retaliation across the region.
USS Abraham Lincoln will stop in Thailand on its way home
The US aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln will make a stop in Thailand after its grueling deployment in the Middle East, Thai officials said.
The Lincoln was supporting the US war against Iran, and its deployment included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 250 days. Concerns have grown about the Lincoln’s lengthy deployment following reports of deteriorating mental health among the crew and shortages of supplies including food and hygiene products.
Thai defense ministry spokesperson Surasant Kongsiri said that the Lincoln will stop in Thailand next week for rest and recovery before returning to its US base.
Iran urges Qatar to address fate of missing Iranian pilots
Iran said Qatar has told Tehran it is unaware of the fate of Iranian pilots missing since their aircraft were shot down after entering Qatari airspace, and urged Doha to step up efforts to determine their status, according to state media.
Tehran said it had followed up through diplomatic and military channels but had yet to receive a clear response from Qatar on the pilots' fate.
Lebanon accuses Israel of burning forest, farmland in south
Lebanese officials and residents have accused Israel's military of systematically sparking blazes that have burnt swathes of forest and farmland in the country's south.
An AFP photographer this month saw multiple fires raging in south Lebanon, mostly inside Israel's self-declared "security zone", which runs around 10 kilometres deep inside Lebanese territory along the border.
Lebanon's governmental National Council for Scientific Research (CNRS) says Israeli military activity has caused 160 square kilometres of land, half of it agricultural, to go up in flames since hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah began in October 2023.
Iran says 'US will achieve nothing' with economic pressure
"Given the measures the government has undertaken, America will not achieve anything with economic pressure at this stage, just as it was unable to achieve anything in the war," Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said, according to ISNA news agency.
Gulf expats hunker down between bouts of war
Six months into the Middle East war, the army of foreign workers and expats in the Gulf has largely stayed put -- hoping to ride out the uncertainty caused by conflict rather than return to dim prospects back home.
"I stayed because I had no other option," a Syrian woman told AFP. "Most of us are here because... it was just unlivable where we came from."
For most of the oil-rich Gulf states, foreigners from Global South countries make up the majority of the population, forming the bedrock of the economy as high-end consultants, manual labourers, healthcare professionals and everything in between.
Sri Lanka tracks 11 US-sanctioned Iranian tankers off coast
Sri Lanka's maritime authorities were monitoring a fleet of 11 US-sanctioned Iranian oil tankers just off the island's southern coast, the foreign minister said Wednesday.
The tankers were spotted close to the Galle harbour where an Iranian frigate, IRIS Dena, was sunk by a US submarine in March, killing 104 sailors. Sri Lanka's navy rescued 32 Iranian sailors from that frigate.
Iranian vessels have been in limbo, unable to return to their home port because of a US blockade. Sri Lanka's Foreign minister Vijitha Herath said the tankers were in international waters where they had freedom of navigation.
Netanyahu says no diplomatic deal possible with Iran 'savages'
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said a diplomatic deal was not possible with the "savages" who rule Iran as he hailed US President Donald Trump's new campaign of economic pressure.
Recounting a recent meeting with Trump, Netanyahu told an event late Tuesday that they had discussed the possibility of diplomacy with Iran and said: "I doubt, however, that an agreement can be reached with that group there, with those savages. I tell you - an agreement cannot be reached."
Israel takes control of UN training centre for Palestinians
Israeli forces took control of a vocational training centre run by the UN agency for Palestinian refugees in an east Jerusalem suburb on Tuesday, in its latest move targeting the beleaguered organisation. The raid drew condemnation from UN chief Antonio Guterres, and followed warnings by UNRWA that Israeli authorities were threatening its Qalandia training centre. The centre was established in 1952 and offers vocational training to around 340 Palestinians from the occupied West Bank every year, according to UNRWA.
Supertankers with 4 million barrels of Saudi oil head for China, data shows
Two supertankers carrying 4 million barrels of Saudi crude are bound for China after loading the cargoes via ship-to-ship transfers off Oman, shipping data showed on Wednesday.
Britain backs US measures for diplomatic solution on Iran
British Finance Minister John Healey said on Tuesday that the country supports U.S. efforts to secure a diplomatic solution on Iran and welcomed steps to increase pressure, including the expanded sanctions on Iran announced Monday.
Healey also called on Iran to cease its "de-stabilising activity" across the region, including in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran says Hormuz strait still closed despite transit corridor talks
Iran and Oman are discussing a temporary transit corridor and mine-clearing for the Strait of Hormuz, but Tehran warned on Wednesday that the vital waterway will not be reopened unless the United States ends the war.
During talks in Tehran, foreign ministers from Iran and Oman discussed a "phased framework" that included setting up a "joint temporary navigational corridor through the Strait of Hormuz and an agreement to implement a joint project to clear the Strait of mines," according to a statement.
The two countries, both coastal states bordering the strait, have sought to hammer out a plan to regulate transit through it, as laid out in a June US-Iran memorandum of understanding.
Gulf ship traffic via Strait of Hormuz hovers below 10-day average
Five commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, broadly unchanged from a day earlier but well below the 10-day average of 15, preliminary shipping data showed on Wednesday.
Two tankers carrying liquefied petroleum gas and one tanker carrying bitumen exited the strait, while two empty product tankers entered the waterway, initial data from shiptracker Kpler showed at 0408 GMT.
The figures could change as some ships typically switch off transponders during the voyage.
Yesterday's key developments:
- United Nations chief Antonio Guterres on Tuesday condemned an incursion by Israeli forces on a training center run by the UN agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA) in an east Jerusalem suburb.
- Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi said on Tuesday that he hoped his country and Iran would soon announce the establishment of a temporary shipping corridor in the Strait of Hormuz after weeks of negotiations.
- US President Donald Trump has said that all mines within the international waters of the Strait of Hormuz have been removed or detonated, and that Iran had been notified that any ship or boat placing new mines would be destroyed.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP, AP and Reuters)

articles.title: Iranian attacks caused billions in damages to US intelligence sites and hardware - report
articles.body:
Iranian attacks on US intelligence posts and hardware during the course of the recent war caused billions of dollars of damage, NBC reported on Wednesday citing four people with knowledge of the matter.
Missile attacks and drone strikes on US assets in the Middle East has forced the US Congress to allocate funding towards repairs, the report cited two of the sources as saying.
Further, some of the sites and equipment targeted by Iran are shared with the US military, the sources said, adding that this war signifies an unprecedented threat to the CIA and other US intelligence agencies.
Some of the intelligence-linked sites hit throughout the war include a Riyadh CIA station, a site in eastern Iraq, and other radar and surveillance equipment throughout the region, NBC reported citing US and Gulf officials familiar with the matter.
These strikes raised questions within the US military and intelligence community about the country's ability to defend its assets, the report added.
Iran attacked radar systems in the early days of the war, lacks interceptors
The CIA maintains dozens of bases throughout the Middle East, the report said, including so-called "stations" at embassies.
The CIA, along with the State Department and the White House did not respond to the network's request for comment.
Iran has attacked US allies in the Gulf region with thousands of drones and missiles since the start of the war in late February, targeting mainly US bases and forces.
In the first days of Operation Epic Fury, Iran targeted multiple US air defense battery radars, satellite imagery and photos spread online showed.
This footage showed a destroyed AN/TPY-2 radar system in Jordan, a destroyed AN/FPS-12 phased array radar in Qatar, as well as damaged systems in the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Saudi Arabia.
In July, the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) published a report estimating that between February and July about 65% of Patriot interceptors had been expended and that the number of THAAD ballistic missile interceptors in US stockpiles was at least 38% lower than at the start of the war.
Patriots and THAADs are systems that detect and destroy incoming missiles and are among the most effective in the country's arsenal.
Anna Ahronheim, Jerusalem Post Staff, and Reuters contributed to this report.

The information was presented during a briefing by Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the Ukrainian president’s sanctions policy commissioner, according to a Militarnyi correspondent.
Russia developed the missile based on the 48N6 family of surface-to-air missiles to strike ground targets and overwhelm enemy air defenses.
In recent months, Russia has increased its use of RM-48U missiles during large-scale combined attacks against Ukraine.
In early June, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence reported that Russia had more than doubled the production rate of these missiles. In 2026, the Russian leadership planned to produce more than 480 RM-48U missiles.

The RM-48U missile also uses 12-channel Kometa antennas containing U.S.-made components.

articles.title: Russia Converted Up to 17 S-400 Launchers for Strikes on Ukraine — DIU
articles.body:
Russia has converted up to 17 launchers of the S-400 air defense system for missile strikes against targets in Ukraine.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (DIU) said this in response to a UNIAN request.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, the Russian command operates five special missile groups deployed in the Bryansk and Rostov regions.
“The total number of converted launchers of this air defense system that the enemy can use to conduct strikes is up to 17,” the intelligence service reported.
Russia is actively using RM-48U missiles to strike Ukraine, with the missiles launched from converted S-400 launchers.
S-400 air defense system missile launch. Photo credits: TASS
The DIU also reported increased use of these missiles. From January through June, Russia used about 15 RM-48U missiles per month, while it used 46 of them in the first 20 days of July alone.
The intelligence service links the increase to an expansion in ballistic strikes against targets in Kyiv.
“The decision to increase the use of RM-48U missiles is linked to their lower cost compared with Iskander-M missiles, as well as a significant stockpile of these missiles — about 400 units,” the DIU noted.
Russian defense industry enterprises can currently produce new S-400 launchers and upgrade existing ones.
The RM-48U missiles, which are essentially ballistic missiles developed from the 48N6 family of surface-to-air missiles, have been found to contain French 3SP Technologies laser modules.
The missiles carry high-explosive fragmentation warheads weighing about 150–180 kg. The first confirmed use of the missile occurred on the night of January 20, 2026. They were subsequently used in combined strikes against Ukrainian cities.
In 2026, the Russian leadership planned to produce more than 480 RM-48U missiles.

articles.title: Ukraine expects sanctions against Russian ballistics manufacturers in coming months – presidential commissioner
articles.body:
Ukraine has provided partners with information on Russian ballistics manufacturers, as well as foreign technical and chemical components used by Russia to produce ballistic missiles, reported Commissioner of the President of Ukraine on Sanctions Policy Vladyslav Vlasiuk.
"And, accordingly, one of the first points of our plan (to counter ballistics – IF-U) is maximum synchronization. That is, in all jurisdictions of countries that adopt sanctions against Russia, all entities identified as manufacturers of Russian ballistic strike weapons must be sanctioned," Vlasiuk told journalists on Wednesday.
According to him, this involves more than 100 Russian enterprises involved in ballistics production.
"Accordingly, in September-October, we expect all Russian manufacturers of ballistic strike weapons to be added to the sanctions lists. We are talking about 100 plus enterprises," he said.
Separately, the presidential commissioner reported that Ukraine handed over information to partners regarding foreign technical components used by Russia in the production of ballistic missiles. According to him, among the countries where companies associated with supplying such components are registered are the US, Switzerland, China, France, Great Britain, Taiwan, Japan, and Germany.
Ukraine also provided partners with information regarding chemical components on whose import Russian ballistics production depends.
"We handed over substance files to our partners and expect decisions in the coming months. All these files are also being transferred. For each item, we disclosed in detail there how exactly this item is used for ballistics production," he noted.
According to him, Ukraine expects partners to introduce corresponding restrictions on the export of such components to Russia in the coming months.
At the same time, he emphasized that this year there were successful cases of blocking the export of foreign components to Russia thanks to US assistance.
The presidential commissioner reported that in the near future he may pay a visit to the US to promote a sanctions bill by the late Senator Lindsey Graham.
Vlasiuk also noted that Ukraine expects several intermediate sanctions packages from the European Union prior to the adoption of the 22nd package, which, according to him, is expected no earlier than the end of October.
"We would like them (the EU – IF-U) to adopt several intermediate packages before this large 22nd package. That is no earlier than the end of October. We would like them to adopt a small intermediate package as early as September, specifically aimed at countering ballistics sanctions packages. Then another package in October," he said.
According to Vlasiuk, the EU’s 22nd sanctions package should address, in particular, the Russian military-industrial complex and measures aimed at countering Russian ballistic capabilities.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Reboot of ‘fortress belt’ defences as Zelenskyy visits frontline
articles.body:
- 
  Volodymyr Zelenskyy has appointed two of Ukraine’s most prominent commanders to oversee and strengthen defences of the “fortress belt” of industrialised cities in the Donetsk region. Visiting the frontline, Zelenskyy said Third Army Corps leader Andrii Biletskyi and Denys Prokopenko, commander of the First Corps Azov, would head new groupings. Both units are known for embracing Nato-style doctrine and new technology.
- 
  Russian forces are putting pressure on the cities of Kostiantynivka, Kramatorsk and Sloviansk – all critical strongholds for Ukraine. According to open-source mapping group Deep State, Moscow’s troops have been infiltrating deeper into Kostiantynivka, with the Ukrainians weeding them out from houses, basements and ruins. Russia was also stepping up its air and artillery attacks on Kramatorsk and Sloviansk to prepare for a targeted offensive on those cities, Deep State said.
- 
  Ukrainian military analyst Mykola Bielieskov told Reuters the appointments were “the right move” in giving Ukraine’s new commander in chief, Mykhailo Drapatyi, greater scope for strategic planning. His predecessor, the “Soviet-era” general Oleksandr Syrskyi, was criticised for micromanagement. Ukrainian drone forces commander Robert Brovdi, a leader of Kyiv’s mid and long-range strike campaigns, praised the appointments as an important step towards “network-centric warfare … This is exactly what ‘Smart War’ is,” he posted.
- 
  Ukraine hit 16 sites in Russia over the past day including oil facilities and logistics, Zelenskyy said on Wednesday. The targets also included airfields, a missile unit, a military enterprise and infrastructure that Moscow uses to launch attacks against Ukraine. Ukraine’s military general staff said its forces struck a Lukoil refinery overnight in Kstovo, in Russia’s Nizhny Novgorod region, setting it on fire. The refinery can process 125m barrels annually. Long-range Ukrainian drones burned a Wildberries warehouse to the ground in the Tambov region south-east of Moscow, Russian authorities said on Wednesday.
- 
  A Russian guided aerial bomb attack seriously damaged a combined heat and power plant in Ukraine’s southern city of Kherson, the plant’s owner, Ukrainian energy company Naftogaz, said on Wednesday. The extent of the damage would be assessed as soon as the security situation allowed, Naftogaz said.
- 
  There were explosions in the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv early on Thursday, a Reuters witness said. Around the same time, Russia attacked an industrial facility in the central Ukrainian city of Kryvyi Rih with ballistic missiles, injuring two people, said Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of the city’s defence council. It came after Bloomberg reported that Russia was considering stepping up its ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv, including targets in the city centre, and on critical infrastructure elsewhere in Ukraine after concluding that efforts to negotiate a peace deal had reached a dead end. While Ukraine has repeatedly offered ceasefires and negotiations, the Kremlin has not altered its demands – chief among which is total control of Ukraine’s Donbas region.
- 
  Volodymyr Zelenskyy has awarded Ukraine’s Order of Freedom to Elon Musk, whose SpaceX has provided Starlink satellite internet to Ukraine’s military. Musk has restricted its use over Russian territory – a policy Zelenskyy hopes to change so that Ukrainian weapons can use Starlink to navigate to their targets.
- 
  Ukraine freed 10 Russian prisoners of war, Russia’s human rights commissioner said on Wednesday. On Monday, Russia released 10 Ukrainian prisoners of war who were previously thought to be missing.
- 
  A pro-Russian hacker group on Wednesday claimed responsibility for a cyber-attack on Digdir, the Norwegian government’s digital services agency. The denial-of-service (DDOS) attacks tried to overwhelm the agency’s computers to block services, including one that enables citizens to use one login across multiple public services. A Digdir spokesperson said the agency still managed to keep the services running “practically all the time”. The pro-Russian hacker group Server Killers said it attacked because Norway renewed its security cooperation with Ukraine on 23 August.

articles.title: Trump downplays Moscow visit by CIA director as ‘semi-routine’
articles.body:
Donald Trump has downplayed a visit to Moscow by the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, as “semi-routine” after he turned up in the Russian capital unannounced, triggering a wave of speculation about the reasons for his trip.
Ratcliffe was reported to have flown to Moscow on a government transport plane on Tuesday in a rare visit after taking off from the Andrews air force base in Maryland.
The White House, CIA, Pentagon and the US air force all declined to comment on the visit, which was confirmed on Wednesday by a Kremlin spokesperson, Dimitry Peskov.
Interviewed by the conservative radio host Glenn Beck, Trump poured cold water on speculation that Ratcliffe had travelled in response to fears that Vladimir Putin, the Russian president, was planning to “test Nato resolve” or to win Moscow’s cooperation for intensified US sanctions on Iran.
“None of the above,” the US president said in response to Beck, who referred to the speculation as “crazy”.
“He’s there, you know, very sort of semi-routine. I hate to disappoint people. We would like to see the war with Ukraine end,” Trump said.
“John Ratcliffe is a fantastic guy. He’s the head of the CIA, and he is not in there for any of the things that you said. Now something may come … out of it. We’re working very hard to get that war ended, and frankly, they both want to see it ended at this point.”
On Wednesday, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people briefed on the visit, that the reason for the spy chief’s surprise visit was to warn Russia not to attack Nato countries.
Ratcliffe’s visit was the first from a CIA director since his predecessor Bill Burns travelled to Moscow in November 2021 to warn Putin of the consequences of attacking Ukraine.
The Russian leader went ahead with the attack regardless in February of the following year. Trump’s efforts to end the war – which he once vowed to bring to a conclusion on “day one” of his second presidency – have proven unsuccessful, despite his friendly personal relations with Putin.
Peskov, the Kremlin spokesperson, said Ratcliffe did not meet Putin during his visit.
Washington and Moscow have found themselves on opposite sides following Trump’s decision last February to go to war with Iran, with Russian satellite technology said to have been used to help Iranian forces with precise targeting of US and allied bases in the Gulf and beyond.
With military hostilities at an impasse, the US treasury department this week unveiled a new program of economic warfare against the Tehran regime involving secondary sanctions against countries that trade with it. To be effective, it would need the cooperation of allies of Iran such as Russia and China, experts say.
Peskov did not give a reason for Ratcliffe’s visit, but described forecasts that it would lead to an upturn in US-Russian relations as “premature”, the Washington Post reported.
“Contacts through intelligence-service channels are in themselves a positive phenomenon, a positive process. These contacts often continue even in the most difficult moments of bilateral relations,” Peskov told reporters. “But whether this will affect, on the whole, the process of bringing our bilateral relations out of the deep crisis they are in – it’s premature to say at this point.”
In recent days, Ukraine has targeted Russia’s energy infrastructure and online retail facilities in long-distance strikes, while Russia has intensified drone and missile attacks on Kyiv.

articles.title: Ukrainian Military Adds Jet-Powered 'Alexa Spatium' Interceptor Drones to Its Arsenal
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense said it is procuring “Alexa Spatium,” a domestically produced jet-powered interceptor drone, to help engage Russian drones and other ground targets.
The ministry called it the “first Ukrainian jet-powered drone interceptor” added to the military’s arsenal in a press release published on Friday, Aug. 22.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
It said the “Alexa Spatium” is a modular drone designed to engage Russia’s Geran-3, Geran-4, Geran-5, and Shahed-131 jet-powered drones, as well as “small aerial, ground, and surface targets.”
The ministry remained tight-lipped about the drone’s performance but noted that it measures approximately 1.5 by 1.7 meters (5 by 5.5 feet) and is launched by mobile catapults that allow deployment “within minutes.”
In a video shared by the ministry, the drone can be seen launching from a short, narrow catapult system a few meters long.
The ministry said it could reach a “high” altitude with a “substantial” range without providing the figures.
It’s built from “lightweight, durable composite material” and is powered by a “powerful turbojet engine,” the ministry said.
When it comes to onboard armaments, the drone can be equipped with high-explosive fragmentation, shaped-charge, or thermobaric warheads, depending on the mission needs.
China Helps Russia Upgrade Shaheds Into a New Threat for Ukraine
In terms of targeting, the drone is said to come with “TV and infrared search and targeting systems.”
While the ministry boasted that it can fly via “pre-programmed coordinates or direct guidance,” it added that it also comes with “reliable control and video transmission systems.”
It can also return to base to be reused if it “does not complete the mission,” the press release says.
The press release did not elaborate on the drone’s manufacturer or the origin of its name.
Various Ukrainian arms makers have unveiled similar jet-powered interceptor drones as Russia’s use of high-speed jet-powered drones became more frequent, with the military warning in June that half of the Russian drones used in future attacks could be jet-powered.
Military expert Oleh Katkov noted in a recent interview with RBC Ukraine that the new, jet-powered Geran drones are approaching cruise missiles in design and capability.
In July, Firebolt Engineering, a UK-Ukrainian arms maker, said its Griffen jet-powered drone successfully destroyed a Russian Shahed drone in the first interception of its kind in Ukraine.
Firebolt Engineering said the Griffen can fly faster than 350 kph (217 mph), with an operating altitude of over 7,500 meters (24,606 feet) and a range of up to 120 km (75 miles).

articles.title: Belarus Orders Surprise Military Readiness Check as CIA Chief Visits Moscow
articles.body:
Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko has ordered a surprise combat-readiness inspection of the country’s armed forces as CIA Director John Ratcliffe makes an unannounced visit to Moscow.
One Belarusian brigade will leave its permanent base and carry out a series of undisclosed tasks as part of the inspection, Alexander Volfovich, secretary of Belarus’ Security Council, said on Aug. 26.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We will not talk about them for now,” Volfovich said, adding that the tasks would depend on decisions by Belarus’ military leadership and General Staff.
The exercise will focus in particular on ways to strike a potential enemy, taking into account “the experience of military conflicts in Ukraine and Iran,” Volfovich said.
The stated goal is to test whether Belarusian military units can conduct combat operations under modern battlefield conditions. Volfovich urged the public not to assume that “something extraordinary is happening.”
The announcement comes a day after Ratcliffe’s arrival in Moscow for an unannounced visit, with the Kremlin saying he did not meet Russian President Vladimir Putin and instead held “contacts between intelligence services.”
The Wall Street Journal, citing people familiar with the matter, reported that Ratcliffe’s trip may have been linked to US intelligence about Putin’s potential next moves.
Belarus Opposition Waits for Its Solidarity Moment
According to the report, Russian forces recently conducted mobilization-preparation exercises in the Kaliningrad region and other areas, testing whether military infrastructure could receive, equip and feed new recruits.
US intelligence has also gathered information suggesting Putin may seek to test NATO’s resolve, the WSJ reported.
“The goal may have been to say: ‘We know what you are planning, and you’d better not do it,’” former US Deputy Director of National Intelligence Beth Sanner told the newspaper.
Belarus has also been strengthening its military posture near Ukraine.
Belarusian Special Operations Forces Commander Alexander Ilyukevich said earlier this month that Minsk had begun forming a new air-assault brigade near the Ukrainian border, reportedly in the Gomel region.
The WSJ previously reported that Putin had been pressing Lukashenko to open a new front against Ukraine. Moscow was also considering using Belarusian territory for operations against neighboring NATO states, including drone launches, according to the report.
French President Emmanuel Macron has warned Lukashenko against being drawn further into Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has also pointed to Belarus’ construction of military infrastructure along the Ukrainian border, warning it could be used for aggression against Ukraine.
