articles.title: Sweden seeks to seize Russian-owned land by naval base
articles.body:
Sweden’s Armed Forces have asked the government to expropriate a strategically placed property at the entrance to Muskö Naval Base, arguing that its Russian ownership and location create an unacceptable national security risk.
The Swedish Armed Forces have asked the government to expropriate a Russian-owned property overlooking an approach to Muskö Naval Base, saying control of the site is necessary to strengthen protection of the installation against surveillance and drone threats, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The Swedish Fortifications Agency submitted the application on behalf of the Armed Forces on 25 August, seeking government permission to acquire the property through compulsory purchase. Swedish defence officials say the site occupies a unique position at one of the approaches to Muskö, south of Stockholm, and is the only property in the immediate area required for the base’s protection that is not already available to the military.
The property is owned by an individual holding Russian citizenship whom the Swedish Armed Forces say they assess to pose a security threat. Open-source discussion of the site has drawn particular attention to its position on the inlet leading towards the naval area, but the Armed Forces’ formal case rests on the combination of its location, current ownership and the changing threat from uncrewed systems.
Lieutenant General Carl-Johan Edström, Chief of the Defence Staff, said, as quoted in a Swedish Armed Forces news update: “Nothing is more important than Sweden’s security. We are facing the most serious security situation since the end of the Second World War, and the threat to Sweden and the Alliance is real.”
He added: “Against this backdrop, the Swedish Armed Forces have instructed the Swedish Fortifications Agency to apply to the Government for permission to expropriate the property in question.”
Swedish defence officials are placing particular emphasis on the rapid development of Russian drone warfare, arguing that military installations now need protection not only from conventional airborne surveillance and attack but also from small aerial and maritime uncrewed systems that can approach sensitive sites from directions which were previously less difficult to monitor.
The Armed Forces say the property at Muskö represents a gap in that defensive arrangement. Because the surrounding locations are already available to the military, acquiring this final site would allow protection measures around the entrance to the base to be planned as a continuous system rather than around privately controlled land.
Edström said: “A strong defence is essential to our freedom. Unmanned systems can be employed in many different ways—for surveillance and intelligence gathering, as well as for direct attacks. That threat is real and must be countered, not least by establishing robust systems capable of detecting and countering drones around our military bases.”
He continued: “The current security environment requires us to act and not accept the risks associated with the property’s current ownership. The present situation does not benefit Sweden or NATO—it benefits Russia.”
The language used by the Armed Forces is unusually direct, with the application explicitly linking the owner’s Russian citizenship and the military’s security assessment to the case for expropriation. The Swedish authorities have not merely argued that the land would be useful for expansion; they describe it as critical to the effective protection of Muskö Naval Base and say its present ownership creates a risk that can no longer be accepted.
The request also reflects Sweden’s wider adjustment to the security environment since joining NATO, with military infrastructure now considered not only in terms of national defence but also its role in protecting Alliance assets and operations. In its statement, the Armed Forces repeatedly referred to both Swedish and NATO security when setting out the need to bring the property under state control.
The Swedish Fortifications Agency has now submitted the application to the Government Offices of Sweden, which must now consider whether to authorise the compulsory acquisition and determine the next steps under Swedish law.

articles.title: Latvia lands $233 million explosives plant near Russia’s border
articles.body:
- Wolfram Europa plans a $233 million explosives and warhead complex near Jēkabpils, Latvia, close to Russia's border, with construction starting in 2027.
- At full capacity, the site aims to produce 200,000 warheads and 100,000 anti-tank mines a year to help close Europe's explosives supply gap.
A European company plans to build a $233 million explosives and warhead factory in Latvia, a NATO ally that sits just 175 miles (280 km) from Russia’s border, in a project aimed at closing a supply gap that has left Europe dependent on outside sources for the raw materials behind its weapons.
Wolfram Europa announced the €200 million ($233 million) project Wednesday at an event in Jēkabpils, a city in eastern Latvia. The company plans a 40-hectare (99-acre) site, secured under a long-term land agreement with Latvijas Valsts Meži, the Latvian state forestry company, with construction happening in three phases starting in 2027.
For American readers, the scale is easier to picture in terms of output. At full capacity, the plant is designed to make enough explosive material to fill 200,000 warheads and 100,000 anti-tank mines every year. It will also produce RDX and HMX, two explosive compounds used across NATO munitions, including artillery shells and missile warheads.
Wolfram Europa was registered in Latvia’s commercial register in January 2026 with initial capital of just $3,260, according to Latvian outlet Dzentlmenis.lv. The jump from a startup-sized registration to a $233 million industrial project happened in a matter of months.
The company describes itself as a European defense manufacturer building explosives, warheads and counter-mobility products, meaning items like anti-tank mines, without relying on long international supply chains. Once fully operational, the project is expected to create 200 jobs in the region.
Company officials say the plant is designed to meet NATO explosive safety standards and will be licensed under Latvian regulation. They describe it as a low-footprint, relocatable design meant to let production scale up or move if needed during a crisis.
The project has the backing of Latvia’s government. Latvian Minister of Economics Viktors Valainis, Minister of Smart Administration and Regional Development Edgars Tavars, Ministry of Defence State Secretary Airis Rikveilis, and Jēkabpils County Municipality Chairman Raivis Ragainis all attended the announcement alongside Wolfram Europa CEO Magnus-Valdemar Saar.
“Investments of this scale represent a significant step forward in the development of Latvia’s defence industry and, at the same time, demonstrate Latvia’s ability to attract strategically important industrial projects to its regions,” said Viktors Valainis, Minister of Economics.
For American readers less familiar with the issue, Europe’s explosives shortage has become a significant concern within NATO. Company officials point to a widening gap between Russia’s explosives output and Europe’s, arguing that European countries have spent billions on missiles, artillery shells and drones in recent years but have not scaled up the raw explosive material those weapons ultimately require.
“For the last 35 years, Europe has been scaling down its explosives and munitions industry, and technological development has stalled with it,” said Magnus-Valdemar Saar, CEO of Wolfram Europa. “Now Europe is rearming, but investment is still focused mainly on platforms and final assembly. That is the explosives gap: Europe is scaling its weapons faster than the explosives and warheads that make them effective.”
Saar said Latvia is meant to be the first of several sites Wolfram Europa builds across the continent.
“Jēkabpils will not serve Latvia alone. Latvia will host strategic production capacity for Europe. It will be our first major site, but not our last,” Saar said.
“The establishment of such a company strengthens the involvement of Latvia’s defence industry, promotes the development of technologies and expertise, and demonstrates Latvia’s ambition to become a significant regional hub for defence industry and technology development,” said Airis Rikveilis, State Secretary of the Ministry of Defence.
The Wolfram Europa project is one of several recent defense manufacturing investments in the Baltic region, an area U.S. policymakers watch closely given its proximity to Russia. Rheinmetall, the German defense contractor, signed a separate memorandum of understanding with Latvia’s government in March 2026 for an artillery shell factory, structured as a joint venture with Rheinmetall holding 51 percent and the Latvian State Defence Corporation holding 49 percent. That plant is expected to produce between 60,000 and 80,000 shells (155mm, or 6.1 inches, in caliber) a year once construction begins in spring 2027.
Rheinmetall has also signed a $350 million deal for a similar shell plant in neighboring Lithuania, which broke ground in November 2025 with a target of 100,000 shells a year by 2027.
“My task is to ensure that unnecessary bureaucracy does not stand in the way of this project and that the investment can flow into Jēkabpils,” said Edgars Tavars, Minister for Smart Administration and Regional Development.

articles.title: CIA director was on ‘semi-routine’ mission in Russia, says Trump
articles.body:
CIA director warned Russia not to attack NATO members: US media
- CIA Director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow to warn Russia against attacking NATO members amid fears of a possible limited assault.
- The visit was described by President Trump as "semi-routine" and focused on efforts to end the Ukraine war and discuss Iran sanctions.
- Kremlin confirmed Ratcliffe met with Russian intelligence but not President Putin, with talks seen as a positive step despite ongoing tensions.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - A highly unusual trip by the CIA director to Moscow this week was to warn Russia against any attack on NATO member states, US media reported on Aug 26, after US President Donald Trump sought to downplay the visit.
The Wall Street Journal and CBS News reported CIA director John Ratcliffe aimed to dissuade Russia from attacking NATO members amid US intelligence assessments that Moscow could seek to test the alliance.
The Journal specified that Putin could test the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation with a “limited assault” in the next few years.
The White House did not respond to multiple AFP requests for comment on the matter, and Trump said Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow on Aug 26 was “semi-routine,” implying that the intelligence chief was in the Russian capital to discuss the Ukraine war.
“He’s there, very sort of semi-routine. I hate to disappoint people. We would like to see the war with Ukraine end,” Trump said, during an interview with conservative radio host Glenn Beck.
Ratcliffe is one of the highest-ranking US officials to visit Russia since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine started in 2022.
His Aug 25 visit came amid an escalation in Moscow’s offensive in Ukraine, with attacks this summer increasing the civilian death toll, while US-brokered peace talks have stalled.
During his visit, Ratcliffe also discussed the war with Iran, warning of additional sanctions if the Strait of Hormuz doesn’t reopen to shipping traffic, CBS News reported, citing multiple people familiar with the matter.
The Kremlin said on Aug 26 that Ratcliffe had “contacts” with Russia’s special services on his visit to Moscow but did not meet President Vladimir Putin.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin was briefed on the talks but refused to say whether the Ukraine war was raised.
“Contacts through the intelligence services are a positive development in and of themselves. It is too early to say how this will affect the process of resolving the crisis in our relations,” Peskov said.
The last time a CIA director visited Moscow was in November 2021 – when William Burns warned Russia against sending troops into Ukraine.
Weeks later, the Kremlin launched its attack that turned into Europe’s worst conflict since World War II.
The CIA has also been involved in prisoner swap deals with Russia, including a major exchange in mid-2024.
The war in Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands and the Kremlin has refused to ease its maximalist demands of seizing the rest of eastern Ukraine and keeping Crimea.
Trump dismissed suggestions that Ratcliffe was discussing other issues such as Russia testing the resolve of NATO or the US campaign to ramp up economic pressure on Iran.
“He is not in there for any of the things that you said, now something may come out, you know, out of it,” Trump told Beck.
“We’re working very hard to get that war ended, and frankly, they both want to see it ended at this point,” the US president said. AFP

articles.title: Glide bomb then infiltrate. This is Russia’s new way of war.
articles.body:
- In 2022, Russians fired artillery then advanced in vehicles
- Four years later, they launch glide bombs then advance as small teams of infantry
- Ukrainian drones stand in their way, and that's why drone operators are the main targets of Russian firepower before and during the advance
On Monday, a small team of Russian infiltrators reportedly slipped 10 km behind the line of contact between Russian and Ukrainian troops just north of Kostiantynivka in eastern Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast.
Sneaking into the town of Druzhkivka, 10 km north of Kostiantynivka along the H20 highway, the Russians reportedly ambushed, captured and executed a group of three or four unarmed Ukrainian drone operators.
It's possible the drone operators had just arrived in Druzhkivka when the Russians appeared. According to analyst and mapper AMK Mapping, Ukrainian drone operators pulled out of the village of Oleksijevo-Druzhkivka—which lies between Kostiantynivka and Druzhkivka—owing to the increasing threat from Russian KAB glide bombs. "It's likely that Russian forces monitored the withdrawals of Ukrainian drone operators and sent in [an infiltration group] after the new position was identified," AMK Mapping concluded.
The atrocity underscores the Russian military's new approach to ground warfare as Russia's wider war on Ukraine grinds through its 54th month. An army that once counted on its own artillery to suppress enemy artillery in order to allow mechanized forces to advance now uses precision bombs, small cruise missiles, tiny drones, and, yes, some artillery to suppress the Ukrainian drone teams that represent the main obstacle to a swift Russian advance.
And when the Russian firepower manages to suppress Ukrainian drone operators, allowing small teams of infantry to advance, the infantry's objective is often to take out the same drone operators whose suppression was a necessary pre-condition of any successful assault.
In short, the Ukrainians largely defend with drones. That means the Russians are fixated on first striking the drone teams in order to prevent them from launching their tiny lethal robots—and then, when they can, assaulting the drone teams' positions in order to capture or kill them. Or capture then kill them, as reportedly happened in Druzhkivka.
The Russians have learned the hard way that they can't advance without first finding and attacking Ukrainian drone operators. That hard experience has driven a profound transformation of the Russian way of war in just the last few years.
Precision suppression
As 2025 wore into 2026, Ukrainian forces finally deployed enough $500 drones to effectively halt any sustained Russian advance along the 1,200-km gray zone stretching across eastern and southern Ukraine. Between February and July, the Russians captured around 260 sq km of Ukrainian soil, according to a tally by the Black Bird Group. That's barely a fifth as much ground as they seized in the same six months in 2025.
Realizing they couldn't just fire an artillery barrage and then roll out the tanks the way they used to, the Russians have mostly parked their thousands of armored vehicles. Now they advance in small teams of lightly equipped infantry that, Russian commanders reason, stand a better chance of avoiding detecting and destruction by drones.
"Broadly speaking, current Russian military theory appears to emphasize restoring the ability to maneuver," Sidharth Kaushal and Sam Cranny-Evans wrote in a new study for the Royal United Services Institute in London. But the infantry infiltrators who do most of the maneuvering these days don't march out without support. A lot of it.
In the early months of the wider war in 2022 and 2023, the Russians counted on artillery—lots of artillery—to support the maneuver forces. But massed artillery is just as exposed to drone attack as massed tanks are, so Russian fire support has had to evolve, too.
Trending Now
Today, the Russians still fire artillery from fewer but more spread-out guns. But they also launch their own drones, small cruise missiles, and—perhaps most important—KAB glide bombs to force Ukrainian defenders, including drone teams, into their dugouts before the infantry dash across the gray zone. "Russian theorists appear to see the solution in highly mobile units designed to exploit lower-risk tunnels created by
precision strike," Kaushal and Cranny-Evans explained.
It's explosive choreography requiring careful communication between the infantry, the artillery, drone teams and the air force. "Sustaining momentum in the face of adversary precision strike is a considerable challenge," Kaushal and Cranny-Evans wrote. But a necessary one as the Russian military "contemplates how it can break the current positional deadlock" in Ukraine "and avoid future ones."
But when it works, it works to catastrophic effect for Ukrainian defenders. As those unfortunate, murdered drone operators found out.
The suppress-then-advance method, but with precision munitions and small teams of infiltrators, works for both sides, of course. The Ukrainians can do it, too—and they recently did in some unspecified sector of the gray zone.
On the same day the Russians executed those drone operators, fellow Ukrainian drone pilot Dmytro Putiata reported a small Ukrainian mechanized advance. "At one of the direction at the front line, one of the Ukrainian brigades used four [infantry fighting vehicles] during the attack," Putiata wrote. "They have managed to break through up to three km; dismounted infantry and all of the vehicles managed to retreat."
They break through with the help of friendly drones units that suppressed Russian troops along the assault route, Putiata explained. "How did they manage not to be targeted by drones? The battlefield was prepared for that."

articles.title: US Senator Blumenthal hopes bill imposing sanctions on Russia to be passed in Sept
articles.body:
U.S. Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal expressed hope that the House of Representatives will pass the bill he co-sponsored with Lindsey Graham to strengthen sanctions against Russia and Iran this September.
According to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent, he made this statement at a press conference in Kyiv on Tuesday.
Blumenthal said that during his previous visit to Ukraine in May, he had pledged to redouble efforts to secure passage of the sanctions bill. Now that the Senate had approved it, he said he was returning with even greater determination to ensure that the House of Representatives also passed the legislation, expressing hope that this would happen in September.
He said the House would resume work in September and said he was in close contact with its leadership. Blumenthal expressed hope that a decision on the bill would be taken then, adding that the efforts he had promised during his previous visit had indeed been intensified.
The senator also said he had met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and encouraged him to remain open to talks with members of the House of Representatives, just as he had communicated with senators. According to Blumenthal, Zelenskyy was willing to speak with House members.
Blumenthal recalled Zelenskyy's visit to the United States, during which the Ukrainian president met senators behind closed doors and was present for the vote on the bill. He said Zelenskyy's reaction to the vote had been inspiring and moving, and expressed hope that he would engage with members of the House in the same way. Blumenthal added that when he suggested this, Zelenskyy readily agreed.
He said he hoped Zelenskyy might hold such talks during a visit to New York and the United Nations, or at another suitable time.
Blumenthal concluded that he would return to the United States with concrete evidence of how important the sanctions bill was.
As reported, on August 7, the U.S. Senate approved Lindsey Graham's bill to strengthen sanctions against Russia and Iran. The bill was sent to the House of Representatives.
Graham, a Republican from South Carolina, has been among Ukraine's most outspoken allies in Congress during the long-running conflict with Russia, and this bill aims to increase economic pressure on Moscow over its military invasion of Ukraine.
The bill also includes expanded sanctions against Iran, which President Donald Trump had insisted upon.
The bill calls for the imposition of 100% secondary tariffs against countries that continue to purchase Russian oil and gas. This primarily refers to China and India.
In addition, the bill provides for sanctions against Russia's "shadow fleet" of tankers, Russian financial institutions – including the Central Bank of Russia – as well as major state-owned energy projects, specifically Yamal LNG, Arctic LNG-1, Arctic LNG-2, and Arctic LNG-3.
Before the vote, Ukrainian President Zelenskyy, who was at the Capitol, met with all the senators and urged them to support the bill, which was introduced by the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham. Afterward, Zelenskyy was present in the chamber during the vote.

articles.title: France is not ready to face cheap drones yet, warns top general
articles.body:
PARIS — France is not yet ready to face cheap, mass-produced threats like drones, the country's chief of defense staff, Gen. Fabien Mandon, warned Wednesday.
Defending in a financially sustainable manner against low-cost weapons manufactured in bulk, including Iranian-made Shahed drones, has been one of the main challenges for Western armed forces since the war in Ukraine started.
"We have enemies who have developed a large number of low-cost solutions that will wear down our models," Mandon said at an event organized by France's main business lobby Medef. "We’re not there yet. It’s nothing catastrophic, we’re still at peace. But we need to make this move."

NATO arsenals have long been composed of high-tech, sophisticated missiles worth several million dollars each, which land forces, navies and warplanes have been firing against unmanned aerial vehicles worth just tens of thousands of dollars. Now, the main goal is to significantly reduce the so-called cost per kill, meaning how much money has been spent to neutralize a threat.
Most recently, the French air force used costly missiles against cheap Iranian drones sent toward Gulf countries.
French legacy arms companies such as MBDA, as well as startups including Alta Ares and Harmattan AI, are working on lower-cost, mass-producible weapons to counter such threats.
"Our defensive weapons are not produced in sufficient quantities to stop these waves of saturation," the French general said. He added that he was working to accelerate the French armed forces' use of drones.
Defense companies "have to be hungry and adaptable in a fast-paced world, where our competitors adapt quickly," Mandon told the audience.

articles.title: What to Know About the Apparent Iranian Threat Against Barron Trump
articles.body:
The U.S. Secret Service said it was aware of a video broadcast by Iranian state media that appeared to threaten President Donald Trump’s youngest son, Barron.
“The U.S. Secret Service is aware of the video and investigates anything that can be perceived as a threat toward our protectees,” Secret Service spokesperson Nate Herring said in a statement. “Out of concern for operational security, we do not discuss matters of protective intelligence.”
According to the U.K.-based news outlet Iran International, the nearly three-minute clip—which starts with a graphic that reads “Where to Kill Barron Trump”—describes efforts to reach the President’s 20-year-old son, whom the video narrator claims is under surveillance.
The video also references several locations related to Barron Trump, such as his place of study and the Trump Tower in New York, as well as his security arrangements. The narrator also suggests a $10 million reward connected to efforts against Barron Trump.
TIME could not independently verify the claims made in the video, which provided no evidence that Barron Trump was actually under surveillance or that anyone had successfully compromised his security. The White House referred TIME to the Secret Service when asked for a response to the apparent threat against Barron Trump.
CNN first reported that the Secret Service was aware of the segment, which aired over the weekend on state-run Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting. IRIB operates under the Supreme Leader's control.
The segment follows a similar video released in July by the IRGC-affiliated Tasnim News Agency that focused on First Lady Melania Trump. That video depicted purported vulnerabilities in her security and ended with the words: ‘Barron Trump, wait for us!’”
Trump has been the subject of such threats from Iran since his first term. Iranian officials have repeatedly threatened Trump since he ordered the airstrike that killed Iranian General Qasem Soleimani, the commander of Iran’s elite Quds Force, in early 2020.
Threats intensified after the U.S. and Israel launched strikes against Iran in late February, killing Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei during the opening phase of the war. His son and successor, Mojtaba Khamenei, has vowed to avenge his death.
Images depicting the deaths of Trump and members of his family have since featured prominently in Iranian calls for revenge.
Last month, a mural in Tehran’s Palestine Square depicted members of the First Family above coffins draped in American flags. The same month, in Enqelab Square, the site of pro-Khamenei demonstrations, a billboard appeared to show Trump’s body in a coffin.
“I don’t think it’s any secret—it’s been in the media that Iran has publicly said they want to kill President Donald Trump,” U.S. Secret Service Deputy Director Matt Quinn told reporters at an event in July.
Earlier this month, the President confirmed that he had secretly switched planes as he left a NATO Summit in Türkiye in July based on a possible Iranian threat.
In response to the Iranian threats on his life, Trump has warned that any Iranian attempt to assassinate him would result in the ‘decimation’ and ‘destruction’ of Iran.

articles.title: Iskander Russia fired at Kyiv Oblast in July held 62 American parts. Ukraine has now named more than 100 Russian ballistics producers and wants its allies to sanction all of them
articles.body:
Ukraine has drawn up a list of those who build Russia's ballistic missiles and wants all of them sanctioned by its allies. Kyiv is asking partners to impose sanctions on more than 100 Russian ballistics producers, presidential sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk said at a press conference in Kyiv, according to Ukrinform.
The demand rests on physical evidence. An Iskander that Russia fired at Kyiv Oblast on 10 July held more than 140 foreign components, 62 of them American, alongside parts from Switzerland, Germany, Taiwan, China, and Japan, Vlasiuk reported in July. Most were made recently, which means the parts are still reaching Russia. Naming the factories is Ukraine's attempt to close the gap at the production end rather than chase each shipment.
The plan runs on synchronization
The commissioner laid out several parts of the plan at the press conference. The first is getting the same producers sanctioned everywhere at once, so a firm blocked in one country cannot operate through another. He said the files were handed to partners a few weeks ago, and Ukrainian specialists expect to identify every producer on allied lists by September or October.
The plan also covers what Vlasiuk called kinetic sanctions, meaning strikes on Russian defense-industry sites. He named the Kamensky Combine, which makes components for rocket fuel, as one such target.
The critical parts are still foreign
Ukraine keeps finding Western microelectronics in identified Russian ballistics, including Iskander-M missiles and those used by the S-400 system, with parts traced to the US, Japan, Germany, Taiwan, France, Britain, and Switzerland. The most sensitive elements are the Kometa satellite navigation system and autonomous inertial guidance units, which run on American, Swiss, and French microelectronics.
Ballistics is the most demanding product for quality and precision, Vlasiuk said, which is why those two systems are the chokepoint.
Ukraine wants smaller packages, sooner
The commissioner asked partners to adopt more stringent export controls, up to licensing or banning the export of sensitive components to third countries that help Russia evade sanctions. Ukraine has also compiled a list of more than 10 critical materials, including ammonium perchlorate, aluminum powder, and tungsten, as well as the numerically controlled machine tools Russia needs to build the missiles.
The EU has already begun work on a large 22nd sanctions package. Ukraine is urging it not to wait, asking instead for an interim ballistics package in September and another in October, moving in small steps as Ukraine, Britain, and Canada already do.

articles.title: Qatar PM to visit Tehran to pursue mediation efforts
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Qatar PM to visit Tehran to pursue mediation efforts
Qatar's prime minister will visit Tehran on Thursday in an effort to relaunch diplomacy after the US and Iran traded recriminations over Washington's promise to increase economic pressure on Tehran by targeting its trade partners for sanctions.
Qatar, a Gulf neighbour of Iran and a US ally, has served as a back-channel negotiator for the warring parties and played a direct role in securing the June ceasefire that briefly led to a cessation of hostilities.
The visit comes as the war nears its sixth month with fighting largely paused but no diplomatic breakthrough in sight. The two sides remain at odds over control of the Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint for global oil supplies that Tehran has used as leverage.
The memorandum of understanding broke down in part because of differences over the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman where one-fifth of the world's oil supplies passed before the war began on 28 February. The guns have gone mostly silent - the US military's Central Command has not reported any attacks on Iran for nearly a month. Washington appears to be leaning more on economic pressure by announcing plans to cut Iran off from its trading partners with increased sanctions.
Hormuz oil flows have fallen to a three-month low, with just 5 million barrels per day transiting on Monday, according to the latest ship-tracking data. Before the war, the strait carried roughly 20 million barrels per day of crude oil. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday that Iran and Oman had agreed how to share the waterway and its revenues, but a senior Iranian source later said the two countries were still working on the details of an agreement.
Despite an aerial bombardment earlier in the war that severely diminished Iran's conventional forces, Tehran has maintained enough missile and drone capability to attack Gulf neighbours that house US military bases and disrupt oil tankers in the strait.
The UN's International Maritime Organization has reported 70 incidents in the Strait of Hormuz since 28 February that have killed 19 seafarers.
Thousands of others have died, mostly in Iran and Lebanon, since the US and Israel attacked Iran with the stated goals of overthrowing the Iranian government and destroying its nuclear and missile capabilities.
Mediator
Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman al-Thani will discuss the continuation of Qatar's mediation efforts and other developments in the region during his visit to Tehran on Thursday, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said.
Qatar's Foreign Ministry spokesperson said on X that Sheikh Mohammed would also address freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the need to return to the status quo before 28 February, while also discussing with Iranian officials ways to "de-escalate tensions and create the conditions conducive to dialogue."
The international waterway was open to free navigation before the war, but Iran has retained its control of the strait as leverage and a revenue source, seeking to charge ships a commission, which the US has opposed.
"An agreement with Oman over the Strait of Hormuz has not been finalised," the senior Iranian source told Reuters, adding that the talks were continuing on the details of an accord.
That seemed to contradict a statement by Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesperson for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, who said Iran and Oman had "reached results that are acceptable to both sides" on controlling the strait and its revenues.
Mohebbi said the strait would remain shut unless the US met Tehran's conditions under the interim ceasefire, or memorandum of understanding, that the two sides signed in June before it unravelled. Those conditions include an end to the US blockade on Iranian ports, compensation and removal of sanctions.
Iran and Oman have held on-and-off talks for weeks about controlling traffic through the strait. Tehran and Washington have each tried to assert control over the channel, imposing separate blockades.
(Reuters)

articles.title: Zvook covers Ukraine’s skies for under €50 million. Now, it has started testing hydrophones underwater
articles.body:
The Ukrainian company that taught Ukraine to hear Russian drones is now learning to listen underwater. Zvook, which develops acoustic systems for detecting drones and missiles, has begun testing hydrophones to detect vessels and other underwater objects by sound, the company said on LinkedIn.
Zvook built its name on land. Its acoustic sensors cover Ukraine at 1,000 meters and below for less than 50 million euros, a system NATO's assistant secretary-general for operations, Tom Goffus, called crazy for its cost-effectiveness. Lithuania chose the same Ukrainian acoustic technology for deployment in 2026 after Russian drones entered its airspace.
The approach stays passive
Zvook says its underwater method emits nothing, unlike traditional sonar. Active sonar sends sound into the water and listens for its return. The company's system only listens to the acoustic environment and uses the information already present in it.
That principle is familiar to the company from the air. Underwater, almost everything else changes: sound propagation, background noise, reflections, environmental conditions, and acoustic signatures create a different detection problem.
Testing comes before any product
The company says its focus now is not a finished product but real-world data. It is working out which objects can be reliably detected and classified, and where a distributed passive underwater acoustic system could have practical value.
Possible applications range from maritime security and vessel awareness to the protection of ports and critical underwater infrastructure, the company explained. Zvook added that it is seeking commercial joint testing with defense organizations, maritime operators, and infrastructure owners.
The company frames it as one method across domains
Zvook cast the shift as continuity rather than a new line of work. From listening to the sky to acoustic tracking, and now beneath the surface, the domain changes, but the principle stays the same: passive, always listening, emitting nothing, the company said.

articles.title: Why August 1991 failed to bring peace between Russia and the West
articles.body:
Why August 1991 failed to bring peace between Russia and the West
Thirty-five years have passed since the dramatic events of August 1991 in Moscow which marked, more clearly than any later declaration or diplomatic ceremony, the end of the era we call the Cold War.
The failed ‘August Coup’ attempt to preserve the Soviet Union made continuation of the old confrontation impossible given one of its principal participants had effectively left the battlefield. Everything that followed, including the formal dissolution of the USSR in December 1991, merely recorded a change that had already taken place.
The essential fact was that the Soviet Union, and subsequently Russia, could no longer sustain the material and political foundations required to continue the struggle. There were many reasons for this, but foremost among them was the exhaustion of the Soviet model of state governance.
Moscow therefore chose to end the confrontation. This was historically unusual because Russia hadn’t been defeated on the battlefield or forced to surrender, and the Cold War ended because of internal political change and a voluntary decision by the Soviet leadership.
Paradoxically, this peaceful ending helped make a future confrontation more likely. The principal reason was simple: the Western powers, led by the United States, regarded the end of the Cold War as a victory, but Russia didn’t regard itself as a defeated country. That contradiction became one of the central problems of the post-Cold War order.
Great nuclear powers such as Russia, the United States, and China cannot realistically be defeated militarily without risking mutual destruction, thus the greatest threats to such states therefore tend to come from within through political dysfunction, economic weakness, poor governance, and social instability.
We can see something similar today in the United States. It remains the strongest individual power in the international system, but domestic conflict increasingly limits the effectiveness of its foreign policy. Meanwhile, China places internal stability and development at the center of its strategic thinking precisely because its leaders understand that domestic cohesion ultimately determines external strength.
The same logic shaped the Cold War because once Washington and Moscow accumulated enormous nuclear arsenals, direct military conflict became irrational. The confrontation instead developed according to what George Kennan described as containment in restricting Soviet influence and applying pressure across numerous fronts while avoiding a direct war between the superpowers.
But we shouldn’t romanticize this arrangement because the Cold War was still a war in the political sense and the objective of the Soviet Union’s adversaries wasn’t simply peaceful coexistence, rather it was the containment and ultimately neutralization of their opponent.
From Moscow’s perspective, this amounted to a struggle against Russia itself, which at that particular historical moment existed politically and economically in the form of the Soviet state.
The relative stability created by nuclear deterrence certainly encouraged a degree of mutual respect as it forced both sides to search for peaceful solutions even during serious crises. However, none of this removed the fundamental Western strategic objective which was victory over the Soviet adversary.
When the Soviet Union disappeared, therefore, Western capitals naturally interpreted the event as the achievement of that objective, but the victory was incomplete.
Russia had lost the geopolitical struggle but had not been defeated in the traditional sense. Its territory hadn’t been occupied and its armed forces hadn’t surrendered, so Russians could therefore reasonably believe that the changes of 1989-91 were the result of decisions taken in Moscow rather than terms imposed by a victorious enemy and that distinction proved enormously important.
It also explains why comparisons with France after 1815 or Germany after 1945 are misleading as both countries were militarily defeated before being incorporated into new international systems established by the victors.
France was reintegrated into the European order after Napoleon because Russia, Britain, Austria, and Prussia quickly developed disagreements of their own so Paris could therefore play a useful balancing role within the Concert of Europe.
Nothing comparable existed after 1991 when the Western coalition was unusually united and organized around NATO under American leadership and there was no internal balance of power in which Russia could become an indispensable partner.
The comparison with West Germany after 1945 is even less convincing. West Germany entered NATO and the emerging European institutions while foreign troops remained on its territory and its sovereignty was sharply constrained by the consequences of military defeat. No comparable arrangement could conceivably have been imposed upon Russia.
After 1991, the central problem was never resolved given that the West saw itself as the victor of the Cold War and wanted to construct a political order reflecting that victory. Russia, on the other hand, saw itself as a sovereign great power that had voluntarily abandoned the previous confrontation and expected to participate in the new order on that basis and these expectations were fundamentally incompatible.
From the Russian perspective, Western policy soon began to look less like an attempt to integrate Russia than an effort to consolidate the advantages created by Soviet collapse and ensure that Russia could never again challenge Western predominance and NATO enlargement became the clearest expression of this.
The decision to begin moving the alliance eastward was taken in January 1994, barely two years after the dissolution of the Soviet Union. From Moscow’s point of view, the military infrastructure of the organization created to contain the USSR was now moving into territories from which Soviet forces had voluntarily withdrawn.
Western governments insisted that enlargement was defensive and that sovereign states had every right to choose their alliances, but those arguments were never persuasive in Moscow. Russian policymakers increasingly interpreted NATO expansion as the construction of a territorial and military base that could be used against Russia in a future confrontation and this was the contradiction created by 1991.
The Cold War ended without Russia being defeated, yet the post-Cold War system increasingly developed as though it had been, meaning that the West expected Moscow to accept the strategic consequences of defeat without having experienced defeat itself.
Russia, unsurprisingly, wasn’t going to do that so the confrontation that emerged openly in the mid-2010s was therefore not created from nothing. Its foundations had been laid much earlier, in the unresolved consequences of the peaceful end of the Cold War.
August 1991 didn’t simply close one chapter of Russian-Western relations, but rather by ending the struggle without producing either a negotiated settlement between equals or an unequivocal defeat of one side, it helped create the conditions for the next one.
This article was first published by Vzglyad.ru, translated and edited by the RT team.

articles.title: Italy, France agree to supply four Samp-T air defense systems to Ukraine — newspaper
articles.body:
ROME, August 26. /TASS/. Italy and France have agreed to supply four Samp-T air defense systems to Ukraine and will allow Kiev to manufacture Aster 30 missiles, the newspaper La Repubblica writes.
According to the publication, the upcoming 13th Italian military aid package for Ukraine, scheduled for approval in October, will also include Aster 30 missiles from Italian arsenals, as well as Kronos radars and Italian-made Samp-T components.
All new systems are expected to be delivered by the beginning of next year. According to the newspaper, the Ukrainian armed forces already have two Samp-T systems at their disposal, for which ammunition has not been supplied since the summer of 2025 due to the depletion of national stockpiles. However, the domestic production pace has been accelerated, and a decision has been made to transfer Kiev to self-sufficiency.
According to the newspaper, the entire operation will cost 3 billion euros and will be structured as a purchase financed by a loan from the so-called EU for Ukraine Fund.
The publication notes that Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, unlike her European partners, is trying to conceal the fact that military aid is being provided, even though it is intended exclusively for defensive purposes. The government’s official statement on support for Ukraine refers to the supply of civilian-use materials.
The form of the decree--while keeping the list of supplies confidential--will allow the government, on the one hand, to avoid the lengthy procedure for approving arms exports. On the other hand, from a political standpoint, this reduces the risk of friction within the ruling coalition, in which the Lega (League) party has repeatedly spoken out against military supplies.
Meloni is also trying not to irritate public opinion in the year when the election campaign begins ahead of the parliamentary vote, the dates of which could be shifted from the fall of 2027 to the spring, the newspaper writes.

Italy arrests Frenchman after anti-tank missiles found in van

AI generated
ROME - A Frenchman was arrested in Italy on arms trafficking charges after a police check found three anti-tank missiles and other military equipment in his van, authorities said Aug 26.
The man, identified as Regis Normand, 46, was arrested in the southern port of Bari in June and remains in custody, prosecutors told AFP.

articles.title: F-35s from Misawa Deploy for First Red Flag in Alaska
articles.body:
The 13th Fighter Squadron from Misawa Air Base, Japan, deployed its new F-35A fighters to a major exercise for the first time, sending them to Pacific Air Forces’ premier air combat training event: Red Flag-Alaska.
It’s a key milestone in Misawa’s transition to the F-35 from its longtime fleet of F-16 CJs, used for the “Wild Weasel” suppression of enemy air defense mission. Eventually the 35th Fighter Wing at Misawa will get 48 F-35s.
These are the first F-35s the Air Force has stationed overseas in the Indo-Pacific region, and they are based strategically close to China, North Korea, and Russia. They will play a key role there integrating with other services and allies—both of whom also participated in Red Flag-Alaska, a regular two-week exercise that takes place multiple times a year
At this edition, the 13th Fighter Squadron focused on its SEAD mission. Alongside it, the 90th Fighter Squadron out of Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Alaska, flew its F-22s. Marine Fighter Attack Squadron 225 out of Marine Corps Air Station Yuma, Ariz., used their F-35Bs for counter-air and strike missions in the exercise, and Marine Fighter Attack Squadron 251 from MCAS Cherry Point, N.C., flew F-35Cs for joint force integration and homeland defense measures.
The 65th Aggressor Squadron out of Nellis Air Force Base, Nev. flew its F-35As as “red air” operating against U.S. and allied paricipants, as did the 18th Aggressor Squadron of Eielson Air Force Base, Alaska, using their F-16s.
This is the third and final iteration of Red Flag-Alaska this year. The exercise mainly takes place in the Joint Pacific Alaska Range Complex with 77,000 square miles of airspace, compared to the main Red Flag exercise at Nellis Air Force Base, Nev., which uses theNevada Test and Training Range and its 12,000 square miles of airspace.
“The tactical execution performed at Red Flag-Alaska complements that at Nellis by allowing forces to project power across massive distances, much like the Pacific theater,” Air Force spokesperson Capt. Grace Banas told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email. “These maneuvers help refine rapid power projection over intercontinental distances, ensuring our forces remain resilient and prepared to respond to dynamic regional security challenges.”
The JPARC also challenges exercise participants with “movable electronic threat emitters to mimic the complex digital signatures and tactical mobility of adversarial Integrated Air Defense Systems,” Banas wrote. These emitters give participants realistic electromagnetic training, a key challenge when conducting missions against peer-level adversaries in real-world combat.
Red Flag exercises started in 1975, growing out of the Vietnam War exercise that ran from 1969-1973 known as Exercise Coronet Organ, which sought to solve the problem of the first 10 combat flights being the most dangerous for fighter pilots by putting them into demanding, realistic, simulated combat scenarios.
The F-35 participated in its first Red Flag exercise at Nellis in 2017 and in Alaska in 2020.
Nellis, which typically hosts three editions of the main Red Flag exercise every year, has only hosted one in 2026, in February.

articles.title: Russia’s fleet is set to get 150 uncrewed vessels in 2026, and possibly 230. Sanctions are holding the build back
articles.body:
Russia is trying to build the weapon Ukraine used against it. The Russian fleet is set to receive more than 150 uncrewed surface vessels in 2026, with the state order possibly rising to 230 units, Ukraine's Defense Intelligence told Oboronka.
Ukraine's naval drones drove Russia's Black Sea Fleet out of its main base. Magura strike drones operated by Defense Intelligence sank or damaged more than a dozen Russian vessels and forced the fleet to relocate from Sevastopol to Novorossiysk, roughly 300 kilometers east.
Russia is now ordering the same class of weapon in volume, three years after Ukraine first attacked Sevastopol with drone boats in October 2022.
Intelligence lists Russia's priorities
Ukraine's Defense Intelligence has identified what Russia is prioritizing in its uncrewed surface vessel program. Those are building universal drones from Russian-made components, integrating protected communications and artificial intelligence, and increasing the vessels' operating range.
Sanctions slow the build
Russian production is held back by a shortage of electronic components caused by sanctions, according to the agency. Moscow is finding it harder to import and to develop communications resistant to electronic warfare, Ukraine's Defense Intelligence said.
Limits on Starlink access may also have shaped Russia's naval drone development, the agency added. Russian forces had actively used the terminals to control uncrewed systems.
The imitation runs behind the original
Ukraine unveiled the Magura V11, the largest boat in the family, at its Independence Day drone parade on 24 August.
Rather than ramming ships like the one-way craft that cleared the Black Sea Fleet from Sevastopol, the V11 carries and launches other drones and stays at sea up to seven days.
UFORCE said the drone carries up to 2,200 kg (about 4,850 pounds) and can stay at sea for up to seven days. The company built it for reconnaissance, surveillance, support of landing operations, and resupplying fuel and equipment to other naval drones.

articles.title: US Navy funds new CHAOS anti-ship weapon
articles.body:
The US Navy has awarded two contracts to develop the CHAOS maritime strike system, a low-cost exportable weapon intended to enter production in a ground-launched configuration by 2028.
The US Navy has awarded development contracts to CoAspire and Zone 5 for a new affordable maritime strike weapon intended from the outset for use by allied and partner nations, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The Coalition Heterogeneous Affordable Offensive Strike programme, known as CHAOS, is being managed by the Navy’s Precision Strike Weapons programme office, PMX-201, under Program Acquisition Executive Munitions. According to a US Navy news update, the objective is to produce a low-cost, scalable precision-strike capability that can be supplied rapidly to international partners facing growing anti-ship requirements.
CoAspire and Zone 5 are described by the Navy as non-traditional defence industry entrants. Their contracts were placed through Other Transaction Authority arrangements, a procurement mechanism frequently used by the Pentagon for prototype and development activity outside some of the requirements associated with conventional acquisition contracts. The Navy says the approach is intended to accelerate development while maintaining competition and bringing new suppliers into the precision-weapons industrial base.
Captain Sarah Abbott, PMX-201 programme manager, said, as quoted in the news update: “As adversaries increasingly deploy advanced area denial systems, coalition and allied forces face significant challenges in maintaining credible, modern, and affordable anti-ship capabilities.”
She added: “CHAOS closes this capability gap, by delivering a highly capable, adaptable, and exportable maritime strike solution that overcomes present day obsolescence and supply chain challenges.”
The programme differs from many previous US weapon developments in that international release requirements are being considered from the beginning rather than after a system has first been designed around American requirements. The Navy describes this as a “partner-first” acquisition strategy, with foreign governments being invited to help shape requirements through Foreign Military Sales cases while the weapon remains in development.
Van Hendrey, Portfolio Acquisition Executive Munitions, said: “These awards are the next milestone in developing an affordable maritime strike capability for security assistance partners, while expanding the defense industrial base through competition and accelerating a new entrant into the Navy’s precision-strike portfolio.”
He continued: “We saw significant demand from our international partners and worked with them to understand and incorporate their requirements from the outset. By building in exportability on day one, we are positioned to deliver an affordable warfighting capability to our partners at speed.”
The Navy has not disclosed the value of the two development awards, nor has it published detailed performance characteristics for CHAOS such as range, speed, seeker configuration, warhead or expected unit cost. It has, however, set out an initial pathway for fielding. The first configuration is planned as an expeditionary ground-launched weapon, with production expected to begin in 2028. Surface-launched versions are intended to follow, while an air-launched configuration could be developed if operational demand justifies it.
CHAOS is being built around the Modular Open Systems Approach and Weapon Open System Architecture standards. According to the Navy, that design philosophy is intended to make it easier to modify software and hardware as requirements change, rather than locking the weapon into a single fixed configuration. It could also allow different partner nations to integrate components or supporting systems according to their own industrial and operational requirements.
The service is explicitly leaving open the possibility of co-assembly and local integration, potentially allowing participating countries to carry out part of the manufacturing or final integration process domestically. That approach could make the programme attractive to governments seeking both a new maritime strike weapon and a greater degree of national industrial involvement.
Rear Admiral Ray Owens, Director of the Navy International Programs Office, said: “Our priority is building real, integrated capability with our allies and partners.”
He added: “We’re working to advance interoperability, strengthen joint deterrence, and enhance fleet readiness at the speed of relevance, while remaining fully aligned with our fleet’s operational needs.”
CoAspire and Zone 5 will now develop their respective solutions under the prototype contracts as the Navy works with interested partner governments on future requirements. The first major target remains production of an expeditionary ground-launched maritime strike capability in 2028, followed by expansion into naval surface launchers and potentially aircraft if the programme progresses as planned.

articles.title: CIA director warned Russia against attacking NATO members during Moscow visit - report
articles.body:
CIA Director John Ratcliffe's recent visit to Moscow was for the purpose of warning Russia against attacking any NATO members, sources familiar with the matter told CBS on Wednesday.
Ratcliffe also discussed Iran while in Russia, telling intelligence officials there that additional sanctions would be implemented by the US unless the Strait of Hormuz was reopened for shipping, the sources said.
A source familiar with the details of Ratcliffe's trip told The Jerusalem Post that Trump administration officials asked Ukraine several days ago to pause any strikes against Moscow and other cities from Monday through Wednesday.
CIA director did not meet with Putin during Moscow visit, Kremlin claims
Ratcliffe held talks with Russian intelligence officials during his visit to Moscow, but did not meet President Vladimir Putin, the Kremlin said on Wednesday.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Putin had been briefed on the outcome of Ratcliffe's talks, but declined to provide further details.
Peskov said it was also too early to say whether such contacts between the two countries' intelligence agencies could help pull US-Russia relations out of what he described as a "deep crisis."
Reuters, Jerusalem Post Staff, and Amichai Stein contributed to this report.

Ukraine Hammers Russian Missile Unit in Sweeping 16-Target Deep-Strike Barrage
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian missile unit along with airfields, oil facilities, military infrastructure and logistics sites as part of a sweeping long-range operation that hit 16 targets inside Russia over the past 24 hours, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on August 26.
The missile unit was among infrastructure Ukraine says is routinely used to launch attacks against Ukrainian territory, making it one of the most significant targets disclosed by Zelenskyy in the latest round of deep strikes.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Over the past day, our warriors imposed sanctions on 16 targets in Russia. In particular, there were long-range responses against oil facilities—Russia’s oil wallet that finances the war. They also struck airfields, a missile unit, and infrastructure that is constantly used to launch attacks against Ukraine. Our sanctions also hit a military enterprise and Russian logistics,” he said.
Zelenskyy has repeatedly referred to Ukraine’s long-range strikes as “sanctions,” arguing that attacks on oil infrastructure and other strategic facilities directly reduce Moscow’s ability to finance and sustain its war of aggression against Ukraine.
The latest campaign appears to have combined strikes against Russia’s military capabilities with attacks intended to increase the economic cost of the war.
“The war must return to where it came from. Ukraine responds to Russian strikes, and we do so in a way that ensures the cost of the war for the aggressor inevitably rises. We are justly reducing Russia’s capacity for aggression. I thank all the warriors involved for their accuracy! Glory to Ukraine!” Zelenskyy wrote.
Separately, Ukraine’s General Staff reported a series of strikes against Russian military infrastructure across occupied Ukrainian territory on August 25 and overnight into August 26.
In Kacha in occupied Crimea, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Kasta radar system. Another operation hit a Russian drone training center in occupied Luhansk.
Ukraine also targeted a Russian repair and recovery base in Pervomaiske in occupied Crimea, according to the General Staff.
A series of strikes hit Russian supply infrastructure, including a fuel and lubricants depot in Prychepylivka in the Luhansk region and logistics warehouses in Svobodne in the Donetsk region and Novoivanivka in occupied Crimea.
Ammunition depots were also struck in Staryi Krym and Velyka Novosilka in the Donetsk region.
In Chornomorske in occupied Crimea, Ukrainian forces hit a ground relay station used to support Russian Geran and Gerbera drones.
The General Staff said assessments of the damage caused by the strikes were still underway.

articles.title: Israeli arms, Iranian drones, Turkish oil: Azerbaijan’s high-stakes balancing act
articles.body:
“We cannot close our eyes and say there is no Iran, there is no Russia. There are.”
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Nargiz Mammadova, a research fellow in international relations at the CASPIA Center, was describing the reality Azerbaijan confronts whenever it looks at the map. Speaking with The Media Line in Jerusalem, she said decisions made in Moscow or Tehran cannot be dismissed as distant developments. Both countries border Azerbaijan, placing instability in either one directly inside Baku’s security calculations.
Mammadova was among 13 Muslim professionals from Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan brought to Israel by Sharaka, a nongovernmental organization founded after the 2020 Abraham Accords to promote people-to-people diplomacy between Israelis and communities across the Arab and Muslim worlds.
Holocaust remembrance and meetings about Israeli society were part of the visit, but regional security was never far from the discussion. For the Azerbaijani participants, Israel is one element of a crowded diplomatic picture that also includes Russia, Iran, Turkey, Armenia and the wider South Caucasus.
The result is a foreign policy built less around choosing sides than keeping several doors open. Azerbaijan buys Israeli weapons, regards Turkey as a vital ally, trades with Russia, shares a long border with Iran and is pursuing peace with Armenia after decades of conflict.
Azerbaijan is surrounded by countries at war
“If you look to the map in the South Caucasus, Azerbaijan has five neighbors, and two of them are into war situation, or kind of war situation,” Mammadova said.
She described the ability to work with competing powers as a defining characteristic of Azerbaijani diplomacy. Baku, she argued, cannot afford to organize its foreign policy around one dominant relationship.
Mammadova applied the same reasoning to Armenia, saying agreements between governments must be accompanied by “building bridges between people” and greater trust between the two societies.
Farid Shukurlu, an international law and security researcher and nonresident fellow at the Research Institute for European and American Studies, told The Media Line that his criticism was directed at the Iranian regime and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), not at Iranian society.
IRGC targeted Azerbaijan
“Even though Azerbaijan’s position was formally neutrality, the country was still targeted by the IRGC in the Nakhchivan enclave,” he said.
Nakhchivan is an Azerbaijani exclave separated from the rest of the country by Armenian territory. Azerbaijan said four drones arriving from Iran struck the region on March 5, injuring four people and damaging Nakhchivan International Airport and a school. Iran denied responsibility and promised an investigation.
The incident demonstrated, in Shukurlu’s view, that avoiding direct participation in a conflict does not necessarily protect Azerbaijan from pressure or military spillover from its southern neighbor.
Those concerns have contributed to stronger defense ties with Israel. Azerbaijan has purchased Israeli weapons for years and used Israeli-made systems during its conflicts with Armenian forces over Nagorno-Karabakh.
Shukurlu said “the military cooperation between Azerbaijan and Israel is at an all-time high,” but rejected suggestions that Baku would allow the relationship to turn Azerbaijani territory into a base for military action.
“It’s also in Azerbaijan’s national security concept not to get dragged into regional conflicts,” he said. “Azerbaijani territory will never be used against a third state.”
Balancing relations with Israel, Turkey
Baku faces a different balancing problem when relations deteriorate between Israel and Turkey. Ankara remains one of Azerbaijan’s closest political and security partners, while Israel has become an important supplier of military technology.
Shukurlu said Azerbaijani officials see no reason to sacrifice either relationship.
“Azerbaijan is not going to give up on Israel, Azerbaijan is not going to give up on Turkey, because these countries are equally important to our security, to our existence, and to our image in the international arena,” he said.
Energy makes the triangle even harder to separate.
Ibrahim Mammadov, head of the Turkic-Western Engagement Initiative and a visiting research fellow at the Danube Institute, pointed to the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline, which carries crude oil from Azerbaijan through Georgia to Turkey’s Mediterranean port of Ceyhan. Some of that oil is then loaded onto tankers bound for Israel.
“I do not believe that it will ever stop because, for Azerbaijan, it’s an extremely important pipeline,” he told The Media Line.
Closing the route would hurt Azerbaijan by restricting one of its principal export channels and Israel by reducing a major source of crude oil. Turkey receives transit and port benefits, while the state-owned Turkish Petroleum Corporation holds a stake in the pipeline consortium.
The same network that binds the three countries together economically also gives Baku a reason to prevent disputes between Israel and Turkey from becoming direct confrontations.
Azerbaijan has already hosted several rounds of talks between Israeli and Turkish officials seeking to prevent clashes in Syria, where both countries maintain competing security interests.
“We know that there have been formal and informal talks that were held in Baku,” Mammadov said.
He wants Azerbaijan to continue serving as a meeting place when its two partners cannot speak easily elsewhere.
“I hope they can be found in the middle ground.”
