articles.title: UK weapons and fighting vehicle jobs rise 51%
articles.body:
Employment supported by Ministry of Defence spending in weapons, ammunition and military fighting vehicle manufacturing rose from around 3,900 to 5,900 jobs in 2024/25, new government estimates show.
The number of UK jobs supported by defence spending in weapons, ammunition and military fighting vehicle manufacturing rose by around 51% in 2024/25, increasing by approximately 2,000 roles to 5,900, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The figures form part of the Ministry of Defence’s latest MOD-supported employment estimates and come as the Government seeks to expand domestic production of artillery ammunition, missiles and other weapons. The increase from roughly 3,900 to 5,900 jobs represents one of the sharper rises within the defence industrial figures, although the statistical category cited by the MOD combines weapons and ammunition manufacturing with military fighting vehicle production.
Across the wider defence economy, the Government estimates that MOD expenditure and the defence sector supported 26,000 more UK industry roles than in the previous year. The North West recorded nearly 4,000 additional jobs supported by defence expenditure, while the South East saw an increase of more than 3,000. The figures include both employment directly associated with defence activity and jobs supported through the wider supply chain.
The MOD says defence now accounts for or supports around 462,000 roles when Armed Forces personnel, civil servants and industry employment are considered together. The figures are estimates of employment associated with defence activity rather than a count of newly recruited MOD employees, and the geographical totals reflect the economic effects of defence expenditure across different parts of the UK.
The rise in weapons-related manufacturing employment comes as the Government attempts to rebuild what it describes as an “always on” sovereign munitions production capacity. The policy is intended to increase the ability of British industry to manufacture weapons such as artillery ammunition and missiles at sustained higher rates, rather than depending on production lines configured principally around smaller peacetime orders.
Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard said, as quoted in a news update: “These figures show that a rising defence budget is creating more good jobs across the UK. Defence is an engine for growth and our investments are driving reindustrialisation. As we increase our military readiness and capabilities we are generating good well-paid jobs nationwide.”
The employment increase comes alongside a broader expansion of planned defence industrial spending. The Defence Investment Plan commits £298 billion to UK defence over the next four years, with expenditure spanning munitions, shipbuilding, nuclear programmes and advanced technologies. How much of that expenditure ultimately flows to British manufacturing employment will depend on individual procurement decisions, supply-chain content and the pace at which planned programmes move into production.
The Government has placed particular emphasis on restoring domestic munitions capacity as European countries reassess stockpile requirements and the rate at which weapons could be consumed during a high-intensity conflict. Sustained production also affects the ability to replenish weapons supplied to allies and partners while maintaining sufficient stocks for Britain’s own forces.
The MOD separately points to the recently announced £8.4 billion commitment for the next generation of nuclear deterrent submarines, with the wider Defence Nuclear Enterprise supporting an estimated 47,000 jobs and more than 6,000 suppliers across the country. Shipbuilding, nuclear engineering and weapons production therefore account for distinct parts of the wider defence employment picture rather than a single manufacturing sector.
The 51% increase should consequently be read against the relatively small starting size of the weapons, ammunition and fighting vehicle category. An additional 2,000 supported jobs produces a large percentage rise, but the resulting total of 5,900 remains a small proportion of the 462,000 roles the Government associates with defence across the Armed Forces, Civil Service and industry.

articles.title: The German Far Right Is Poised for a Breakthrough
articles.body:
The German Far Right Is Poised for a Breakthrough
The AfD could do something next month that would mark a first in the country’s postwar history.
Imagine that it’s October 2026, and one of Germany’s 16 federal states has come under the control of a far-right government for the first time since the Nazi era. With an absolute majority in the state Parliament and one of its own installed as state premier, the Alternative for Germany, or AfD, quickly begins implementing its agenda. The interior minister announces an emergency remigration program: abolishing asylum, revoking the residence permit of any foreigner convicted of a crime, pledging to review all naturalization decisions made during this century, and incarcerating those designated for deportation. The government stops classifying Ukrainians as war refugees and ends their social benefits. European Union flags disappear from public buildings. The mainstream press is shunned in favor of influencers aligned with the party’s ideology. The government authorizes vigilante groups to act as an auxiliary police force in regions with high crime rates.
This hasn’t happened, but it’s not merely hypothetical either. The AfD is projected to win an election next month in Saxony-Anhalt, a central German state of some 2 million people. An anti-racism NGO in Berlin, the Amadeu Antonio Foundation, created this scenario based on the far-right party’s own election manifesto and the statements of its representatives. For decades, right-wing politics have carried particular weight in Germany, where atonement for the Holocaust includes mandatory education about the rise of National Socialism. The far right was long relegated to the fringes, its most ardent members easily identified as skinheads decked out in leather. But the AfD, founded in 2013 as a mild euroskeptic party led mostly by conservative economists opposed to eurozone bailouts, is now Germany’s most important right-wing force since the Nazis.
At the national level, the AfD is the most popular party, supported by more than a quarter of voters in recent polls. It leads both of the traditional broad-based parties, the center-right Christian Democrats and the center-left Social Democrats. Its base of support is in the formerly Communist east—generally poorer, older, and angrier than the rest of Germany. And that’s where it’s poised for a breakthrough later this summer. In past state elections, other parties have contorted themselves to keep the far-right faction out of governing coalitions, maintaining a so-called firewall even when the AfD has won the most votes. That may not be possible in Saxony-Anhalt, where ahead of a September 6 vote, the AfD is polling at more than 40 percent. If smaller parties fail to reach the required 5 percent threshold to enter Parliament, this kind of showing by the AfD could be enough for it to win an outright majority, meaning that it wouldn’t need cooperation from other parties to govern. Suddenly, Saxony-Anhalt would become a testing ground for AfD policies.
If the AfD doesn’t reach that threshold, the spotlight would turn to the Christian Democratic Union, the party of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. The Christian Democrats would face a dilemma: whether to breach the firewall and work with the AfD or join hands with the far-left party Die Linke in a last-ditch effort to keep the far right from taking power. In fact, the Christian Democrats have a policy, formalized in 2018 and known as an incompatibility resolution, against working with either party. Andreas Rödder, a historian who previously headed the center-right party’s fundamental-values commission, told me that the decision didn’t generate much controversy within the party at the time because the matter was mostly symbolic; the center-right party, then dominated by Chancellor Angela Merkel, had other choices for governing partners. At that time, German politics remained fairly stable, relatively speaking, as anti-establishment forces shook up other Western democracies. For many in Germany, this was a point of pride, a sign that the country had learned from its history, that it knew where political fanaticism led.
Less than a decade later, Germany no longer appears immune to extremism, and the stable politics that once attested to its moral redemption are “on the brink of being fundamentally shattered,” Rödder said. The country’s domestic intelligence agency has classified Saxony-Anhalt’s branch of the AfD as a right-wing extremist group. Some voters support the party because of that hard-right agenda. Others are drawn to it for contrarian reasons: to register their dissent against elite gatekeepers, whether in the security service, the judiciary, or the media. In this way, their vote is a version of the declaration once made by the Russian literary critic Vissarion Belinsky: “Negation is my god.”
“Every organ of elite opinion tells people they can’t vote for the AfD,” a German diplomat told me. “And many people respond by saying, ‘Hell yes, we can.’”
Why does an election in a relatively small German state matter? Because what happens in Germany matters. That’s been the nature of the German problem for almost two centuries—what to do with this country, larger and more prosperous than its neighbors, that has caused so much torment for Europe and for the world. The problem arose with the Franco-Prussian War and the unification of Germany in 1871. It returned in monstrous form during both world wars. And it recurred with German reunification in 1990.
The German question is back as the country breaks with postwar taboos. Germany is rearming, spending billions to turn its army into the strongest in Europe. Its steadfast support for Israel has been shaken by the extremism of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government. And in Saxony-Anhalt as well as other German regions, even if not yet nationally, the far right appears on the cusp of claiming power.
Germany’s situation isn’t unique; what’s striking in a country where historians have debated whether a Sonderweg, or “special path,” produced destructive nationalism is how much it mirrors what’s happening elsewhere in Europe. Marine Le Pen, the far-right French firebrand, is leading in polls ahead of a presidential election next year. Nigel Farage’s Reform UK remains in a strong position in Britain. Giorgia Meloni already leads a far-right government in Italy, representing a party that traces its roots to the country’s postwar neofascist movement. Saxony-Anhalt is following these same trends. But the circumstances command greater attention. As Henry Morgenthau Jr., President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s treasury secretary, titled his postwar book on the defeated Axis power, Germany Is Our Problem.
Saxony-Anhalt is sometimes called the heartland of German history. It’s the birthplace of the Protestant Reformation, where Martin Luther nailed his 95 theses to the church door in Wittenberg. Cities such as the capital, Magdeburg, were important centers of the Holy Roman Empire. In the 20th century, modernism flourished in the region, which has Germany’s highest concentration of Bauhaus architecture. It’s long been a hub of the chemical and coal-mining industries. During the Cold War, the territory fell on the eastern side of the Iron Curtain, and the state still faces structural problems left over from post-reunification deindustrialization and out-migration, including higher rates of poverty and unemployment than the national average. The psychic effect also lingers. Until 1990, there was no genuine democracy; freedom and civil rights were curtailed. “In some quarters,” Detlef Gürth, a member of the ruling Christian Democrats in Saxony-Anhalt’s state Parliament, told me, there is still a “pronounced desire for a ‘strongman,’ a messiah who dictates the course of action and takes care of everything.”
Two recent events crystallize the state’s misfortune and the feeling among many residents that things aren’t working. In December 2024, a Saudi-born doctor drove a rented SUV through a crowded Christmas market in Magdeburg, killing six people and injuring hundreds more. Authorities said the perpetrator was an anti-Islam activist sympathetic to far-right groups, but terrorist violence of any kind, the facts notwithstanding, played into the far right’s hands. The following year, the California-based Intel Corporation canceled plans for a €30 billion chip factory in Magdeburg, which would have been the biggest-ever foreign direct investment in Germany. The episodes were unrelated; the company said it had simply grown too fast, although a government minister also found an explanation in “Donald Trump’s ‘America First’ philosophy.” Together, however, they contributed to a gathering feeling of precarity and bad luck.
The AfD promises to shake up the system. Its 35-year-old front man, Ulrich Siegmund, is a perpetually smiling social-media sensation. He is a salesman by trade, the founder of a fragrance company called Berlin-Duftet, whose name means literally “Berlin smells good.” Der Spiegel, the prestigious German news magazine, recently branded him “the most dangerous man in Germany,” which turned out to be great publicity; at campaign events, he autographed copies of the magazine cover.
As Siegmund racks up likes on social media, he leaves the most incendiary topics to others in the party. When some members of the state AfD branch traveled to the United States last year to attend a gala of the Trump-aligned New York Young Republican Club, Siegmund stayed home. The party’s ideological engine in Saxony-Anhalt is said to be Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, a member of the state Parliament who has likened Islam to a fungus, condemned the “sacralization of the Holocaust,” and suggested that Jewish institutions are using Muslim immigration to achieve the “abolition of our people.” He has called AIDS patients the “price we pay for a decadent social model” and argued that the Bauhaus movement “raped the human need for comfort.” On foreign policy, Tillschneider sides with Russia in its assault on Ukraine, praising President Vladimir Putin as “a real man with a sound set of values” and insisting that Moscow is “defending itself.”
When I asked Tillschneider to explain his party’s success in the region, he said it didn’t stem from one particular issue or another but amounted to a rejection of the mainstream’s whole approach to policy making. He argued that the “established parties have formed a consensus against the interests of the citizens” and refuse to entertain ideas that go against their orthodoxy. The AfD is testing the limits of what’s acceptable in German political culture, especially on immigration. The party’s election manifesto declares ominously, “Our streets and squares are no longer safe.” And it promises a “deportation and remigration offensive.” The term remigration, once a fringe concept linked to ethnic cleansing, is now a focus of far-right immigration discourse, and has flexible meanings. Tillschneider defined it as “the maximum possible deportation within the framework of the constitutional order.” In addition to a “180-degree turn” in migration policy, the party is also vowing to revamp education and art, instill pride in German identity, and end the country’s “guilt complex.” The AfD also objects to the established parties’ anti-Russia policies and seeks to expand Russian-language instruction in schools and revive student exchanges with Russia.
The Christian Democrats, who currently govern Saxony-Anhalt in a coalition with the Social Democrats and the liberal Free Democrats, have struggled to respond. The state premier, Sven Schulze, took umbrage at the far right for “constantly belittling Saxony-Anhalt and acting as if everything here is doomed to failure.” AfD representatives can sense the desperation. Tillschneider said the firewall had become a “tomb wall” that the Christian Democratic Union has built for itself. He envisioned only two possibilities after the September election: either an AfD government or an “all-party government against us.” On this there seems to be some agreement. Gürth, the Christian Democratic lawmaker, said his party can’t justify cooperation with the AfD, which “operates like the Nazi Party” in its methods: “It exaggerates real or perceived problems, taps into public discontent, and paints a dystopian picture of Germany teetering on the brink of collapse. All other parties are blamed, and only the AfD can save Germany.”
In the scenario outlined by the Amadeu Antonio Foundation, an AfD-led government soon turns the state into a platform for international self-promotion, hosting conferences and opening offices in Washington and Moscow. Vice President Vance, who met with an AfD leader on the sidelines of the Munich Security Conference last year, visits the state and offers to support American companies that choose to invest in Saxony-Anhalt. In the next federal election, in 2029, the AfD wins. The party may soon get the chance to give this scenario a shot.

articles.title: Rebuilding Hope from War: South Korea's Heritage Strategy Offers Iran Key Lessons
articles.body:
Rebuilding Hope from War: South Korea's Heritage Strategy Offers Iran Key Lessons
How South Korea documented, restored, and revitalized war-damaged heritage
TEHRAN- Historical monuments are not merely symbols of a nation's identity; they are also testaments to that nation's resilience against the vicissitudes of history and narrators of its past experiences. Although in recent years, especially after the two World Wars, historical monuments have come under the umbrella of international protection, obligating global sensitivities for warring parties to preserve these sites in each other's territories, the inherently destructive nature of war, combined with its objectives which tend toward the annihilation of the enemy and consequently the erasure or at least weakening of their identity, has meant that this sector has not been spared from the negative effects of war damage.
Examining South Korea's approach to managing cultural heritage and reconstructing historical identity may offer a lesson for all those who have faced this predicament. This document is published as a strategic report by the Iran-South Korea Joint Chamber of Commerce, aiming to optimize and learn from this country's successful experience in overcoming the effects of war.
Rebuilding cultural heritage means clinging to history to restore the collective self-confidence of a society and holding onto a single unifying thread for social cohesion, despite all the ethnic, cultural, linguistic, and even religious diversity within a society.
In the Korean War (1950–1953), at least 351 Buddhist temples were damaged, 240 of which were completely destroyed; along with dozens of palaces, historical gates, and royal tombs. Nevertheless, seventy years later, South Korea has not only restored the vast majority of this heritage but has also turned cultural heritage preservation into an independent economic sector valued at 9.05 trillion won in 2025, with a cumulative target of 100 trillion won by 2030.
This report analyzes South Korea's strategy across five policy pillars—preventive documentation, pre-restoration engineering diagnosis, intergenerational transfer through technology, economic regeneration of ruins, and selective preservation of war scars—examining it within the context of its institutional structure, public-private financing models, and the broader vision of South Korea's Ministry of Culture, "Culture-K 2030". Subsequently, this experience is juxtaposed with the new reality confronting Iran's cultural heritage this year: damages from the recent war between the US and Israel against Iran affecting over 140 historical sites and monuments, including at least five sites inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. The report concludes with six specific and adaptable lessons for cultural heritage policy, financing, and economic regeneration in Iran.
It should be noted that this document is the fifth strategic report published by the Iran-South Korea Joint Chamber of Commerce, made available to the public for the benefit of experts, researchers, policymakers, and other interested parties.
1. Introduction: Dimensions of War Damage to Korea's Cultural Heritage
The Korean War did not only devastate cities and villages; it also targeted the historical memory of a nation. Royal palaces were damaged, Buddhist temples burned, and hundreds of valuable structures were reduced to rubble. At the war's end, South Korea was one of the poorest countries in the world; a nation that had simultaneously lost its economic infrastructure and a significant part of its historical identity.
A precise and unified monetary estimate of the total cost of post-war cultural heritage reconstruction in Korea is not available in public sources; however, the indicator presented later in this report—the growth of the 'Heritage-K' industry to a value of 9.05 trillion won in 2025—shows that the country transformed reconstruction from a 'restoration cost' into a 'productive economic asset'.
Korea's seventy-year experience on this path is summarized in five policy pillars, each examined below with evidence, supporting institutional structures, and considerations applicable to Iran.
2. Institutional and Financial Architecture: The Role of Government and the Private Sector
2.1. The Central Institution: Korea Heritage Service (KHS)
The Korea Heritage Service—operating until 1999 as the 'Cultural Properties Administration' and renamed in 2024—is under the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism. It plays a pivotal role in designating national treasures, financing restoration, and issuing permits for any changes to registered structures. This organization provides direct subsidies for the maintenance and restoration of 'nationally designated' properties and offers parallel financial support for seven strategic heritage regions (including the Baekje Historic Areas).
2.2. Public-Private Partnership Model
Research in cultural heritage governance identifies three contractual models in the experiences of countries like Korea, whose application varies depending on the type of asset:
· Service Contract: The private sector participates in conservation research, specialized restoration, or equipment maintenance; ownership and ultimate responsibility remain with the government.
· Construction and Restoration Contract: The private sector performs the physical restoration work, accepting execution risks; financing and long-term maintenance are the government's responsibility.
· Lease or Operation Contract: The asset is temporarily transferred to the private sector or a local entity for economic use (café, gallery, accommodation); the economic risk of operation is transferred to the private sector, but ownership and conservation standards remain with the government.
In other words, South Korea firmly retains 'ownership and determination of conservation standards' in government hands but delegates 'execution, economic operation, and technological innovation' largely to the private sector, local institutions, and community participation. A prime example of this model is the regeneration of the Bukchon neighborhood, implemented through financial cooperation between the government and private owners of traditional houses.
To strategize decision-making regarding cultural heritage, understanding the institutional structure that implements these policies is crucial, because without this architecture, none of Korea's technical solutions can be understood or replicated.
3. Five Strategic Pillars of South Korea's Experience
3.1. Pillar One: Save the Memory Before Reconstruction
Since the 1990s, South Korea has initiated a national project for the digital documentation of historical monuments. Using laser scanners, drones, and photogrammetry technology, thousands of historical structures have been recorded in 3D to create a digital backup of the country's history. This approach effectively acts as a 'national historical memory insurance'.
This approach's utility has been tested in recent crises: in the unprecedented spring 2025 wildfires in North Gyeongsang Province, Gounsa Temple (built in 681 AD) was severely damaged, leaving only 9 of its 30 buildings intact; however, the existence of prior 3D documentation enabled the formulation of a precise restoration plan—before the memory of the building's true form faded. South Korea also emergently evacuated and relocated 15 national treasures from endangered temples during these same fires.
3.2. Pillar Two: Examine the Building Before Restoration (HBIM)
Many mistakes in hasty reconstructions during the first post-war decades stemmed from a lack of precise information about structural conditions, materials, and hidden damages. To solve this, South Korea adopted HBIM (Historic Building Information Modeling) technology.
If 3D scanning can be considered 'photographing' a building, HBIM is essentially its 'complete medical file': material types, age of components, deterioration rate, repair history, column and beam conditions, moisture, and cracks are recorded in an integrated digital model. This allows experts to simulate and compare various restoration scenarios—in terms of cost, structural soundness, and preservation of historical authenticity—before any physical intervention.
This is a solution that could also be effective for Iran. In many of the country's historical monuments, damage from deterioration, earthquakes, moisture, or various incidents is not detectable by the naked eye. Deploying technologies like HBIM before any national reconstruction program—especially for structures damaged by the Imposed War in the western and southwestern regions—could prevent additional costs and non-transparent decision-making.
3.3. Pillar Three: Show History's Wounds to the New Generation
Newer generations of Koreans have not experienced the war and may take historical heritage for granted. Korea's solution was Augmented Reality (AR) technology. At many historical sites, visitors can scan a QR code and point their phone's camera at a structure, viewing various layers of its history—from its initial glory, through war destruction, to restoration phases—displayed on the screen. In this way, history transforms from an abstract narrative into a vivid and tangible experience.
3.4. Pillar Four: Turn Ruins into Economic Opportunities
One of South Korea's most creative actions has been repurposing war-torn and abandoned military spaces into art galleries, concert halls, cafés, museums, and cultural centers.
· Camp Greaves: This former US Army base near the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), occupied by US forces from 1953 to 2004, was transformed from 2013 onwards by the Gyeonggi Province initiative under the 'DMZ Peace Platform Project' into a cultural-artistic complex with public accommodations; its ammunition depot, bowling alley, and barracks now host exhibitions, traditional music concerts, and educational programs focused on commemorating peace.
· Bukchon Neighborhood, Seoul: The government implemented an extensive program to revitalize the historical fabric of this neighborhood by providing financial aid to private owners of traditional hanok houses. The result was unprecedented tourism growth; according to recent reports, in 2023 and 2024, the neighborhood hosted approximately 6.4 million visitors annually, compared to only about 6,100 local residents. This growth has been so remarkable that the main challenge for Seoul's city management in this area is now managing 'overtourism' and implementing time-based visitor restrictions, not a lack of tourists.
The message from the experience of revitalizing war-torn and neglected sites is that every ruin or abandoned military structure is not necessarily just a cost; it's a strategy for many war-affected areas. By converting barracks, bunkers, or damaged urban fabrics in war zones into cultural-tourist spaces—while simultaneously designing a financial and managerial structure—they can become sources of local income and employment instead of draining public funds. This is provided that planning involves the local community and private sector from the outset, rather than being solely a top-down government project or revenue model.
3.5. Pillar Five: Don't Erase All the Wounds
In Cheorwon, the former office building of the Workers' Party of Korea, severely damaged during the war and still showing bullet and destruction marks on its walls, was not fully restored but transformed into a venue for music festivals, art exhibitions, and peace programs.
This approach perhaps contains the deepest lesson from Korea's experience, resting on a clear policy principle: one hundred percent restoration is not always the desirable goal; some structures should remain in their damaged state to serve as living documents of collective memory.
The decision-making process regarding which building should be 'fully restored', which should be 'preserved in a semi-restored state', and which should be 'maintained as a ruin' must itself be a formal part of the cultural heritage policy framework—not an ad-hoc or subjective decision.
4. From Restoration to Industry: Economic Dimensions of Korea's Cultural Heritage
The turning point in South Korea's experience is transforming cultural heritage preservation from a 'budgetary expense' into a 'sustainable revenue stream' and a 'measurable economic sector'. In December 2025, the Korea Heritage Service for the first time officially announced the market size of the national heritage sector and presented a plan for its development.
The figures above indicate that South Korean policymakers place cultural heritage within the budgetary category of 'national strategic industries'—on par with AI and technology—rather than under peripheral cultural expenditures. This budgetary framing is a political prerequisite for securing parliamentary and private sector support for long-term restoration programs.
5. Roadmap 2025–2030 and the Culture-K 2030 Vision
5.1. The Future: Protecting History with Artificial Intelligence
In 2026, the South Korean government unveiled a five-year plan covering 2025–2030, utilizing cutting-edge technologies—Artificial Intelligence, digital twins, smart robots, drones, blockchain, and virtual reality—for cultural heritage preservation.
5.2. Beyond Heritage: The Larger Culture-K 2030 Blueprint
The five-year cultural heritage plan is part of a much larger initiative. In the summer of 2026, South Korea's Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism presented President Lee Jae-myung with a strategic document titled 'Revitalizing Regions and Expanding Globally with Korean Culture, Sports, and Tourism'. The main goal of this document is to attract 40 million foreign tourists annually, a significant jump from the estimated 23 million for the current year. This document has three main axes:
· Developing the Culture-K Industry as an Economic Engine: South Korea is strengthening its content industries—publishing, music, video games, and cinema—as a pivotal future economic sector, moving from solely government-led, competition-based financing towards more diverse support mechanisms (including social insurance for artists).
· Cultural Decentralization: The plan emphasizes making regions outside the Seoul metropolitan area more attractive through developing cultural and sports facilities and deploying local specialists.
· Direct Link with the Cultural Heritage Strategy: The Culture-K 2030 vision aligns with the five-year cultural heritage plan; both define culture as a 'strategic export' and not merely a 'conservation responsibility'.
Iranian media have highlighted this parallel: according to a Tehran Times report, the Korean model of social security for artists could be a model for supporting Iranian cultural activists, and Korea's cultural decentralization policy aligns with Iran's reality—cities like Tabriz, Mashhad, and Shiraz, with their distinct cultural identities, could be developed as 'regional cultural capitals' to stimulate local economic growth and distribute tourism income more equitably.
6.ApplicaIran's Cultural Heritage in the Mirror of the 2026 War: Why This Experience is Now Urgent
South Korea's experience is no longer just a theoretical or historical lesson for Iran. During the US-Israel war against Iran, which began on February 28, 2026, a significant number of the country's historical sites and monuments were damaged. According to a report by the head of the Iranian National Commission for UNESCO, at least 140 cultural and historical sites across the country were affected by this conflict, at least five of which are inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. According to UNESCO and international media reports, at least four to five of Iran's 29 UNESCO World Heritage sites have been affected by this war. On March 31, 2026, Iran formally submitted documentation of damage to over 131 sites to UNESCO, citing violations of the 1954 Hague Convention for the Protection of Cultural Property in the Event of Armed Conflict.
The financial situation for reconstruction finds itself at a point similar to South Korea's starting point in the 1950s: as of May 2026, the Iranian government had not introduced any specific, publicly announced budget line for reconstructing damaged cultural heritage, and officials have spoken of the difficulty of long-term planning 'as long as the shadow of war remains over Iran's skies.' Precisely this vacuum—the absence of a central institution with an explicit budget line and a clear framework for private sector participation—is where South Korea's seventy years of experience can offer a practical roadmap.
Applicable Lessons for Iran
Iran's cultural heritage has suffered significant damage both during the eight-year Imposed War with Iraq and in the recent war with the US and Israel, and remains exposed to natural (earthquake, flood) and human risks. South Korea's experience offers six distinct lessons for Iran, not as a one-to-one corresponding import model, but as an adaptable policy framework:
6.1. Policy Sequence: Document First, Then Restore
The first step in any national reconstruction program is not commencing construction operations, but creating a 'National Digital Archive' of the current state of at-risk sites. Without this archive, even in the event of an incident, accurate and authentic reconstruction will be impossible. The prioritization of this archive should be based on risk mapping (earthquake, decay, border and conflict zones). Given the recent damage inflicted on Golestan Palace, Naqsh-e Jahan Square, and Isfahan's Jameh Mosque, the top priority is the immediate 3D documentation of these sites and other monuments at risk of repeat attacks.
6.2. Separating Government and Private Sector Roles Instead of the 'Public or Private' Dichotomy
Korea's experience shows the right question isn't 'public or private?' but 'which role for which actor?': Ownership of national heritage and the formulation of conservation criteria must remain with a powerful central body (similar to the Korea Heritage Service), but the technical execution of restoration, tourism operation, and economic development of sites can be delegated to the private sector and local institutions through service, construction, and lease contracts. This separation prevents corruption and damage caused by short-term profit motives, while simultaneously bringing private sector efficiency and capital into the reconstruction cycle.
6.3. Independent Budget Line for Heritage Restoration
The lack of a formal budget line for reconstructing heritage damaged in Iran's recent war (Section 6) is precisely the weakness South Korea faced in the 1950s, but seventy years later transformed into an 'industry' with clear quantitative targets (Section 4). The Korean model—defining specific economic indicators (employment, tourism, foreign exchange earnings) for the heritage sector—could provide a framework for Iranian chambers of commerce and economic policy institutions to advocate for a transparent budget line, rather than deferring the issue to 'when conditions stabilize.'
6.4. Economic Regeneration of War-Damaged Urban Fabrics
War-damaged areas in Khuzestan, Ilam, and Kermanshah provinces, and even parts of Tehran, similar to Camp Greaves and Bukchon, possess the potential to become destinations for memory and cultural tourism; provided that a financial model is based on the participation of local owners and the private sector, not merely the allocation of government funds for physical reconstruction without a long-term economic utilization plan.
6.5. Formal Policy for Selective Preservation of War Sites as National Memory
Institutions responsible for cultural heritage and the Sacred Defense in Iran could, akin to the Workers' Party building in Cheorwon, compile an official and criteria-based list of war structures that, instead of being fully restored, are maintained as memorials and cultural sites—a decision that should be made within the framework of a written policy, not in a scattered, localized manner.
6.6. Pre-Restoration Diagnostic Technology (e.g., HBIM) to Reduce Costs and Execution Errors
Given the high cost of erroneous or hasty restorations, initial investment in modeling historical building information can reduce total reconstruction costs in the medium term and enable transparent, auditable decision-making for oversight and funding bodies (whether governmental or reconstruction charities).
7. Concluding Remarks: Rebuilding Hope is More Important than Rebuilding Walls
The story of South Korea's cultural heritage is not just the story of restoring a few palaces and temples; it is the story of a nation that, in the aftermath of one of the most devastating wars of the 20th century, decided not to forget its past and to turn it into an economic and identity asset for the future. Seventy years ago, many thought the ruins of the Korean War would never be compensated for; today, that same country has become one of the world's most successful examples in cultural heritage preservation and one of the few nations that places cultural heritage in the budgetary category of strategic industries, on par with artificial intelligence.
Today, Iran, with Golestan Palace, Isfahan's Jameh Mosque, and Naqsh-e Jahan Square listed among its war-damaged sites, stands at a point similar to where South Korea stood seventy years ago. The shared lesson for both, and for any country that has tasted war, crisis, or devastation, is that true reconstruction is not merely about rebuilding walls; it is a combination of scientific documentation, a clear separation of government and private sector roles, industrial and transparent budgeting, and a conscious choice between complete restoration and preserving historical wounds.

articles.title: Ukraine strikes Russian radar, drone training center and military supply hubs
articles.body:
Ukraine strikes Russian radar, drone training center and military supply hubs
According to Ukrinform, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this on Facebook.
On August 25 and overnight into August 26, Ukrainian Defense Forces units struck a number of Russian military facilities.
In Kacha, temporarily occupied Crimea, a Kasta radar station was hit.
A UAV training center was struck in Luhansk.
A Russian repair and recovery base in Pervomaiske, Crimea, was also hit.

The extent of the damage is being assessed.

According to President Volodymyr Zelensky, these included oil facilities, airfields, a missile unit and infrastructure routinely used to launch attacks against Ukraine.

articles.title: Saildrone USV completes live-fire weapons test
articles.body:
Lockheed Martin and Saildrone have fired two rounds from an uncrewed Surveyor vessel during RIMPAC 2026, using US Navy targeting data and a remotely operated combat system to engage a surrogate high-speed surface threat.
Lockheed Martin and Saildrone have completed a live-fire demonstration from an uncrewed surface vessel during RIMPAC 2026, launching two rounds from a Surveyor-class platform fitted with a Joint Air-to-Ground Missile dual launcher, according to the company.
The demonstration near Hawaii paired the Saildrone Surveyor with Lockheed Martin’s JAGM Dual Launcher and the US Navy’s Adjunct Remote Engagement System, or ARES, for fire control and command and control. Working in coordination with the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group, the uncrewed vessel acted on targeting information relating to a surrogate high-speed surface craft.
Lockheed Martin said the system progressed from concept to live demonstration in six months, with the work sponsored by the US Navy Fleet Experimentation Program during Exercise Rim of the Pacific. The announcement does not state the precise configuration of the rounds fired, beyond identifying the platform as integrated with the JAGM launcher, nor does it describe the engagement result in detail.
The companies also used the Surveyor to demonstrate a passive electronic warfare capability during the exercise. Operating alongside an MH-60S helicopter, the uncrewed vessel detected, classified and identified a surrogate threat radar system, according to Lockheed Martin. The activity therefore combined remote weapons employment with a separate sensing role rather than focusing solely on the launcher.
Paul Lemmo, vice president and general manager of Sensors, Effectors and Mission Systems at Lockheed Martin, said, as quoted in a news update: “Lockheed Martin and Saildrone are leading the way to leverage the strength of industry to deliver autonomous platforms with containerized capabilities for our national defense. We will continue to invest in new capabilities ahead of need to accelerate and de-risk deployment of urgently needed defense technologies.”
Saildrone founder and chief executive Richard Jenkins said, as quoted in the same news update: “This successful live fire demonstration was the result of pairing one of the most tried and trusted munitions with the most operationally deployed class of USV on the planet.”
He added: “Not only does this deliver mission-ready, kinetic USV capability today, but it also de-risks and accelerates our journey of fitting more sophisticated kinetic capabilities, like the Mk70 launcher, to our larger platform, the Saildrone Spectre.”
The Surveyor test is intended to form the first of several trials involving Saildrone vessels integrated with US Navy combat systems. Lockheed Martin and Saildrone are also looking towards the larger Spectre-class USV, which the companies say is being designed to accommodate heavier containerised payloads. Planned examples include the Lockheed Martin Mk 70 launcher and the Surveillance Towed Array Sensor System, or SURTASS.
The Mk 70 is a containerised derivative of the US Navy’s Mk 41 vertical launch architecture and would represent a substantial increase in weapon capacity and missile size compared with the JAGM installation demonstrated aboard Surveyor. The companies have not announced a completed Mk 70 live-fire integration on Spectre, and the August trial should not be read as demonstrating that future configuration.
JAGM itself uses a dual-mode seeker combining semi-active laser and millimetre-wave radar guidance. Lockheed Martin is promoting the weapon for a wider range of missions, including counter-UAS applications, as it examines ways of adapting existing missiles and launchers to uncrewed maritime platforms.
Further testing is planned to expand the types of payload carried by Saildrone vessels and examine how larger uncrewed platforms can be incorporated into Navy combat systems. The Surveyor firing establishes that a commercially derived USV can receive targeting information through the ARES architecture and conduct a remotely controlled live-fire engagement at sea, while the more heavily armed Spectre configuration remains a subsequent development objective.

articles.title: Finland Orders €14 Million Worth of FPV Drones for Conscription Training
articles.body:
The Finnish Defense Forces have ordered €14 million worth of FPV drones to train conscripts.
The multi-year agreement was signed with Finnish company Insta Group, which shared the news on its website.
The procurement is part of a long-term program to develop the Finnish military’s unmanned aerial vehicle and unmanned systems capabilities.
The delivery of the new FPV drones will allow training in their use to be expanded to all brigade-level units.
This will significantly expand Finland’s capabilities in drone warfare.
The contract includes personnel training, spare parts, and technical maintenance for the drones.
Insta Group currently produces 7- and 10-inch FPV drones. In addition to training, the drones can carry warheads and other payloads.
The Finnish Army began training conscripts to operate FPV drones at the Finnish Defense Forces’ Military Academy in autumn 2025. Since early 2026, the training has been expanded to other brigade-level units across the country.
Together with Ukrainian specialists, Insta Group developed and presented the Steel Eagle ER strike drone for the Ukrainian Defense Forces in early 2025. It is equipped with a specialized munition containing pre-formed fragments that detonates in the air above the target.
Last week, Ukrainian developer Airlogix and Finnish company Innokas signed a letter of intent to establish production facilities in Finland for manufacturing drones based on Ukrainian technologies.
On August 23, Finnish company Patria and Ukrainian company General Cherry signed a letter of intent to begin joint drone production in Finland for Ukraine and Europe.
Ukrainian company Tencore and Finnish company Insta will also establish a joint venture to manufacture TerMIT 2.0 unmanned ground vehicles.

Ukraine is also expected to receive one SAMP/T system and new air defense radars from France this fall.

articles.title: Der Spiegel: The weapons cache found outside Berlin was left there by a 24-year-old Ukrainian man arrested in Romania

Der Spiegel: The weapons cache found outside Berlin was left there by a 24-year-old Ukrainian man arrested in Romania
The weapons cache found in a forest outside Berlin, which German media reported on in August, was set up by a 24-year-old Ukrainian identified as Vadym S., according to the German magazine Der Spiegel. Citing intelligence services, the magazine said he was part of a group preparing acts of sabotage in European countries on orders from Russian intelligence.
Polish law enforcement agencies, which had tracked Vadym S.’s movements, determined that on October 1, 2025, he traveled by bus from Poland to Berlin, picked up two packages there, and placed them in the cache in the forest. When the cache was opened, the packages were found to contain two pistols and ammunition.
From Berlin, Vadym S. returned to Poland and soon afterward traveled to Romania. He was detained in Bucharest on October 16 after leaving two packages containing incendiary devices at a local branch of the Ukrainian delivery company Nova Poshta.
A second Ukrainian was detained along with Vadym S., according to Der Spiegel. In keeping with German media convention, the magazine did not identify either man further. The independent Russian investigative outlet Agentstvo found records showing that two Ukrainians were arrested in Romania on October 16, 2025: 24-year-old Vadym Shcherbakov and 21-year-old Bohdan Filipchuk.
The Romanian outlet Libertatea said in June that Russian intelligence services had overseen the attempted firebombing of the Nova Poshta branch and that Shcherbakov had received his assignments from his uncle. Libertatea also said both men were born in the Kherson region, now partly occupied by Russia, and moved to Poland in 2025.
German intelligence officials had also said earlier that the cache might have been intended for Russian agents carrying out “kinetic operations.” But they stressed that the investigation was still underway.
The cache was placed under surveillance, but for a year no one came to check on it. The Russian Embassy in Germany, in comments to the Russian business news outlet RBC, called reports linking the cache to Russian intelligence services “speculation.”

articles.title: Air Force Football to Sport B-21 Themed Uniforms vs. Navy
articles.body:
For its latest special uniform celebrating the heritage of airpower, the U.S. Air Force Academy football team is looking to the future: the B-21 Raider.
The Academy unveiled the new outfit Aug. 25, replete with the B-21’s lambda wing silhouette and other visual details from the new sixth-generation bomber. The Falcons will wear the uniform Oct. 10 when they welcome Navy to Colorado Springs, Colo.
In keeping with the secrecy around the B-21 and its stealth nature, the new uniforms are minimalist and the Academy provided a relatively short list of details explaining the visual references.
“The uniform draws from the bomber’s distinctive shape, stealth, and advanced technology, with Air Force aviation details woven throughout the design,” Northrop Grumman said in a statement.
The uniform is mostly black, with lettering and numbers rendered in a metallic silver. The helmet has an oversized B-21 silhouette rendered in grey against a camouflage background, plus another silhouette across the back. The silhouette also appears as a shoulder patch, on the thigh of the pants, and on the players’ gloves.
The helmet has “B-21” on the front bumper just above the face mask, and “Northrop Grumman,” the B-21 manufacturer, across the back bumper.
Each of the uniforms features one of three patches on the collarbone: Air Force Materiel Command, Air Force Global Strike Command, and the 412th Test Wing. Those emblems are all on the test B-21s currently being flown out of Edwards Air Force Base, Calif.
Instead of the players’ names on the back, the jerseys will feature either the phrase “Strategic Deterrence” or “Power Projection,” reflecting the B-21’s nuclear and long-range strike missions. “B-21 Raider” will run vertically down both pant legs.
One detail sure to please aviation enthusiasts: red “Remove Before Flight” towels.
This is the 11th edition of the Academy’s Air Power Legacy Series of uniforms, always worn for a game against a rival service academy. Previous versions have touched on every era of Air Force history, from World War II (the Tuskegee Airmen and Doolittle Raiders) to Vietnam (Operation Linebacker II) to the present day (the F-35 and the Space Force).
Air Power Legacy Series
- 2025: F-16
- 2024: Air Force Special Operations Command
- 2023: Doolittle Raiders
- 2022: Space Force
- 2021: B-52 Stratofortress and Operation Linebacker II
- 2020: Tuskegee Airmen
- 2019: C-17 Globemaster III
- 2018: AC-130 Spooky
- 2017: F-35 Lightning II
- 2016: Tiger Shark Teeth nose art
Air Force enters the 2026 season seeking its 22nd Commander-in-Chief’s Trophy, awarded to the top service academy. It starts play Sept. 5 against Duquesne, faces Navy on Oct. 10, and takes on Army on Nov. 7.
The B-21, meanwhile, is progressing through testing and is expected to arrive at its first operational base, Ellsworth Air Force Base, S.D., in 2027.

articles.title: Ukraine’s new commander-in-chief has been picking technical chiefs. Adviser who knows them says he is putting most competent people
articles.body:
Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, advisor to the president on the development of defense technologies, has highly praised the recent personnel changes in the new Ukrainian commander-in-chief's staff. He says that Mykhailo Drapatyi is appointing the most competent people available to the Armed Forces' technical directions, adding that "after many years of war, he knows most of the army's technical specialists."
The endorsement comes from Beskrestnov, an adviser to former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, considered the most effective in Ukraine's history. After the dismissal, he became a non-staff adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The technology war moves weekly
Beskrestnov rates the new appointees on temperament as much as expertise.
"The main thing is that these new heads are energetic, modern, and good communicators," he wrote.
In a war of technologies, everything changes literally every week, and "we have to react to all the enemy's challenges just as fast. Analyze, forecast, respond, and act a step ahead of the enemy," he added.
Drapatyi arrived in the same reshuffle
Zelenskyy named Drapatyi commander-in-chief on 21 July, replacing Oleksandr Syrskyi, and said in the same address that he had offered Fedorov a leadership position bringing together Ukraine's technological capabilities.
Fedorov's removal drew street protests across Ukraine. Drapatyi commands the General Staff rather than the ministry, so the appointments Beskrestnov praises sit outside the structure he left behind.
Change will be slow, he expects
"I believe big positive changes are ahead of us, but this will not happen fast, because a great deal has to change," Beskrestnov said.
He did not name any of the new appointees or their posts.
Earlier, Beskrestnov disclosed Russia's new tactics in its drones. According to him, while Ukraine's cheap interceptor drones have been knocking Russia's nightly attackers out of the sky, Russia has now bolted a jammer onto some of its own drones to blind them.

articles.title: Hungary labels Russia a ‘threat’
articles.body:
Hungary labels Russia a ‘threat’
Hungary considers Russia a “threat to Hungary, Europe and the global order,” according to a foreign policy directive published by the country’s new pro-EU government. The statement marks a dramatic shift from the pragmatic relations pursued by former Prime Minister Viktor Orban.
Signed by Prime Minister Peter Magyar on Tuesday, the document states that “Hungary condemns Russian military aggression and fully supports Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders, and recognizes Ukraine’s right to self-defense.”
“Russia’s behavior poses a threat to Hungary, Europe and the global order, and also puts the Hungarian minority living in Transcarpathia in serious danger, therefore we support all efforts aimed at initiating negotiations towards sustainable peace and long-term security guarantees,” it continued.
Hungary had not formally designated Russia a “threat” at any point since 1945.
This new position is almost identical to that of the EU, which also backs “sustainable peace and long-term security guarantees,” but only if they recognize Kiev’s maximalist demands – a return to Ukraine’s 1991 borders, freedom for Ukraine to pursue NATO and EU membership, and NATO-like security guarantees provided by European and American forces.
Since taking office in May, Magyar has worked to align Budapest’s foreign policy with Brussels’. He has ended Hungary’s opposition to EU accession talks with Ukraine, backed the bloc’s 21st package of anti-Russian sanctions, and lifted Budapest’s veto on a €90 billion loan package to Kiev.
Magyar’s predecessor, Viktor Orban, condemned Russia’s military operation in Ukraine. However, he also condemned the “war policies” of the West that provoked the conflict, and refused to help arm Kiev, arguing that Ukraine cannot hope to defeat Russia and should seek an imperfect peace deal instead. Orban argued that the EU’s self-imposed embargo on Russian energy would “kill off the European economy,” and lent support to its sanctions packages only after securing exemptions that would allow Hungary to continue purchasing Russian oil, gas, and nuclear fuel.
Hungary still imports energy from Russia under Magyar. Andrey Kolesnik, a member of Russia’s State Duma committee on defense, Andrei Kolesnik, suggested that Russia could cut these supplies in response.
“They’ve given [Magyar] the order to now treat Russia poorly,” he told Gazeta.ru. “They’re trying to gain some benefits. I think that oil supplies to Hungary, and energy supplies to Hungary from Russia, are now in question after such statements.”
Orban’s government viewed Kiev, not Moscow, as the most pressing threat to Ukraine’s Hungarian minority. Under Vladimir Zelensky’s rule, ethnic Hungarians in Transcarpathia have had their language rights restricted and been subjected to brutal forced conscription.
In June, Magyar struck what he called a “formal agreement” with Zelensky to protect the rights of Ukraine’s ethnic Hungarians. However, no documents concerning the agreement have been published to date, making it completely unclear what protections Zelensky has agreed to.

articles.title: Iraq renames Jurf Al-Sakhr city to Al-Nasr City
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iraq renames Jurf Al-Sakhr city to Al-Nasr City, what does that mean?
The local government of Babil province, south of the Iraqi capital Baghdad, announced on Monday, 24 August, that it had changed the name of Jurf Al-Sakhr, a town controlled by Iran-aligned militias, to "Al-Nasr City".
The decision came after weeks of growing political and rights demands in Iraq for the return of tens of thousands of residents displaced from the town and living in displacement camps for more than 12 years.
The local government, headed by the Asaib Ahl al-Haq group led by Qais al-Khazali, responded to the demands with legal action and rejected calls to restore the area to its previous state amid the influence of armed factions over local decision-making in the province.
A statement from the Babil Provincial Council said it had voted to change the name of Jurf Al-Sakhr to "Al-Nasr City", claiming that the vote "came in appreciation of and loyalty to the blood of the martyrs and their great sacrifices in defending the homeland and holy sites".
The decision to change the name comes as controversy has again emerged over the situation in Jurf Al-Sakhr district, about 60 kilometres south of Baghdad.
Iraqi forces and armed factions regained control of the area from Islamic State in October 2014, before armed militias, most notably Hezbollah Brigades, took control of it and prevented its residents from returning ever since.
Adnan al-Janabi, a sheikh of the Janabi tribe, had called for displaced people to return to their areas, describing what happened on 25 Oct. 2014 as an "occupation" rather than a "liberation".
He spoke of the demolition of thousands of homes and "killing, looting and enforced disappearance", as well as the continued prevention of residents from accessing their land and property.
The comments prompted responses from parties and factions in Babil.
The Babil Provincial Council said al-Janabi's comments contained "an insult to the council and inaccurate facts that could stir discord and incite public opinion".
As a result, a lawsuit was filed against him before the Hilla Investigative Court.
Babil Gov. Ali Turki al-Jamali also ruled out the return of displaced people in comments, claiming that the land had been subject to expired government agricultural contracts.
The New Arab spoke to several displaced residents of the town living in neighbourhoods near Jurf Al-Sakhr.
They argued that changing the name of the city is an attempt "to erase its history and existence" and "prevent its residents from returning", by those factions, militias and non-Iraqi groups that have offices and headquarters inside Jurf Al-Sakhr.
Changing the name will not make any difference in Iraqi memory, as the displaced and forcibly uprooted people from it will not abandon their right, the residents added.
One of displaced residents, who currently lives about seven kilometres from his home in Jurf Al-Sakhr, said that "changing the name of our area means nothing to us, because it will remain Jurf Al-Sakhr, and the occupied lands and orchards will remain our lands, and we will continue to demand them".
"Ali al-Zaidi's government is required to open the area and instruct its displaced residents to return to it, and the settlement projects being carried out by armed groups there will not succeed because the right is on our side," he told TNA.
He stressed, as a member of the Janabi tribe, that "changing the name is a provocative act against the displaced residents of the city who want to return to their homes and lands".
"The armed groups are behind it, having instructed and pressured parties in Babil to change the name as part of diluting the issue and ending the suffering of the residents," he added. "Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi faces a test over opening the area and removing the armed groups from it".
Earlier this month, Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered the formation of a government committee to study the security and logistical situation in Jurf Al-Sakhr and to establish mechanisms for deploying regular security forces around the area and at its entrances ahead of beginning the process of reclaiming it.
The process may coincide with the expiry of the deadline given to Iraqi factions to hand over their weapons at the end of September.
But a government source from Babil province said that "government attention towards Jurf Al-Sakhr is inconsistent, particularly as Al-Zaidi is not considering using force to open the area but rather dialogue and understanding, especially in pushing towards restricting the factions' weapons".
Speaking to TNA, the source said that "Al-Zaidi's success in restricting the factions' weapons, particularly the weapons of Hezbollah Brigades, could lead the government to demand the opening of all depopulated areas, including Jurf al-Sakhr".
"But in the near term, it does not appear that the Jurf Al-Sakhr file will end. Rather, it will be diluted. However, it could come under external strikes in the future because it contains large faction headquarters and weapons depots and possibly missile manufacturing facilities," the source added.
Jurf Al-Sakhr, which covers more than 50 square kilometres, was closed 12 years ago by Iran-aligned armed factions. The town is considered a stronghold of Iraq's Arab Janabi tribe, alongside other tribes. Its population, estimated at 180,000, remains displaced in camps and displacement sites.
Despite repeated promises by the governments of Haider al-Abadi, Adel Abdul Mahdi, Mustafa al-Kadhimi and Mohammed Shia al-Sudani to return them, none of those promises has been fulfilled.

articles.title: AI erodes our humanity while elites profit from war – Roger Waters
articles.body:
AI erodes our humanity while elites profit from war – Roger Waters
Pink Floyd co-founder Roger Waters has warned that artificial intelligence and social media are eroding people’s ability to think and feel, while powerful interests exploit technology, politics and war for profit.
Speaking to RT on Wednesday, the veteran musician welcomed Australia’s decision to bar fully AI-generated songs from its music charts, saying streaming platforms have already gutted musicians’ livelihoods with minuscule royalties while concentrating ownership and profits in the hands of Big Tech.
“So that piracy has almost destroyed everything. But if they are then allowed to use AI to produce fodder for their very tame audience who pays so much a month to get any music that they want from anywhere… Unfortunately, we know that a large number of that audience won’t be able to tell the difference between AI and Pink Floyd, or Neil Young, or Bob Dylan, or The Beatles or anything else.”
Waters broadened his criticism beyond the music industry, accusing social media platforms of manipulating users’ emotions and political attitudes through addictive algorithms, while warning that reliance on AI assistants was undermining independent thought.
“It reduces the size of your brain and your capacity to think and your capacity to feel,” Waters said. “In fact, it reduces everything human about anybody who goes in that direction.”
“So where do you draw the line? I’m not sure,” he added. “Wouldn’t it be great if we had a factual, you know, a sort of fact-based library, if that’s all there was? But it’s not. It’s controlling our political motivations and our feelings and our emotions, and also releasing dopamine.”
Waters then widened the argument to global politics, saying the same pursuit of power and profit had produced a world increasingly governed by force rather than international law.
“We live in a world that is controlled now by gangsterism,” he said. He cited Israel’s destruction of Palestinian communities in Gaza and the occupied territories, as one example, while accusing Washington of openly stealing Venezuela’s oil wealth through coercion.
Turning to Ukraine, Waters blamed the failure to implement the Minsk agreements and the collapse of the 2022 Istanbul peace talks, accusing Western governments of preventing a negotiated settlement.
Waters warned that the Ukraine conflict has since escalated “in a very, very dangerous way” and increasingly resembles the future of warfare, dominated by drones and missiles.
“Just who gets killed, nobody cares anymore,” Waters said, “because all they’re interested in is making money.”

articles.title: Lockheed fires rocket from Kodiak container launcher
articles.body:
Lockheed Martin has completed the first live-fire test of its Kodiak containerised launcher, demonstrating a system designed to carry up to 12 GMLRS rockets and deploy from air, land or sea platforms.
Lockheed Martin has completed the first integrated live-fire test of its new Kodiak containerised launcher, using a Reduced-Range Practice Rocket to demonstrate offensive fires from the system, according to the company.
The test, announced by Lockheed Martin, involved loading and launching an RRPR from the containerised unit. RRPR is the training round used by HIMARS and M270A2 Multiple Launch Rocket System crews for live-fire training associated with GMLRS and the wider MLRS Family of Munitions.
Kodiak is intended to provide a transportable launcher for offensive fires while retaining the external form of a containerised system. Lockheed Martin says each unit can accommodate up to 12 GMLRS rockets and can be deployed from air, land or sea platforms, potentially allowing missile launchers to be positioned without relying solely on conventional dedicated launch vehicles.
The company is presenting the system as part of a wider effort to develop both offensive and defensive containerised launch capabilities. The Kodiak test follows a series of demonstrations involving Lockheed Martin’s GRIZZLY system, with the company arguing that placing launch equipment inside standardised container-like structures can give military users greater flexibility in where weapons are transported, positioned and employed.
Randy Crites, vice president and general manager of Lockheed Martin Advanced Programs, said, as quoted in a news update: “Achieving a live-fire launch from our Kodiak containerized system in under six months showcases the speed and agility our customers demand.”
He added: “Completing all mission requirements on our first attempt reinforces our commitment to delivering a ready-to-fire solution that keeps pace with the evolving battlefield.”
The company describes Kodiak as a “plug-and-play” launcher, although the announcement does not detail the full set of interfaces, command-and-control arrangements or external sensor requirements needed for operational deployment. Nor does it identify a customer, procurement programme or fielding timetable. The live-fire event therefore demonstrates that the launcher can successfully employ a practice rocket, rather than confirming an operationally deployed capability.
Containerised launchers have attracted increasing interest because they can potentially complicate an adversary’s targeting problem and broaden the range of platforms able to carry missiles. Their effectiveness in service, however, depends on more than the launcher itself, including targeting data, communications, reload arrangements, platform integration and the ability to safely store and operate munitions from different locations.
Lockheed Martin says Kodiak can hold as many as 12 GMLRS rockets, giving it a larger magazine than a single standard HIMARS launcher, which carries one six-round launch pod. The company did not state in the announcement whether Kodiak is restricted to GMLRS-family weapons or whether other munitions could ultimately be integrated.
The Reduced-Range Practice Rocket used in the trial is intended for training rather than operational strike missions. Its use allowed Lockheed Martin to test the containerised launch sequence while drawing on an established rocket already associated with HIMARS and M270A2 training.

articles.title: U.S. Navy awards Castelion $90 million for hypersonic weapon
articles.body:
- The Navy awarded Castelion $89,997,162 to advance the Blackbeard hypersonic weapon to Early Operational Capability, funding 50 weapons.
- The order supports Blackbeard's transition to a Navy Program of Record and includes work to speed potential exports to allies.
The U.S. Navy awarded Castelion Corp. nearly $90 million to advance its Blackbeard hypersonic strike weapon toward Early Operational Capability, the company announced August 25.
The order funds engineering, technical, logistics and manufacturing work supporting 50 early operational capability weapons and the missile’s transition to a formal Navy Program of Record.
The contract also funds Defense Exportability Features, design modifications intended to speed up potential sales to U.S. allies and partners. Work will be performed in Torrance, California, and is expected to be completed by August 2028.
The order falls under a Small Business Innovation Research Phase III effort tied to the topic “Low Cost Highly Manufacturable Long Range Strike Weapon Production.” Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division in Lakehurst, New Jersey, is the contracting activity, and the action was not competitively bid. Funding includes $50 million in fiscal 2026 defense-wide research funds, roughly $15.8 million in fiscal 2026 Navy research funds, and about $24.2 million in fiscal 2025 Navy research funds, the last of which expires at the end of the current fiscal year.
Blackbeard is designed to fly faster than Mach 5 while maneuvering within the atmosphere, built for both air launch from aircraft such as the F/A-18 and a parallel ground-launched variant compatible with HIMARS. The Navy selected Blackbeard in February as the first weapon candidate under its Multi-mission Affordable Capacity Effector program, known as MACE, which aims to field large quantities of lower-cost, longer-range strike weapons rather than relying solely on smaller numbers of expensive, exquisite systems. The Navy confirmed that link in April, tying the missile to a rapid prototyping effort structured within the fiscal 2026 Navy research budget as part of its Precision Strike Weapons Development Program.
Castelion has received a rapid sequence of expanding Navy contracts for Blackbeard over the past year, each building on the last. Following initial integration awards from the Army and Navy in October 2025, the Navy awarded the company nearly $50 million in February 2026 to fund full-scale prototypes and flight testing at Point Mugu Sea Range. That was followed in April by a $105 million contract modification to integrate the missile onto the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and support live-fire testing in the Indo-Pacific Command area of responsibility, with work expected to run through January 2028. In June, the Navy ordered 50 early operational capability pre-production prototypes and 50 storage and shipping containers under a $23.4 million contract, the first production-style delivery order for a low-cost hypersonic weapon of its kind. Roughly three-quarters of that work went to Castelion’s Project Ranger manufacturing campus, a 1,000-acre hypersonic production site in Rio Rancho, New Mexico, with the remainder handled at the company’s Torrance headquarters.
Castelion was founded in 2022 by Bryon Hargis, Sean Pitt and Andrew Kreitz, all of whom previously worked at SpaceX. The company describes Blackbeard as the first U.S. hypersonic system engineered from inception for industrial-rate output and commercial-style unit costs, built around continuous flight test iteration rather than the long, singular test campaigns typical of legacy hypersonic programs. Castelion has said its longer-term ambition includes multi-year procurement of 500 weapons annually, a production rate intended to shift the program from a development effort into fielded capability at scale. The company operates manufacturing sites in New Mexico, Texas and California, along with offices in Washington, D.C.
Congress increased MACE program funding by more than $140 million in the fiscal 2026 defense appropriations act, more than doubling the program’s base funding, though lawmakers did not specify how the additional money should be spent. Early budget documents for fiscal 2027 show continued funding growth planned for the broader Precision Strike Weapons Development Program that houses MACE.

articles.title: US senator hopes 'sledgehammer' Russian sanctions will pass next month
articles.body:
US senator hopes 'sledgehammer' Russian sanctions will pass next month
KYIV, Aug 26 - A U.S. senator sponsoring a bill for wide-ranging sanctions on Russia said on Wednesday he was hopeful it would pass the House of Representatives next month, and be a "sledgehammer" to President Vladimir Putin's efforts to fund his war in Ukraine.
Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat from Connecticut who met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and senior officials during a visit to Kyiv, said the bill had strong Republican support in the House, after comfortably passing an initial Senate vote last month.
"Putin understands only force," Blumenthal told a news conference. "And the Russia sanctions bill is a sledgehammer that can have the kind of force Putin understands."
Though Democrats are broadly supportive of the sanctions, some have expressed concern that it would give Republican President Donald Trump leeway to impose additional tariffs, including on U.S. allies.
The bill would sanction top Russian officials and allow Trump to set tariffs of up to 100% on the top buyers of Russia's oil and gas, which include China and India, in an effort to stem revenue flows to Moscow.
Blumenthal said exemptions in the bill would spare European allies from the imposition of tariffs, allaying concerns raised by some Democratic legislators.
Blumenthal said he had asked Zelenskiy to lobby members of the House of Representatives to support its passage.
Zelenskiy spoke to several senators in Washington last month ahead of the vote on the bill, which took place on the day of the funeral of its co-author, the late Senator Lindsey Graham.
Blumenthal said Zelenskiy had "heartily and readily agreed" to his request. Ukraine's presidency did not immediately respond to a request for comment. REUTERS

They were launched from the areas of Kursk, Orel, and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia, as well as the temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in the temporarily occupied Crimea.

articles.title: “This is smart war”: Ukraine is reinforcing two Donetsk groupings, as Russia pushes at fortress cities. Azov commanders will lead both
articles.body:
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy has announced a reinforcement of Ukrainian positions in Donetsk Oblast. This comes amid a Russian offensive against the fortress cities that have defended the region since 2014. Zelenskyy announced the decision after a meeting with Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has ordered his army to seize the entire territory of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts by the end of this year, Zelenskyy said earlier. This comes amid plans in Russia to mobilize 300,000 Russians in the autumn, UNIAN reports.
After speaking with the military and hearing General Staff reports, Zelenskyy said he, Drapatyi, and Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara determined the next steps to strengthen Ukrainian positions. Two renewed groupings in Donetsk Oblast will be reinforced.
Two Azov commanders take the groupings
The groupings will be led by Hero of Ukraine Denys Prokopenko and Hero of Ukraine Andrii Biletskyi, Zelenskyy said. Prokopenko commands the 1st Azov Corps of the National Guard and led the defense of Mariupol in 2022. Biletskyi founded the Azov movement in 2014 and now commands the 3rd Army Corps.
Prepare for the worst
Robert “Madiar” Brovdi, commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, has commented on the decision.
“This is Smart War. Total synchronization with the Unmanned Systems Forces grouping, the shortest possible ‘sensor-to-shooter’ chain,” he said, adding that Russian forces should prepare for the worst possible consequences.
Analysts urged the move before it came
Earlier, two experts had also called for such a decision: Oleksandr Kovalenko of Information Resistance and Yurii Butusov, a drone company commander in the National Guard’s Khartia Corps.
"The eastern flank of the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration is taking on an increasingly threatening character," said Kovalenko, suggesting Andrii Biletskyi's 3rd Army Corps, often described as one of the most capable formations in Ukraine's forces, can be used to stop the catastrophe.
Yurii Butusov said that if Ukraine's forces retreat from Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, it could ultimately lead to the loss of the Donbas.
