articles.title: Hungary declares Russia a ‘threat’, breaking with Orbán policy
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin meets with the Minister of Industry and Trade of Russia (unseen) in Moscow. | Pool photo by Mikhail Metzel/AFP via Getty Images
´Hungary’s government has formally condemned Russia’s military aggression and announced its support for Ukraine’s territorial integrity, according to policy guidelines published late Tuesday — marking a sharp break with the Russia-friendly policies of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.
“Russia’s conduct poses a threat to Hungary, Europe and the global order,” the document says, adding that Moscow puts the Hungarian minority in Ukraine’s Transcarpathia region “in serious danger.”
The guidelines, signed by Prime Minister Péter Magyar, set Budapest’s foreign policy priorities for next month’s U.N. General Assembly in New York.
Advertisement
“Hungary condemns Russian military aggression and fully supports Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders,” the document reads. It also recognizes Kyiv’s right to self-defense and backs negotiations toward “sustainable peace and long-term security guarantees.”
Magyar has steadily shifted Budapest’s foreign policy since ousting Orbán this spring. He moved to repair ties with Brussels, secured a deal that unlocked €16.4 billion in frozen EU funds and lifted Hungary’s vetoes on reimbursing EU countries for weapons sent to Kyiv.
He also announced a review of Orbán’s landmark Paks II nuclear deal with Moscow earlier this month. Orbán signed the agreement with Russia’s Rosatom in 2014, backed by up to €10 billion in Russian financing.
However, Magyar's government still opposes fast-tracking Ukraine’s EU membership and has sought to slow down accession talks between Brussels and Kyiv.
Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said that if negotiations are completed, a referendum would take place to decide whether Hungary agrees to accept Ukraine into the bloc.

articles.title: Trump comments for the first time on CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s ‘semi-routine’ visit to Moscow
articles.body:
Trump comments for the first time on CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s ‘semi-routine’ visit to Moscow
U.S. President Donald Trump has commented for the first time on CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s August 25 trip to Moscow. “He’s there on … you know, very sort of semi-routine [business],” Trump said in an interview with radio host Glenn Beck. “I hate to disappoint people. We would like to see the war in Ukraine end.”
Trump denied reports that Ratcliffe had been sent to Russia because Putin planned to “test the resolve” of NATO.
Still, Trump said that something “may come out of” the CIA director’s visit to Russia. “We’re working very hard to get that war ended … Frankly, they both [Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky] want to see it ended at this point,” he said.
Journalists linked Ratcliffe’s trip to reports that Washington intended to deliver a “warning” to Putin. The Kremlin said Ratcliffe had come for “contacts between intelligence services” and had not met with Putin.

articles.title: Trump sends Saudi nuclear deal to Congress – media
articles.body:
Trump sends Saudi nuclear deal to Congress – media
US President Donald Trump has reportedly submitted a landmark nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia for congressional review and renewed demands that Riyadh normalize relations with Israel as part of the deal.
According to US media outlets, citing unnamed administration and congressional sources, the document was sent to Congress on Monday. The White House has yet to publicly confirm the move.
Lawmakers now have 90 session days to review the US-Saudi pact. If they attempt to block it, Trump is expected to use his veto powers to push it through. A two-thirds majority in both chambers would be required to overrule the president.
The agreement was originally signed last month and aims to allow American companies to play a major role in developing Saudi Arabia’s civilian nuclear energy program. The 30-year deal is expected to involve the construction of US-designed nuclear reactors in Saudi Arabia and could be worth tens of billions of dollars.
Riyadh says it wants nuclear power to meet the growing domestic energy demand, reduce the amount of oil consumed at home, and free up more crude for export.
However, the deal has raised concerns over nuclear proliferation. Unlike a similar US deal with the United Arab Emirates, the pact does not permanently bar the kingdom from reprocessing nuclear fuel or enrichment, which could potentially be used to make weapons.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman previously suggested that the kingdom could seek a nuclear weapon if Iran ever acquires one.
Trump has also tied the nuclear agreement to Saudi Arabia formally joining the Abraham Accords and establishing diplomatic relations with Israel. The condition was unexpectedly announced by Trump late last month after the agreement had already been negotiated and signed.
An administration official cited by Reuters on Wednesday said Trump’s position on the issue “has not changed.”
The Abraham Accords, brokered during Trump’s first term, established diplomatic relations between Israel and several Arab and Muslim-majority countries, including the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, and Morocco.
The US has also pushed for Saudi-Israeli normalization, but the efforts have stalled since the outbreak of the Gaza war in 2023. Saudi Arabia has repeatedly said it will not normalize relations with Israel without an irreversible path toward the creation of a Palestinian state.
